his generation, the fall of the berlin wall and the collapse of communism were defining events, and the driver behind his essay "the end of history." now it has looped back to the start: many of the people who actually lived through those countries want to reverse that outcome. his explanation is that the biggest driver of people valuing liberal democracy is negative experience — living under tyranny. the joy eastern europeans felt back then was concrete, because being surveilled and being punished for your speech were real. but the one or two generations that grew up after the berlin wall fell have no such experience, so they easily take peace and prosperity as things that exist by nature, and even see the eu as the world's largest tyranny. francis fukuyama the end of history is not my phrase fukuyama clarifies: "end of history" is hegel's wording, and here history is capitalized h, equivalent to what we today call modernization or development; end means a goal or endpoint, not "nothing more will happen." the question is: what kind of society will eventually emerge from this long evolution. marxists took over hegel's concept of history and said the endpoint is communism; by the late 1980s fukuyama judged that communism was out, so the endpoint landed on what communists called bourgeois democracy plus a market economy. he admits the book's choice of words was his own mistake — the real other half is "the last man," from nietzsche, who detested the idea that history has an endpoint, because the victory of english-style liberalism looked to him like a boring, flat world where everyone is fed, clothed and content, like cattle grazing in a field. francis fukuyama liberalism has been attacked as dissolving community since birth fukuyama tells the origin of liberalism very concretely: after the 17th-century european wars of religion, christians slaughtered each other over transubstantiation, infant baptism and the like, and the early liberals said we must accept a fact — we do not agree on the highest questions, so let us tolerate each other and live in peace. that is the essence of liberalism: it accepts pluralism and difference. but that is exactly what drives many people crazy: you must tolerate people you genuinely oppose, and you get no intense feeling that "everyone is moving in the same direction." fukuyama says this is where nationalism and religious politics come from. the danger is that people forget what such politics brings — the 20th century was strong national identities asserting themselves and dominating each other, and the result was two world wars; today putin runs on the same logic, unsatisfied with a peaceful, prosperous russia and demanding that ukraine and belarus be inside it too. francis fukuyama h: clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed inside tents four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the laprele site in wyoming; dna protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests. high density of archaeological detail, but it requires patience: the first half is clovis research history and dating debates, the second half — the concrete findings at laprele — is the part that's really worth it. readers interested in american prehistoric archaeology, ice age human adaptation strategies, or hunter-gatherer spatial organization; also suited to engineers following new archaeological techniques like zooms. the ancients the ancients ice age america: the clovis culture archaeology ice age american prehistory clovis culture zooms clovis lasted only a few hundred years radiocarbon dating pins clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago — a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the ice age. the narrowness of that span is itself startling: the ice age operates on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and clovis is only an instant within it. more critically, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire north american continent, from new mexico to wyoming, from washington state to virginia. this combination of "narrow in time, wide in space" is clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, spear points rapidly regionalized. madeline mackey clovis were not the first americans the "clovis first" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the americas, and clovis people were the earliest settlers. but discoveries at sites like monte verde (chile), paisley caves (oregon), cooper's ferry (idaho) and page-ladson (florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people lived in the americas thousands of years before clovis. mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in american archaeology, and pleistocene archaeologists argue about it heatedly. but she also stresses: clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves. madeline mackey one chopper changed the entire nature of the site the laprele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek; mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. in the first season, retired archaeologist rich adams, while helping everyone repair the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. the key point is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. this tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately finding more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. laprele was no longer just a kill site, but a camp where humans had lived. madeline mackey hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment laprele's most striking discovery is four "hearth-centered areas." in the block b area, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small area, indicating a hearth once stood there. even more remarkable is the spatial analysis: if you look down from above at a tent, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by a high-activity zone, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects accumulate — because the wall is a barrier to artifact movement. block b's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an indoor space. in the same area, a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter ochre (hematite) pigment scatter was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire. madeline mackey the bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone the team used zooms (zooarchaeology by mass spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. the results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. mackey notes these animals are all fur-bearing, and their bone thickness may have been just right for making needles. more importantly, these animals were likely caught with traps rather than hunted with spears. this means clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day — they were also taking more common small prey. madeline mackey were clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores north america has about 15 widely accepted clovis sites where they coexisted with megafauna, mostly proboscideans

cross-border e-commerce brand marketing consumer brands australians taking pills is a tradition the soil for australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that self-medicates, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, naturopathic industry organisations dating to the 1920s, and health food stores resembling food-as-medicine shops. stacked together, these four made australians used to "solving health problems without going to the hospital." black moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic; only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — for example, turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into standardised fish oil capsules. the contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation pen pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing of supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the fat-and-gelatin seal of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. in the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (cmo) to cdmo covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. the brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell. registration means nobody looks before it hits the market australia legislated in 1989, putting the tga in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an aust number. most supplements enter the austl category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the tga, only low-level health claims, and a company gets the number just by applying itself — the tga does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. by around 2010 australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% fell under this registration system. only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the austr tier, which requires the tga to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance. it looks strict, but in practice it's loose put the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together and you see that gmp only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced to a batch recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. the tga side only handles declarations and issuing licence numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. so the claim that "australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong in itself, but it is misleading: the method of control is the same, but the degree of control over the efficacy part differs enormously. the whole system does no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effect, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy. the marketing was copied from centrum, not invented ceo radek sali, who took over in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. he did industry research and found the best-selling peer was centrum, and the feedback from retailers was: centrum didn't give the channel much margin, but you couldn't fight the fact that it advertised relentlessly on tv all year, had great athlete endorsements, and consumers walked into the pharmacy and asked for it by name. sali wanted to replicate this at swisse. he first bought into australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain — running very short ad slots only during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even a limited budget could appear at important moments. but the female-dominated sales channel wasn't moved; one buyer didn't watch cricket herself and didn't know the athlete. he asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance variety show, and the h: solo founders aren't alone: the relationship is the product 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone. this episode has medium information density, but dave morin uses three cases — openclaw, pulsia and ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. the mechanics in the second half are worth more than the motivational talk in the first. founders considering going solo or already working alone, and investors who want to understand how the solo-founder support system actually works. solo founders 单人创始人 why you don't need a co-founder to start | dave morin, offline ventures solo founders founder relationships openclaw pulsia venture capital the share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years carta data shows that roughly 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. dave morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone for any waking hour, and ai has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. you used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to ai, explore your own ideas and get input on what to do tomorrow. the "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something youtube and chatgpt can teach. dave morin most startups die from relationships, not products dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. he compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. when your favorite app suddenly gets redesigned and the ui becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made it changed. so he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself. dave morin designing the team matters as much as designing the product when steve jobs died, dave was working on path, jony ive was helping him, and he was helping jony with some apple work. jony told him something he still remembers: designing the team matters as much as designing the product. from that dave derives his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but with customers, audiences and the community that cares about your product. you are not alone. dave morin he fell in love with openclaw within 12 hours in december 2025, dave was in montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called claudebot. he didn't look the first day; he installed it the second, and within less than 12 hours he had that childhood feeling — at age 7 his grandfather put a macintosh on his desk, and for the first time he felt he could create anything. the second time he felt that was seeing facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. this time it was openclaw, and he immediately went to find peter, moving from twitter dms to imessage, talking every day, saying "i don't know what this will become, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs." dave morin peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not a lucky break dave doesn't see openclaw's explosion as an accident. peter did ten years of hardcore pdf engineering and understands mac os details at the engineering level better than most people. so when claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already digested all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. dave's conclusion: this is an extremely well-trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical. dave morin ben built himself a company os on the road after ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to kyoto, hong kong, shanghai and thailand. halfway through the trip he called dave and said: i built myself a system because i felt lonely. he built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a cmo, an engineering vp, a therapist — and he called it company os. dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. three months later pulsia launched. ben later told him that if dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up. dave morin matt applied data science to campsites matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached amazon — at its peak, more than 80% of amazon's top 50 books were ones they published. during the pandemic he and dave talked by a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? national park a ‖ 單人創始人

h: the bottleneck for ai adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains ai's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. aiuc wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance. for founders, investors and operators who care about ai deployment, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. the historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more. founders building ai applications, agent products or enterprise ai, plus investors and risk leads watching compliance, insurance and third-party audit. latent space latent space underwriting superintelligence: backing agents you can sue — rune kvist, aiuc ai compliance ai insurance third-party audit agents confidence infrastructure four years on, waymo still can't get into an airport rune's core evidence is waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. so what constrains ai's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. worse, the problem gets worse as ai gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous, the more valuable, and the larger the risk surface. he traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built the confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. the shared blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the claims, and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it. rune kvist most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimising output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. most companies' architecture is actually right, and they do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. for example, dropping in a classifier that says "if this looks like medical advice, filter it out" — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through every way someone could elicit medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and tricks for getting around ai. aiuc-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, there must be a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers are notified when something goes wrong). rune kvist standards made by nonprofits are a problem rune says outright that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organisations, and he thinks that's a problem. nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — no customers, nobody asking "what do you want" — which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. he gives counterexamples of for-profit standards: moody's, fico credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; ul (underwriters laboratories) was born in an era of electric lights spreading, houses catching fire, and insurers footing the bill, and today ul has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. his conviction is that standards have to come before insurance: whether it's jpmorgan's ciso, cursor's ciso or an underwriter at lloyd's, the first demand is "don't have an incident" — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something. rune kvist the policy is a trust signal to the market rune explains that demand for ai insurance comes mainly from the gap between "the people building ai" and "the people buying ai". buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite says "there is risk here, but it's manageable", and its interests are aligned with the company adopting ai, so it's a good signal to the market. when waymo got its san francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked a huge policy — not because google couldn't afford the loss, but so that the government and a trusted third party could look at the data and say "we're willing to put some of this on our own balance shee

h: human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state. the first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an ai agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and ai agents. researchers in neurodevelopment or organoids, and engineers and founders building research ai tools, paper agents, and ai agent workflows. nature podcast nature podcast transplanted human brain-tissue takes root in mice without a cortex neuroscience organoids ai agents research tools ethics and regulation no surgery — genetics makes the room in 2022, sergio pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted," unable to get connections or room to grow. this time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic trick that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. the result is that cells are unable to divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and stall in place. the structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. these "pallium-less mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses. sergio pasca four million human neurons take over the vacancy the team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into pallium-less pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells, already differentiated and on their way to forming cortex. the human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, most of the removed tissue replaced by about 4 million human neurons. human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons. sergio pasca they are neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice the team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, pallium-less mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and the xenocortical mice carrying organoids. pallium-less mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither," sitting in a third behavioural state. later experiments backed this up: pallium-less animals had deficits on working memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and human cells very likely contributed some of it, but this is not perfect restoration — it only shows these cells can functionally integrate and produce behavioural consequences. sergio pasca a hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work the team used this system to model brain injury. hypoxia is severe in humans and can bring lifelong disease, while mice tolerate low oxygen far better. after the three kinds of mice were exposed to low-oxygen conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response, while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and pallium-less mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show defects in walking and gait coordination. sergio thinks this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these defects, and that this would be a strong system not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials. sergio pasca a very rare neuron type was grown aparna bhaduri at the university of california studies human brain development and cancer, and she thinks one highlight of the work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could help future therapy development. but she also points out there is a long way to go: the cortex's layer structure and different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach a more human-brain-like state; and the authors themselves note that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex. aparna bhaduri this is not a human brain in a mouse's head asked in other areas of medicine, and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists. this episode has medium information density, but the first half — a firsthand account of how evidence standards in medical ai moved from chaos to norms — is directly useful to anyone building medical ai products. engineers and founders working on medical ai products, clinical validation or regulatory submissions, and researchers interested in how evidence standards for medical ai get established. nejm ai grand rounds nejm ai grand rounds beyond the hype: dr. xiao liu on evaluating medical ai medical ai clinical validation reporting guidelines regulation large models fewer than 5% of ai papers in top journals hold up around 2019, new papers every week claimed ‘ai is as good as radiologists’ or ‘ai beats radiologists at pneumonia detection’, but these conclusions contradicted each other. xiao liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they applied the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years to these ai papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. the paper count was cut down sharply — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. and within that small set, the best models only matched radiologists. this isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature. xiao liu reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did consort, spirit, prisma, stard, tripod — these reporting guidelines are essentially a checklist specifying which items must be reported in a paper. they don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. their function is to put authors, journal editors and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. xiao liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report something, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that's hard to measure. xiao liu guidelines come out of delphi voting; items without consensus get cut consort ai and spirit ai weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion produced a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. that in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those that do are kept. xiao liu says doing this kind of consensus project properly takes at least six months; she tried a rushed version compressed to three months, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multi-round participation, you can't cut corners on time or reach. xiao liu whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fought over at the meeting andy beam recalls that one question in the delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. he and lauren oakden-rayner got up on the little stage and said ‘no, it shouldn't be done at all, for the following reasons’. that debate was later commissioned as a paper by lancet digital health editor rupa, and reach the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects. andy beam being a regulatory consultant without ever working in industry felt insincere at the time, xiao liu was doing academic ai research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. she began to feel she had never stood on the regulated side, and that consulting was a bit insincere. so she joined him in 1890, coley took on 17-year-old bessie dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was eventually diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on january 23, 1891, at just 18 years old, only about 10 weeks after coley first examined her. coley was 28, in his first year as a surgeon. amputation was the only treatment available at the time, and it had not worked, which sent him digging through roughly 90 records of cancer surgery patients at new york hospital from the previous 15 years, looking for something better. tracy v. wilson in one record, the tumor disappeared on its own in the case files, coley found a case from his colleague dr. william t. bull: a small round cell sarcoma of the neck that recurred four times, until at the fifth operation the tumor had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. after surgery the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, then had a second attack two weeks later. within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by the time the patient was discharged the tumor had disappeared completely. the hospital had no follow-up records, so coley went door to door in the german immigrant community and found him; in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the operation. tracy v. wilson he tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins on may 2, 1891, coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with an inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. the tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could swallow only small amounts of liquid. coley exposed the patient to bacteria cultured in the lab, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until in october an injection of a culture a colleague had brought from robert koch's laboratory in germany made the patient gravely ill — but two weeks later the neck tumor had disappeared and the tonsillar tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. by the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins, rather than using live bacteria directly. tracy v. wilson the effect was real, but only in some patients in his papers, coley wrote that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases the improvement was only temporary, and within weeks the tumor regrew and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very few cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly of the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. by 1909 he was recommending the treatment for all inoperable sarcomas (except melanotic ones), for osteosarcoma of the long bones where surgery would mean sacrificing a limb, for primary sarcoma after surgery once the wound had healed as prophylaxis against recurrence, and for all carcinomas after surgery to reduce recurrence. tracy v. wilson jama waited, then declared failure two months later on may 31, 1894, coley read his paper before the american surgical association. in october of that year, jama published an article comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until experts published complete results. but only two months later, on december 15, 1894, jama published "the failure of the erysipelas toxins," saying there was "no longer much question that the engineers wondering whether ai can replace administrative process; and readers who want to understand why the american welfare state is so inefficient. conversations with tyler conversations with tyler annie lowrey on the time tax, fraud, and rationing by paperwork public policy administrative burden ubi ai and government us welfare the irs is legally barred from filing your taxes for you lowrey's central example: in japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries mail you a prefilled return and you just correct the errors. the us could do exactly this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, so their tax situations are fairly simple — but the irs is not legally permitted to. this isn't a technology problem, it's an institutional choice. she defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labor, and unlike a monetary tax it's different in kind: you can earn more money, you can't earn more time. annie lowrey the worst program is tanf, not the irs lowrey singles out tanf (cash welfare) as the worst program in the whole government: nominally it exists to reduce child poverty, in practice it doesn't move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extraordinarily heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. she offers a rule: programs aimed at high-income americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. that yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of its recipients. annie lowrey pandemic fraud isn't something the time tax can prevent cowen raises a common objection: after deregulation in 2020 fraud exploded, so maybe the time tax is just the necessary cost of fraud prevention. lowrey rejects it outright: that fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, plus the fact that ui systems themselves run on ancient cobol infrastructure. her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade ui systems when unemployment is low, so every recession replays the same conversation. the conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not. annie lowrey large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side lowrey points out that medicare and medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. individual fraud has a low ceiling, because the amount you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. so her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organizations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who don't commit fraud. she adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, and thereby get voters to tolerate cuts. annie lowrey fifty hours a year each, and highly unequal lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the american time use survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. she concedes the number is understated — atus can't capture multitasking (cooking while on hold only gets recorded as one thing), and time taxes are scattered across categories without being aggregated. who pays the most? people entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. the rich can "skip" it with subordinates and accountants — with one exception: permits to renovate a house in san francisco, where no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review. annie lowrey ai can fill out forms, but not a urine test cowen asks whether ai agents could handle all of this within five years. lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is an open question; h: the strongest el niño hasn't peaked yet, but no one alive has seen one this big the 2026 el niño already exceeded the peaks of the two strongest events on record, 1982 and 2015, by autumn — and its peak usually doesn't arrive until winter. this is not a climate forecast for the future; it is weather that is happening now. meteorologist marshall shepherd lays out the mechanics of el niño, how it's observed, and what it actually does — and dissects how a un report got misread by the media as a "strategic retreat." dense with information, worth listening to. founders and investors watching turning into an end-of-the-world narrative of "we're done for." but the word "retreat" does not appear in the report at all — the un was in fact doubling down on emissions cuts. what was actually abandoned was only the claim that "we can still hold 1.5 degrees." the report's own text says: every fraction of a degree avoided, every year of overshoot shortened, saves lives, protects ecosystems and reduces economic losses. allie ward climate change isn't coming to knock — it's already at the table shepherd says the framing he heard growing up was "climate change is coming," and that framing is now outdated. in his words, it isn't just sitting at the dinner table — it's eating dessert, the appetizer and all the main courses. he explicitly rejects any narrative that talks about climate who caught no fish at christmas every two to seven years, the pacific trade winds weaken or even reverse, warm water in the western pacific flows back east, and the upwelling of cold water off south america shuts down. peruvian fishermen found they caught no fish around christmas — because the nutrients brought up by that cold-water upwelling had been cut off — and so the name el niño was born. the opposite, cold phase is la niña. shepherd stresses that this is a coupled ocean-atmosphere system, so it takes both meteorology and oceanography to understand. el niño disturbs the upper-level jet stream through "teleconnections," spreading its effects globally; california, georgia, the amazon and the sahel are all on that chain. marshall shepherd no hurricanes in the atlantic, but hawaii issued its first-ever tornado warning el niño suppresses atlantic hurricane activity while strengthening the pacific hurricane season. as of september 8, not a single hurricane had formed in the atlantic, only a few tropical storms, and it was likely to break the record for the latest first hurricane since 1941. on the other side, hawaii got the first tornado warning in the state's history because of hurricane lowell, with gusts on kauai reaching 84 miles per hour. shepherd says this is el niño's two sets of books: the east coast benefits, the pacific islands take the strain. california, meanwhile, faces strong storms, rain and mudslides. marshall shepherd eight degrees of warm water below the surface means there's no turning back the threshold for calling an el niño is meteorological organization data show that by february 2027 this el niño is almost certain to still be going strong. he stresses that he is not a scientist given to exaggeration, but this may be the s: 2026-09-16-sv101-推理芯片绕过cuda是必然-但sram的窗口未必一直开着
h: bypassing cuda for inference chips is inevitable, but sram's window may not stay open forever training is a compute game, inference is a bandwidth game. groq and cerebras both bet on sram, but one discounts for determinism and the other discounts for yield; openai chose the most expensive hbm4 because what it lacks is power, not money. two frontline chip entrepreneurs break down the trade-offs of the three paths taken by groq, cerebras and openai, with plenty of engineering detail and cost accounting, for anyone who wants to understand what inference chips are really betting on. engineers and founders working on ai chips, compilers or inference infrastructure, and investors trying to understand the inference cost equation and heterogeneous approaches. 硅谷101 硅谷101 e251｜推理芯片之战：聊聊groq、cerebras与openai三大路径与bill dally的设计哲学 inference chips sram groq cerebras heterogeneous computing training bets on compute, inference bets on bandwidth in the training era no one could make money from training itself, so costs couldn't be quantified and everyone just wanted to bet on the strongest cluster; in the inference era the math is clear—how much the user pays per million tokens, and how much it costs me to produce those million tokens. more fundamentally, it's about computational density: training has massive data to saturate compute, while the decode phase of inference is strictly autoregressive, producing one token at a time, and each token produced requires reading the entire model from storage into the compute unit. so the core contradiction of inference shifts from compute to memory bandwidth. ziyang sram is the consensus, but the two companies part ways groq and cerebras both saw the bandwidth demand before transformers appeared, and both converged on sram—because sram's absolute bandwidth and bandwidth per dollar are two to three orders of magnitude higher than hbm. the cost is capacity: dram stores one bit with one transistor plus one capacitor, while sram needs six transistors, so per-chip capacity may be two orders of magnitude lower than hbm. thus the system must be scaled up, with hundreds or thousands of chips holding all model weights, and the bottleneck immediately shifts from capacity to cluster communication scheduling. here the two diverge: groq moves all scheduling ahead to compile time, while cerebras simply stuffs a cabinet of chips into a single wafer. mark groq's static scheduling collides with moe's dynamism groq designs hardware around the compiler, pushing determinism to the extreme with no runtime scheduling overhead. but after moe appeared, each token activates 8 out of 128 experts, and which ones are chosen is decided at runtime, unpredictable at compile time. the static approach has only two options: either conservatively send all tokens and let some chips idle; or change the way the model is partitioned, but current models are hard to partition cleanly along dimensions other than experts. idling only affects cost-effectiveness, not the fact that it's still fast, so groq remains a good choice outside of gpus. mark the price cerebras pays for yield the maximum single-chip size is about 800 square millimeters, and a wafer can yield thirty or forty dies, so with 50% yield you still get 20 good ones. but cerebras's entire wafer is one product, and if defects exceed the 30% it can tolerate, the whole wafer is scrapped. this isn't mask cost (masks can be amortized), but rather that out of every 10 made, maybe 9 are unusable. so it may achieve 10x nvidia's bandwidth, but at 3x the cost of hbm, so bandwidth cost-effectiveness is discounted. groq discounts for determinism, cerebras discounts for yield cost, and the discounts ultimately hit token cost. mark in the inference era, cuda will definitely be bypassed tpu and trainium have no intention of being cuda-compatible, yet people still find tpu software hard to use; anthropic can buy in bulk because many of its engineers come from google and know jax. the key change is: in the training era people were willing to pay for good software, but in the inference era the balance tips toward performance and cost-effectiveness. as long as it's not many hard problems but one hard problem, writing all transformer operators on a new chip makes business sense; plus ai coding accelerates operator optimization, greatly lowering the software stack barrier. deepseek would rather write low-level ptx assembly for optimization—that's the logic. ziyang the faster the inference, the smarter the model after agents exploded, a large number of tokens are not for humans to read but for other agents to read; human reading speed tops out at 100 tokens per second. but the significance of inference speed is not faster interaction, but that in the same minute of waiting, the model can use 10x more tokens for more internal thinking, thus becoming smarter. jensen's slide has 'smarter ai' on the horizontal axis and tokens per watt on the vertical. conversely, some applications that give  ‖ 硅谷 硅谷 推理芯片之戰 聊聊 與 三大路徑與 的設計哲學

are budget airlines facing extinction? airlines business models trading down loyalty programs m&a what budget airlines sell is: you get what you pay for the episode opens with a string of passenger complaints that define the category: tray tables too small to hold anything, water costs extra, seats with almost no padding, and random bumping off oversold flights. but precisely because the price is low enough, people who want to travel cheap keep pouring into budget airlines. allison sider says the model peaked around ten to twelve years ago, when it looked like it would become the dominant business model, and the big airlines genuinely felt they had to find a way to respond. allison sider frontier put ulcc right in its ticker symbol frontier is headquartered in denver, with white fuselages and forest-green lettering, and a different animal on the tail of every plane. in the 2010s it went all in on the ultra-low-cost model, and its ticker symbol is literally ulcc (ultra-low-cost carrier) — in allison's words, that is ‘how much it wanted to embody that business model, to own that identity.’ its business model is highly similar to spirit's and shares the same roots. but frontier's operations have long been rough, and it sits at the bottom of the rankings year after year on on-time rates, cancellation rates and bumping passengers off flights. allison sider both mergers failed, and spirit simply vanished in 2022 frontier proposed acquiring spirit, hoping to merge into a national budget airline that could take on the big four of delta, united, american and southwest, with the two route networks complementary — spirit stronger in the east, frontier in the west. but jetblue bid higher, spirit turned to jetblue, and a federal judge then blocked that deal on antitrust grounds. in the end nobody got spirit; it went through multiple bankruptcies and shut down entirely this year. spirit's disappearance opened up market space for frontier, and the company says it has benefited — but it also ran into inflation, high jet fuel costs, and a fading of demand for cheap travel itself. allison sider the big airlines outflanked budget carriers with basic economy delta, american and united all rolled out basic economy — a cheaper, stripped-down fare class below the rest of the cabin. the big airlines' move was not to cut prices across the board, but to take a handful of seats, price them close to budget-carrier levels, and pair them with close-to-bare-bones service, such as no seat assignment in advance. for consumers, that means getting the budget-airline experience on a big airline's routes and reliability. allison says this is the bet most airlines are now making: people want a more premium experience and are willing to pay for it. delta made that bet first, fifteen years ago — wagering that ‘if you have the best product and the most reliable operation, people will come’ — and it worked extremely well. allison sider what actually killed budget airlines is the frequent-flyer credit card the other mechanism big airlines use to keep customers is loyalty programs: co-branded credit cards mean travelers don't shop on price at all. allison's example is that someone chasing miles or elite status might be willing to pay $100 more. that makes it extremely hard for frontier to compete — its route options aren't as broad and its loyalty program isn't as strong. frontier's response has been to start selling bundled products (ticket plus bag plus seat selection), and soon it will add first class and in-flight wi-fi. in other words, it is becoming more and more like an ordinary airline. allison sider frontier's ceo: fix operations first, everything else later frontier ceo jimmy dempsey told allison the company's future is bright, but it has to adapt to the environment — ‘customers are seeking a more premium product, and we're adapting to that.’ some of the actions he lists are very basic: improve operations, be more reliable. allison's read is that reliability is the center that holds up everything else: only with reliable operations, fewer delays and cancellations, and enough flights for backup does it make sense to invest in a loyalty program and a credit card.

h: the milky way's outer disk has slowed down, and both dark matter and mond may have predicted wrong gaia's rotation curve for the milky way's outskirts looks keplerian, while both dark matter halos and mond expect it to stay flat — each side now needs tuned parameters or external field effects to survive. fifteen minutes to get clear on the latest data in the dark matter versus mond fight, with specific numbers and three possible explanations, for anyone who wants a quick read on where the field stands. physicists following dark matter, mond or milky way dynamics, astronomy enthusiasts, and readers who want a fast take on the field's newest controversy. into the impossible with brian keating into the impossible with brian keating dark matter has a problem. so does mond. astrophysics dark matter mond milky way gaia a flat curve is where dark matter starts what vera rubin and others observed is that velocities in the outskirts of galaxies do not fall with radius; they stay roughly constant. by kepler's laws, at the outskirts nearly all the mass is enclosed, so velocities should decay like 1/√r; a constant velocity instead means the enclosed gravitational mass must keep rising with radius. the visible light is fading while the gravitational influence is not, and that mismatch is one of the cleanest reasons dark matter became central to modern astrophysics. the standard explanation is that a larger dark matter halo wraps around the visible disk, emitting almost nothing yet continuing to contribute enclosed mass, which keeps the rotation curve flat. brian keating we are measuring the pitch from inside the stands measuring the milky way has a built-in disadvantage: we are inside it. keating's analogy is inferring the shape of an entire football pitch from inside the stands. gaia delivers precise measurements of stellar positions and motions, but it has no button labeled "true milky way rotation curve." to get a curve you must first choose a model, correct for asymmetric drift, assume equilibrium and symmetry, and then invert for the circular speed. the instrument provides data; the pipeline tells us what those data points mean — revolutionary conclusions require looking at both chapters together. brian keating asymmetric drift bites hardest in the outskirts stars do not travel on perfect circular orbits; they oscillate radially and vertically, which makes the mean azimuthal velocity of a stellar population lower than the circular speed of the gravitational field. that difference is called asymmetric drift. recovering the circular speed requires modeling the random motions. the problem is that the correction matters most precisely in the sparse outer regions, which is exactly where the enclosed mass is largest and the controversy is greatest. the analysis infers a velocity decline of about 30 km/s between 19.5 and 26.5 kiloparsecs from the center, with a fitted outer slope of minus 0.47 plus or minus 0.15. brian keating turning a curve into mass is all geometry assumptions if the circular speed really falls as 1/√r, then the velocity squared falls as 1/r, and plugging that into the circular velocity equation leaves the enclosed spherical-equivalent mass roughly constant — walking outward yet inferring almost no additional gravitational mass, which is awkward for a large extended dark matter halo that should keep adding enclosed mass. but note the phrase "spherical equivalent": the milky way has a disk, gas, a bulge, a warp and a three-dimensional halo, and turning a single curve into mass requires a great deal of geometric insight. brian keating 260 billion solar masses is below most independent estimates the analysis gives a mean total mass estimate of about 2.6×10^11 solar masses, that is 260 billion solar masses, including stars, gas and dust, below many independent estimates that approach one trillion solar masses. that number comes from fitting the measured rotation curve and extrapolating the mass model beyond the region where stars directly constrain it. gaia's rotation curve only constrains roughly 9 to 27 kiloparsecs, while the milky way's halo may extend to about 200 kiloparsecs, so most of the mass comes from the fitted model rather than direct tracers. observation and extrapolation are not synonyms. brian keating there is no radius in mond's formula mond holds that below a characteristic acceleration, the effective dynamics depart from newtonian relations, and in the mond regime the acceleration is approximately the newtonian acceleration times the square root of the mond scale a0. in the low-acceleration limit, the fourth power of the velocity equals newton's constant times the baryonic mass times a0, and there is no radius in the equation — which is exactly why mond naturally yields asymptotically flat rotation curves, and also its fragility. if the milky way's outer curve really is keplerian, mond likewise expects something flatter and does not find it. h: renaissance doctors came in four tiers, and the best healer was called a quack bone-setters worked the market circuit every week, far more practiced than a licensed surgeon who did a few cases a year — and the physicians called them quacks. title and skill were never the same thing. a medical history interview, medium information density. the most valuable parts are the stratification of the medical marketplace, the origins of credential monopoly, and the era when bloodletting, purging and vomiting were enshrined as the three great therapies. listeners interested in medical history, the origins of professional credentials, and the stratification of the medical marketplace; anyone building in healthcare or working on policy should listen to the credential-monopoly section. this podcast will kill you this podcast will kill you special episode: dr. alanna skuse & the surgeon, the midwife, the quack medical history renaissance medical credentials professional stratification public health eighty to ninety percent of medicine was provided free by women erin asks who was practising medicine in this period, and alanna skuse's answer is ‘almost everyone’ — but the real base of supply was women: household healers carried roughly 80%, perhaps 90%, of medical care, and mostly charged very little or nothing. the reason history overlooked them is concrete: they left too little written material behind. knowledge passed down the maternal line — mother to daughter, aunt to niece, sometimes mistress to servant — carried in handwritten recipe books. they also wrote to each other exchanging ‘i found a good remedy’ and ‘i tried this and it didn't work’. this formed a medical network with no licences, no college, and yet coverage of the vast majority of the population. alanna skews first you check your purse: ten shillings a visit the path to care was essentially a price ladder. at the very top was the physician, about 10 shillings a visit, extremely expensive, so only the wealthy called a doctor directly. those without money worked upward from the bottom: first a local woman, a midwife with extra medical skill, or a nearby gentlewoman with leisure and literacy; failing that, an apothecary, whose medicines started at a penny, like today's pharmacist, except nearly every one sold his own secret remedies and sometimes diagnosed and treated patients himself; failing that, or if a leg was obviously broken, a surgeon, about 3 shillings a visit, responsible for everything on the body's surface — lumps, wounds, fractures. skuse states plainly that how sick you let yourself get before seeking care depended on what it cost: ‘the doctor or dinner’. alanna skews the guild monopoly failed, but the idea of credentials stayed skuse characterises the motive behind the college of physicians bluntly as commercial: physicians resented surgeons and barber-surgeons encroaching on their turf and wanted to found a college and then monopolise all medical practice. the college was founded; the monopoly was not obtained — it could not even control london, let alone the country. but the long-term consequence matters more than the short-term outcome: this was the first time the idea that ‘practitioners ought to be credentialed’ took systematic form. skuse draws the line to today at the end: these bodies, initially weak regulators, evolved into organisations like the british medical association and the ama, and our default assumption that doctors share uniform standards and a single opinion starts here. alanna skews colleagues calling each other quacks was the norm, not the exception asked how fierce competition was among doctors, skuse says they were ‘horrifically rude to each other’, and finding two who did not quarrel was rarer — because there was only one pie and everyone wanted the biggest slice. so surgeons insulted apothecaries, physicians insulted surgeons, and everyone called everyone else a quack. she gives an example: someone claimed a certain doctor had gone off to exorcise a woman, when in fact she merely had wind. quack comes from the dutch quacksalver, meaning one who sells salves by boasting of his medical credentials; another word, mountebank, comes from italian, meaning one who climbs onto a stage to hawk cures. the key point is that the word's boundary was filthy: a bone-setter would be called a quack by a physician, because he had no credentials and no fixed shop. alanna skews bone-setters were more practised than licensed surgeons this is the sharpest passage in the whole piece. skuse asks: if you had a complex fracture, would you go to a licensed surgeon who did a few cases a year, or to a bone-setter who travelled a different market every week and did nothing but set bones? bone-setters usually also pulled teeth — teeth rotted badly in that era and there was no option but extraction — so they tended to be physically strong, and brought an equally strong assistant to hold the patient down during the procedure. physicians classed these

you? i am well, thank god.’ the letter travelled by way of the red sea, aden, bombay, suez, alexandria, marseille and london, halfway around the world, and ended up filed by the foreign office in the india office records. no one replied. the emperor waited two years, his expectation turning to suspicion, and concluded that britain was colluding with his muslim enemies. in 1864 he seized the british consul cameron and a group of missionaries, and the hostage crisis began. he claimed descent from solomon, and meant it abyssinia had a legend: a descendant of solomon and david would rise, unify the divided kingdom, defeat the egyptians, and march all the way to jerusalem, and his name would be tewodros. in 1855 kassa, a man of obscure origins who had been a bandit chief, defeated his last rival and proclaimed himself the new emperor, taking the name tewodros ii. he later claimed to be of solomon's line, though he said nothing of it when plowden first met him. this messianic identity was both the source of his legitimacy and the root of his later paranoia. after his wife died he began to lose control in 1858 tewodros's wife tewabech died, and he was grief-stricken. his next wife, the 12-year-old tiruwork, was cold to him and said, ‘i am speaking with a king greater than you — get out.’ he began drinking heavily, sleeping with women in the camp at random, and admitted to the missionaries that he was living ‘a very unchristian and indecent life.’ in 1860 his friend plowden was ambushed by rebels and died nine days after taking a spear wound. britain sent a new representative only two years later, and in the interval the emperor's paranoia deteriorated sharply. the letter cameron carried back became the fuse at the end of 1862, when cameron left the emperor's camp, he took with him a letter in which tewodros asked victoria to arrange safe passage for his envoy, and said, ‘see how islam oppresses the christians.’ cameron returned saying he had received no reply from london, and the emperor began to suspect he had gone off to sudan to collude with the muslims. in october 1863 the missionary stern angered the emperor by publishing his book wanderings among the falashas, and was arrested, whipped and put in chains. in january 1864 cameron and the other missionaries were also seized, and all the hostages realised the nightmare had only just begun. what britain really feared was france the foreign office did not particularly care whether the missionaries lived or died; what worried them was france. suez canal fever was at its height, and if they alienated tewodros he might turn to paris, and france could then control the route from the red sea to india. so they sent hormuzd rassam — mosul-born assyrian, archaeologist, discoverer of ashurbanipal's palace and the epic of gilgamesh, oxford-educated, a convert to protestantism, and fervently pro-british. he set out for abyssinia with a letter from queen victoria and two assistants, dr blanc and lieutenant prideaux. rassam nearly succeeded, then was seized himself in january 1866 rassam, in his blue diplomatic uniform, met tewodros, and after reading victoria's letter the emperor was so excited he could not sleep; the next day he dictated a reply calling the queen ‘the defender of religion chosen by god.’ he agreed to release all the hostages, but demanded that rassam first accompany him on a campaign to put down rebels. along the way the emperor kept sending gifts: muskets, manuscripts, salmon, antelope, two lion cubs, two monkeys and a baboon. in march 1866 the hostages were finally brought to the lake, but on 13 april, when rassam went to say goodbye, he found that he too had been arrested. he held everyone just to get gunmakers why did tewodros seize rassam? there are three possibilities: he had been acting all along; he was overcome at the last moment by his hatred of the missionaries; or he genuinely liked rassam and could not bear to let him go. philip marsden thinks the third most likely — the emperor

it has its own language, its own alphabet, and its religion is georgian orthodoxy, which is not the same thing as russian orthodoxy. the analogy the episode gives is this: a man of georgian orthodox background climbing to the top of power in moscow is equivalent to a man of irish catholic background from some remote place like limerick becoming master of london in the mid-twentieth century. for georgians at the time, being governed by moscow meant being colonized. anita arnon / william de rumpel his father refused to change trades, then started hitting people his father bessarion (nicknamed besso) was a cobbler with his own workshop in gori, and by most accounts a good craftsman. but he refused to keep up with the times: he went on making georgian-style soft leather high boots while the market had already turned to european shoes. he did not adapt; he became bitter, drank heavily, and the violence fell mainly on his wife ekaterina (kiki) and little joseph, who was nicknamed "crazy besso." stalin later told his daughter svetlana one scene: his father was drunk and beating his mother, he grabbed a knife and threw it at his father, missed, his father charged at him, and he ran to a neighbor's house and hid there for several days until his father's rage passed. anita arnon / william de rumpel smallpox, a carriage, and a left arm that was too short around age six he caught smallpox, severe enough that his mother thought he would die — two older brothers had already died in infancy, and the family was too poor to afford a doctor, so they could only call a local folk healer. he survived, but his face was permanently scarred, and every official photograph was retouched. later a runaway carriage hit him and broke his arm; the left arm never healed properly and was noticeably shorter and stiffer for the rest of his life. the episode's formulation is: smallpox did not take him, his father's violence did not take him, and the carriage did not take him either. his mother was extremely devoted to him and had ambitious plans for him. anita arnon / william de rumpel he wrote poetry, and he was good at it in his late teens two things happened at once: he began writing quite good poetry, and he entered the seminary. the episode reads one poem aloud: "the pink buds have already blossomed, toward the pale violet violets; brushed by the breeze, the lily of the valley bends down over the grass. flowers, my georgia. may peace come to my native land, and may you, friends, make our homeland famous through study." anita says that in the original georgian it is quite beautiful. it shows two things: he was a proud georgian, not a russian; startups yc lead qualification cold start send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation the most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. the real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. the problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. so before automating, do at least a hundred outbound attempts by hand — genuinely by hand: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her linkedin and her company page. that homework is where high-converting outbound ideas come from. picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy founders often spend hours tweaking email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or the most carefully polished copy won't land. one winter batch company selling infrastructure products should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual how well the email was written. work backward from closed customers to the target title how do you find the right title? look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal to close, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. you can also look at who has replied to your outbound. if you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer could get fired in a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target. list-building tools will hand you the wrong companies another common mistake is searching in sales navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like a match but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a pile of it implementation consultancies. so use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether it's really your customer. after doing enough outbound, you start spotting the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. job postings are a great thing to watch, since they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, companies under 100 people probably haven't introduced job levels yet, and companies over 500 have probably already set compensation bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own. shake your first customers out of your personal network when closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. really shake the tree — make sure you've covered everyone you know: first your personal network, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of. executives don't care about your product features the single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. figure out the three things that keep your buyer up at night: what could get him fired, what could get him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. when buyers read the email and think "this is exactly my problem," they're likely willing to take the call, even if they 3d scenes, and meshes all had to pass through a gaussian representation before being rendered back to image or video. atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2d/3d fork happens earlier. generating 2d or video output is no longer bottlenecked on a gaussian scene — the model emits 2d pixels directly; only in applications where you genuinely need 3d does it get lifted to 3d. justin johnson gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory justin doesn't think gaussian has been outgrown — it's a tool, and you use it in the right place. vfx's final product is a 2d image or video, and may not need explicit 3d at all. but in real-time applications and on embedded devices, explicit 3d representations like gaussian and mesh still h: making a furin site isn't hard at all — admitting it isn't rare is deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand of a coronavirus population carry insertions, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up. the first half is the quantitative methodology of viral recombination and insertion; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. listeners who want the argument can jump straight to 52 minutes. readers interested in viral evolution, the lab-origin debate, and deep-sequencing methodology; anyone who wants to see a controversy taken apart with quantitative data rather than rhetoric. this week in virology this week in virology twiv 1357: furin, naturally with paul bieinasz virology deep sequencing lab origin furin site coronavirus they changed the gfp sequence and the recombination rate went up the team first built an oc43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carries a frameshifted gfp, so infection with either alone yields only fragments, but co-infection lets recombination stitch green fluorescent protein back together. they expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the gfps would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that once double-stranded rna forms, the strand-transfer events of recombination become more likely because the duplex "breathes." this counterintuitive result later became the reagent starting point for the whole paper. paul bieniasz knock gfp out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. their approach was to put the gfp gene into the viral genome and deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from gfp, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls gfp back into frame. this lets them both count event frequencies and pick out green viruses to sequence and infer the mechanism. that is where figure 1 of the paper comes from. paul bieniasz knocking out nsp15 made insertions go down the original hypothesis came from prior work suggesting that nsp15, a nuclease, affects deletion rates — when you think nuclease, you naturally think deletions, not insertions. but the experiment went the opposite way: viruses with nsp15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pulled gfp back into frame. paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time — it was this accidental result that opened up the entire line of research. paul bieniasz every base sequenced a million times before you talk about frequency they moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrating about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, loading a portion onto a sequencing chip, and producing hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome is read at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when the tube holds only a thousand virions is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample. paul bieniasz eleven nucleotides is the threshold for judging origin short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. they calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch matches the viral genome perfectly, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. the result: over 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in oc43 wild-type virus had 87 times more insertions than the nsp15 mutant, most of them derived from the positive strand. paul bieniasz insertions aren't rare events, they're a few per thousand vincent says that for years he was told insertions are rare, but the data suggest this has been happening all along. paul responds that "rare" is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it's common. the insertion frequency they report is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion out of every thousand virions. that frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. the reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even letha
