h: rome won with a crow: the key to the first punic war rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling carthage's advantage in seamanship; but carthage brought in a spartan to rebuild its army and captured a roman consul in return. this episode tells the first punic war as a war story with mechanisms: the crow bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants — all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density. listeners interested in the roman republic, carthage or ancient naval warfare; anyone who wants to understand specific military mechanisms like the corvus, and how underwater archaeology reconstructs a sea battle. the ancients the ancients the first punic war ancient history rome carthage naval warfare archaeology this was not a war between two equal powers the host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western mediterranean,’ and eve macdonald corrects him on the spot: at the war's outbreak, carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries of alliance networks in western sicily, but it had no strong standing army — it relied on allies and mercenaries. what actually made carthage into a power capable of fighting rome as an equal was this war itself. so the story roman sources tell over and over, of ‘roman adaptability,’ is only half the story; the other half is carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years. dr. eve macdonald mercenaries at messana dragged both powers into war the trigger was not the ambition of rome or carthage but a group of campanian mercenaries called the mamertines. they had seized messana, and after being defeated by hiero ii, king of syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked carthage for help, the other asked rome. carthage acted first from its base in the lipari islands, and rome followed — and not with a small intervention, but a full invasion with two consular armies. eve points out that the roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the romans showed up at messana at the scale of an invading force. polybius treats the romans' first crossing of the sea into sicily as the starting point of roman imperial expansion. dr. eve macdonald the corvus turned sea battles into land battles carthage was the naval power: better oarsmen, ships built fast and well — the romans even built their warships to carthaginian standards. but the romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow,’ a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. once hooked, the carthaginian ship could not move, and roman marines simply crossed over and fought a land battle. at the battle of mylae, the carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and took heavy losses. eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treat it as decisive. at the battle of cape ecnomus, the corvus is again credited as the chief factor, and rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of africa. dr. eve macdonald carthage hired a spartan to rebuild its army after the roman landing in africa, rome advanced steadily and carthage looked finished. carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern mediterranean and to bring in a spartan commander, xanthippus. he reorganised the carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. eve notes in particular that the carthaginians had not used war elephants before; it was only after seeing the indian elephants pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller african elephant of their own they could use. xanthippus's reforms worked: the roman army was destroyed and the consul regulus was captured. this was rome's first devastating defeat of the war, and it became a key event in later roman memory defining the relationship between rome and carthage. dr. eve macdonald the captured consul went back to rome to argue against peace carthage sent the captured consul regulus back to rome to negotiate peace. in the senate, regulus said not to surrender, that carthage was within reach. by agreement, if peace was not made, he had to return to carthage and remain a prisoner. he went back, and died in captivity. eve says the various horrifying versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in carthage, peace was refused, and rome fought on. this passage is a textbook moment of roman self-congratulatory rhetoric. dr. eve macdonald the sacred chickens would not along with the rest. stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class symhc classics: flexner report medical education racial inequality industry standards american history professional associations the report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer abraham flexner was not part of the medical world. in 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote the american college, a criticism, attacking american higher education, which is why henry smith pritchett of the carnegie foundation came to him and asked him to look at us and canadian medical schools with the same critical eye. he spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording each one's admission requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations, and in 1910 delivered medical education in the united states and canada. it was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing. tracy v. wilson medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge in the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic techniques and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no uniform standards. at many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. the result was that the care the doctors they produced gave patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. admission standards were equally chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses. tracy v. wilson he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools flexner set standards first and then scored each school against them: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for practical training; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than physicians who practised on the side. he published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time teachers. in the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. within a decade the number of american medical schools was down to half, the surviving schools reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were substantially modernised. in canada only one school made the closure list, and it ultimately did anyone who wants to see how a single manuscript gets reconstructed into a specific performance setting. the british history podcast british history podcast chansons de geste and 12th century performance sample medieval manuscripts epic dialect studies british history the most complete version is an english manuscript the song of roland is a french epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre chanson de geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century french cultural hegemony to regions including britain. but its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from france itself — it is an english manuscript, catalogued as oxford digby 23. this manuscript was originally bound together with a completely unrelated book by someone later, which is why it is called digby 23 b, and a is that "other book." nobody knows who bound them together; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books. every stanza is a camera position the poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood shifts, you change laisse. the whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut into four plus six in performance: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six syllables fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. recited over and over this becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs to four thousand lines — hours of recitation. at peak emotion, the same action is performed three times this kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially intense or the emotion especially strong, it uses consecutive laisses to tell the same action from three angles, a kind of poetic slow motion. for example, roland's refusal to blow the oliphant is told three times, with almost no gap between them. this is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — for instance, "roland dies, his soul ascends to heaven" is followed directly by "the emperor arrives at roncevaux." the performer's name is left at the end of the manuscript digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; turoldus will not tell more." this line appears before charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, i cannot go on. the name turoldus does not appear in the poem, and he is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this performance. its pocket-book size gives away that it was for work the manuscript is only about six and a half inches by four and a half inches, a pocket book you could carry on your person, not a wealthy man's finely bound volume. it is itself heavily worn and not refined, and it contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. together these features point to a professional performer on the move: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator in a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical performance. such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler. the dialect pins this performer to england the manuscript is not in the french of central france, nor continental french, but in anglo-norman, which suggests this performer was probably anglo-norman, performing in britain or at least in normandy. the dialect features are very specific: continental french o and ou are replaced by u, so roland becomes rulant, l'or becomes l'ur; anglo-norman french was also losing final soft e. these changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven. accent drift alone can date a manuscript scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. the method is similar to scholars reconstructing shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. poetry is especially suited to this kind of reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. for many jongleurs, french was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent, and they spelled by sound. a french

oxide: how faux can you go? emulation hardware internal tools llm open source the test environment is always twenty-seventh in line steve karam says anyone who's done software development or it knows the test environment usually isn't second fiddle — it's twenty-seventh fiddle, ahead only of education and enablement environments and documentation. and when your product is an entire rack, the problem gets especially hard: the rack itself, the fabric, the sleds, the switch zone, the sp, the root of trust — every layer needs one. so oxide has multiple fidelity tiers: dog food racks, the racklet mini rack, single-instance omicron (simulated or physical running on helios) — but it was missing a middle tier that's easier than a racklet yet higher fidelity than a single chassis. steve karam four by two compressed everything into boot time voxel's predecessor was called four by two, and it used a pile of shell scripts to define what the rack should look like, bringing up a virtual rack at boot with cargo bay, shared disks, networking and emulated networking. it did work — ipv6 and unnumbered bgp were first tested on four by two. but steve points out the fatal flaw: doing everything at boot time is a recipe for disaster — boot took forty minutes, it was hard to self-heal, and "you know it's going to crash in the last two minutes of that fortieth minute." so ryan goodfellow proposed a rewrite and came up with the name voxel: virtual oxide emulation labs. steve karam voxel splits build and deploy into two steps the biggest difference between voxel and four by two is the separation of build and deploy: give it an omicron commit, it clones, compiles, produces a perfectly formed sled image and snapshots it, then reuses that snapshot to play every sled and gimlet. the other big change is a full rewrite in rust, shedding shell scripts as much as possible. because one snapshot has to play six roles, something has to tell it what to be — voxel has a built-in agent written in rust, delivered at each sled's boot, telling it "you're the switch," "you're sled 1," "you're sled 2." steve karam llms are great at enumerating registers, bad at judging threads steve says llms are very strong at enumerating registers and finding the bits and pieces that make up a complete system, because nobody can hold an entire rack in their head; with rfds and design docs as context, the results get much clearer. but elsewhere it confidently reaches wrong conclusions: he once had the root of trust and the sp share a single thread for communication, and the llm said that was absolutely not a problem — after splitting them, performance improved 500x, and the rack could finally bring both up at once. steve karam don't touch the main software — that's voxel's bottom line steve says voxel has a creed it tries hard to hold: don't modify the main software. when he worked on multi rack, he stuffed all kinds of hacks into voxel to make voxel and omicron pretend multi-rack was already supported — for instance, creating a port that doesn't exist in omicron at all but magically exists in voxel. robert said on the company channel that you shouldn't create things that don't actually exist in omicron. steve admits he was right: it's putting the cart before the horse, and it's the trap you easily fall into when doing emulation — you start rewriting families who are or have faced decisions about extremely premature infants; anyone wanting to understand how the "viability line" moved from the courtroom into the hospital room. radiolab radiolab 23 weeks 6 days medical ethics premature infants law boundaries of life family the 24-week line was drawn by a court nita farahani explains that in 1973, when roe v. wade was decided, the supreme court wanted to set a limit on abortion rights and chose "viability"—whether a fetus could survive outside the womb. the best medical guess at the time was 24 weeks, because that's when lungs begin forming air sacs and might theoretically allow breathing. but it was only theory; no one had actually taken a fetus out at 24 weeks to test it. in practice, through the 1970s and '80s, most hospitals drew the line at 28 weeks, because it's around then that the lungs start producing surfactant. only in the late 1970s, with the arrival of artificial surfactant, intravenous nutrition, and tiny ventilators, did the line move back to around 24 weeks. nita farahani the doctor gave three numbers: 53%, 20%, 80% at 23 weeks 4 days, the doctor told kelly and tom the baby would be born within 48 hours. the doctor gave them: no matter what they did, about a 53% chance of death; about a 20% chance the baby would be completely fine; and the remaining 80% meant possible lifelong dependence on a ventilator, brain hemorrhage, blindness, or deafness. the doctor asked them to decide before the birth whether to "do everything." because once you see the baby, it's hard to say no. tom said it was the worst night, and they worried they were "torturing this infant for nothing," and that the child would one day hate them for being born. tom french the nurse turned a yes-or-no question into a conditional one nicu nurse diane loissel didn't give numbers. instead she told kelly and tom: this isn't a yes or no decision. the baby could be born first, and if she came out crying loudly and vigorous, they could go all out to save her; if she came out blue and floppy, they could stop, withdraw support, and hold her until she died. that way, the decision was handed to the baby herself. the plan turned an impossible choice into "give her a chance first, then see." diane loissel parents see will; doctors see reflexes "the baby declared herself" is a phrase parents and staff used repeatedly. but the two sides understood it completely differently. what parents saw was will and determination; nurse tracy hullett said she deliberately used more neutral words, because a 23-week baby's brain has almost no folds on the outside—it's basically smooth—and no one knows what it can think or feel. keith barrington was more direct: a baby grasping a parent's finger is actually the grasp reflex, and he never told parents that, because they would think it was intentional. but perhaps it's precisely this ability to "see will" that lets parents make a decision when they can't decide rationally. keith barrington the neonatologist himself was fooled by a reflex keith barrington and his wife annie are both experts in the ethics of extreme prematurity. their own daughter was born at 24 weeks 5 days, weighing 720 grams, in the very nicu where he was director. weeks later, the daughter developed severe complications and didn't move at all for 36 hours, and they decided to let her go peacefully. but when he went back to the nicu to see her, he saw her lips moving—she was sucking on a pacifier a nurse had put in her mouth. he knew it was just a basic brainstem reflex, nowhere near enough to survive. but he still went back to his wife and said: we can't stop, i want to keep giving her a chance. he said if he were more evidence-based, more rational, more scientific, he might have made either choice, but as a father, in that moment, he couldn't let go. keith barrington she opened her eyes, and the doctor decided to operate juniper's intestine perforated again, her blood pressure and oxygen crashed, and even 100% pure oxygen couldn't sustain her. the surgeon refused to operate, considering it futile, and her blood pressure was too unstable—she might not survive the surgery; and the brain shuttle company in the back half is the most valuable part. founders and investors working on neurodegenerative disease, blood-brain barrier delivery, glycobiology or biologics; neurodegeneration bioorthogonal chemistry drug delivery glycobiology was abandoned by its tools in the 1960s and 70s, carbohydrates were taken as seriously as proteins, but once recombinant dna arrived, proteins could be cloned, expressed and studied — sugars could not. sugars are not a product of the central dogma; they are the output of enzymes encoded by hundreds of genes, and molecular biology techniques cannot manipulate them directly. so the field rushed toward whatever could be accelerated, and sugar science, technically hard, was left where it stood. bertozzi says this is not because sugars are unimportant, but because "just because you don't study an area doesn't mean it's not important." carolyn bertozzi she built the flashlight before talking biology when she started her lab at berkeley in 1996, sugar science was missing two things proteins had long had: sequencing (knowing which sugars exist) and live imaging (seeing where sugars are and how they move). her lab's initial goal was to fill exactly those two holes, and it took roughly a decade to develop bioorthogonal chemistry — a chemical reaction that can label sugars inside living cells and is now a general-purpose tool in the life sciences. with a flashlight, you can finally see places no one had looked before. carolyn bertozzi nobody had asked how sugars change with age tony wyss-coray's lab was studying transcriptomic and proteomic changes in brain endothelial cells as they age — standard practice — but nobody had asked about the glycome. sophia, a student who had rotated in bertozzi's lab, moved to tony's lab and brought the sugar imaging reagents with her to compare the vasculature of old and young mice. the result was "absolutely striking" — the sugar changes were far more dramatic than any phenotype observed in the transcriptome or proteome. carolyn bertozzi brain endothelial cells have mucins like a redwood forest mucins on the cell surface are like giant redwoods: tall, stiff, straight, projecting above everything else. the mucin forest on brain endothelial cells is far thicker than on the vasculature of heart, kidney or muscle — a landscape unique to the blood-brain barrier. with age this forest turns into winter: leaves gone, trees bare, you can see straight through. young mice are spring, dense with foliage. sophia found that the enzymes responsible for synthesizing these sugars drop in abundance in old mice; restoring the enzyme with a gene therapy vector restored the mucins, reduced blood-brain barrier leakage, and the mice got through the maze faster. carolyn bertozzi a reagent crossed the blood-brain barrier on its own sophia injected a mucin-binding reagent into mice and found hours later that it first bound the vasculature, then crossed the blood-brain barrier by itself into the brain parenchyma. textbooks say proteins cannot cross the blood-brain barrier alone, and this is the biggest pain point for biologics companies working on brain drugs. the accidental finding made the team realize it could serve as a shuttle carrier — a brain shuttle — delivering cargo into the brain. sophia now has her own lab at harvard, and she, bertozzi, tony and another student are spinning out a company to do brain shuttling. carolyn bertozzi only 15 cns biologics are approved more than 150 biologics have been approved to treat immune disease, and a similar number for cancer, but only 15 treat central nervous system disease — and most go in by intrathecal injection: a lumbar puncture, invasive, a whole day gone, hard to scale. if those drugs could be given as ordinary intravenous injections, it would be transformative for patients. the drug classes that could get into the brain include monoclonal antibodies, enzyme replacement therapies, sirna and antisense oligonucleotides, mrna lipid nanoparticles, and viral and non-viral gene therapy vectors. carolyn bertozzi cd22 is the brake on the brain's immune cells tony's lab found anyone who wants to know why li ning and anta took different paths. 忽左忽右 忽左忽右 500 晋江陈埭镇往事：黄子懿谈改开进程中的中国运动品牌 consumer brands manufacturing family business industrial history jinjiang jinjiang is not the fujian version of the wenzhou model fei xiaotong summed up chinese rural development into four models: sunan had government leading farmers to start factories, wenzhou relied on individual entrepreneurs, the pearl river delta relied on foreign capital plus labor doing processing and assembly. jinjiang appeared last and is the easiest to underestimate. it was not individual entrepreneurs but township enterprises started by several families and friends pooling household funds, with a quasi-private-shareholding character: in 1979, when lin tuqin started jinjiang's first shoe factory, he gathered 14 village households to buy in — these people were both shareholders and employees; in 1982, when they wanted to strike out on their own, they also split from the original factory into five factories. the money came from the minnan-specific biao hui, sitting in a financial gray zone; many companies that later grew big raised their early money this way. the local government also put forward the "five permissions," permitting dividends, share-based fundraising, hired labor, and sales commissions. huang ziyi under the fake-medicine case, the government chose to kill the pests and protect the flowers jinjiang had two early quality crises. one was the "week shoes" and "street-crossing shoes": farmers didn't understand that shoes needed specialized glue, and used ordinary glue to stick soles to uppers, so they came apart after seven days — one consumer said they came apart just crossing the street. the second was the 1985 fake-medicine case: white sugar ground into powder, congealed into blocks, stuffed with white fungus to pass as granules, flowing through gray channels to hospitals, reported nationwide by people's daily. jinjiang goods became notorious, over a thousand ground-promotion salesmen were turned away, and some hotels threw their luggage right out the door. at the time, fujian's first provincial party secretary, xiang nan, was very market-oriented — he expanded the xiamen special economic zone's area and borrowed international loans to build xiamen airport — and called chendai's workshops "a flower of township enterprises," but for this he was criticized as too far left, made five or six self-criticisms within half a year, and then stepped down. on his way out he instructed the people handling the fake-medicine case: kill the pests and protect the flowers; when you pour out the bathwater, you can't throw the baby out with it. huang ziyi li ning's resource endowment became a curse instead jinjiang's shoe factories were all nike's apprentices, but the first to develop the awareness of building a domestic brand was li ning. li ning founded the brand in 1990, collecting sacred flame beneath the snow mountains of the qinghai-tibet plateau and carrying it nationwide, with enormous impact; almost all jinjiang brands' registration milestones came after that — anta applied in 1990 and registered successfully in 1991, peak was originally named fengdeng and changed its name in 1990-1991, and 361° was previously called bieke. but the two paths were completely different: li ning carried a national halo from the very start, and when performance doubled year after year in the mid-1990s it set the goal of spending ten or twenty years to put a chinese brand in the world's number one position; h: the failure of liberal democracy is not economic, it is the distribution of recognition fukuyama says liberalism flattened the human soul into a creature that wants only security and consumption, ignoring the longing to be seen and recognized; trump-style backlash and identity politics both grow from here. fukuyama himself restates the end of history, threading recognition, thumos and state capacity into a single line. information density is high, though the ai section in the back half is looser. founders, investors and policy researchers concerned with why democratic institutions are failing and with the roots of populism and identity politics — especially suited to anyone thinking about ai governance. the ezra klein show ezra klein show francis fukuyama on trump, china and the legacy of 9/11 political philosophy populism recognition politics state capacity ai governance the end of history is not the end of events fukuyama clarifies that the phrase comes from hegel: it means history has direction and a goal, and asks what objective endpoint the process is heading toward — not that big things stop happening. his observation in the late 1980s was that every systemic competitor had either self-destructed or been abandoned by its followers, so things would stop at liberal democracy plus capitalism, the second-to-last station. his challenge to opponents has not changed: can you point to a better alternative that leaves people ultimately happier and more complete. francis fukuyama the foundation of liberalism is not self-preservation, it is recognition fukuyama moves the philosophical basis of liberalism from hobbes and locke to hegel. hobbes and locke ask only for self-preservation and a decent material life; hegel saw deeper: humans also have thumos, an immaterial impulse demanding that others recognize their humanity. he coined two greek words: isothumia is the basic dignity everyone is born entitled to, cashed out through rights; asking for amplification. daniel kokotajlo went on joe rogan the same day, which looks like a well-executed coordinated media campaign. but the author stresses this does not amount to a conspiracy or h: brahminhood is not doghood: how a buddhist philosopher dismantled the metaphysics of caste dharmakirti does not deny that dogs share a universal, "doghood" — he refuses to grant that "brahminhood" exists, because brahmins and shudras do not differ in any perceptible way in body, intellect or capacity, and caste produces no causal efficacy at all. this episode works through one specific metaphysical dispute in the history of indian philosophy: from universal realism to "caste is a cognitive failure," the argument chain is complete, not a vague cultural introduction. people interested in indian philosophy and the metaphysical problem of universals; people who want to understand how the caste system can be dismantled by philosophical argument rather than moral condemnation. philosophy bites philosophy bites nilanjan das on buddhist philosophy and caste indian philosophy buddhism caste metaphysics universals caste has two layers: four varnas plus countless jatis nilanjan das first unpacks the structure of caste: one layer is the four occupational ranks — brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, shudra — corresponding to different occupations; the other is the endogamous social groups embedded within them, the jatis. the former are called varnas, the latter jatis. the key point is that it is simultaneously a hierarchy of social power and political power, with brahmins and kshatriyas at the top and the rest below. and whichever rank you are born into is the one you are: caste is transmitted through lineage, not through any other factor. das also concedes that the history of the caste system's own origins is unclear, appearing roughly alongside the brahmanical forms of the mid-first millennium bce. nilanjan das the opponent's analogy: brahminhood is like doghood dharmakirti's main opponent, kumarila, holds a kind of universal realism: when we watch two dachshunds running in a field, besides seeing particular features like brown color and wagging tails, we also see the shared property of "doghood." such properties, if taken to exist independently of individual objects, are what philosophers of the time called universals, and what they themselves called samanyas or jatis. kumarila's inference is: just as dogs share doghood, brahmins share "brahminhood," and — this is the part das calls most bizarre — we can actually see a brahmin's brahminhood. das admits this looks strange at first: the distinction between dogs and snakes is natural, but saying all brahmins share a property that non-brahmins lack is something else entirely. nilanjan das seeing brahminhood is not the same as recognizing a brahmin here there is a key distinction: non-epistemic seeing versus epistemic seeing. the former is seeing something without seeing it as anything; the latter is seeing it as something. das gives an example: if i had never seen a dog, i might see a dog and its doghood yet be unable to identify it as a dog — identification requires the background capacity to classify and categorize. kumarila would say the same of brahmins: you might see a brahmin together with his brahminhood yet be unable to see him as a brahmin. so even if you put a group of brahmins and non-brahmins into the same identity line-up, wearing the same clothes and the same haircut, das says kumarila would probably hold that he could still pick out who is a brahmin — but there is an important qualification here. nilanjan das dharmakirti's test: structure, properties, causal power what dharmakirti himself says is actually quite basic: we can grasp a natural distinction between objects only under certain conditions — when the objects differ in physical structure, or differ in important properties, or differ in causal power. he cites cows and horses: a cow's shape and structure differ from a horse's, a cow's milk tastes different from a horse's, and a cow can do things a horse cannot, so we can posit a natural distinction between cows and horses. but on dharmakirti's view, no such distinction exists between brahmins and other caste ranks such as shudras: brahmins do not differ from other castes in body, in intellect or in capacity. so there is no reason to think we can grasp a natural distinction between castes. das stresses dharmakirti's general principle: if you want to posit that something exists, it has to "earn its place," by proving that it has causal efficacy and can produce effects in the world. nilanjan das caste is like an occupational surname, not like witchcraft asked whether dharmakirti is saying caste is a social construction, das gives a careful answer. dharmakirti does think that many things we think and talk about — tables, chairs, properties like brown — are constructed through our conceptual capacities, yet they are still true in another sense, because without granting them, everyday activity could not proceed. dharmakirti thinks caste terms like brahmin and shudra are much like occupational terms: h: the first space elevator shouldn't be built on land, but on a ship in the equatorial pacific the core of siting the first space elevator isn't being close to cities, but minimizing the consequences of failure: a mobile offshore platform in the equatorial pacific, with mild weather, far from shipping lanes, where an accident just drops into open ocean. this episode is siting deduction rather than engineering detail, with medium information density; the second half on the moon, phobos, and venus proposals is more counterintuitive than the earth section, and worth listening to. founders and engineers interested in space infrastructure, orbital transport, and geopolitical engineering siting; spendthrifts feel it too weakly and spend more than they ideally would. the scale measures the gap between your "ideal self" and your actual behavior, so a very wealthy person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. on the show, ben retook the test and scored 11, just over the tightwad line; the wider the gap between the two on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, even controlling for household debt and savings. benjamin felix everyone already has a default prenup in ontario it is called a marriage contract; h: a disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the ones born in sin, the ones who have to fight for their rights. this isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people. mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; its value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. skip it if you want methodology and industry judgment. people in charity work, theatre and community workshops; content people who want to understand why integration can't rest on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers working on disability issues. 故事fm 故事fm e909.我们给残障人写「爽文」戏剧，把健全人写成弱势群体 disability theatre nonprofit integration oral history disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary hanyā (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. one of them, a woman she calls jiejie, had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at new year, what she felt was ‘like being walked like a little dog or cat’. later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. another woman, a visually impaired mother, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. these accounts made yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case. yaoyao disabled people's friends are all disabled people a former colleague of yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs; they hung the chairs front and back with belongings and hauled load after load. yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would have been done in half a day. the colleague paused, then said, i don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, ‘you have no chance at integration to speak of’. that was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre. yaoyao writing the able-bodied as the discriminated ones born in sin leyi theatre's first play, huí zhuǎn wèi lái (“逆转未来”), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like; the surviving minority of able-bodied people, guilty of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become the ones born in sin, marginalised by society. yaoyao's logic: since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning every right disabled people now have to fight for into a right the able-bodied have to fight for. she calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. the plot's core: an original-sin father, to spare his son from suffering for his able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to saw off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original-sin people and modified people. yaoyao how the one who can't see and the one who can't hear partner up visually impaired actor wang xiaomin was pulled in as a partner by deaf actor li ning during an audition, and his first reaction was blank: you can't hear, i can't see, how are we supposed to act. li ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was wang's line. director ma yan says blind and deaf performers sharing a stage already exists abroad: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. wang xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, ‘absolutely no way they could ever communicate’, a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and li ning became very good friends. the troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description. wang xiaomin visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impai ‖ 故事 故事 我們給殘障人寫 爽文 戲劇 把健全人寫成弱勢群體

h: inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes, not yet in humans textbooks use the weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small rnas and they still resist viruses their parents met — change only the rna in the brain and you change behavior three generations later. 35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from dna to small rnas, with the experimental designs and the key numbers; on mammals the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply. people working in reproductive health, ivf diagnostics or epigenetics; and biology readers who want to know whether lamarck was entirely wrong. huberman lab huberman lab essentials: genes & the inheritance of memories across generations | dr. oded rechavi epigenetics c. elegans rna interference acquired inheritance reproductive health the genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page every cell carries the same genome. rechavi's analogy is that every room holds an ikea manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out one page, and that page is rna, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. the messenger rna that actually encodes protein is only a small part of rna: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger rna, while a great deal of the rna that gets transcribed does other things, many of them still not understood. this distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — dna determines which instructions can be opened, and the remaining question is whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions. dr. oded rechavi two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? rechavi attributes it to two barriers. the first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century august weismann proposed what is now called the weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. the second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. the reason for the erasure is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being locked into the few pieces one room happened to make. dr. oded rechavi it was opposed and desired, and not entirely for data reasons this barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. rechavi describes two sides: one is theory, the barrier is sitting right there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. he takes schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. but he doesn't push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it has promise’; he only says rna is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field. dr. oded rechavi nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one phd why trust nematodes? the conditions rechavi lists are concrete: a c. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, raised in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; the generation time is 3 days, so one phd can run hundreds of generations of nematodes. under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it. dr. oded rechavi offspring that can't make small rnas still resist viruses the experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, while if it's destroyed it stays black. first let nematodes get infected and clear the virus, then knock out the machinery for making small rnas in their offspring — these offspring have

h: ect is not what you think: a century of drift from back room to routine treatment modern ect is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized. if your image of ect is still stuck on one flew over the cuckoo's nest, this episode will completely reset it. hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account. clinicians, psychiatric and pediatric staff, medical students, and anyone who has doubts about ect or wants to understand the evidence behind first-line treatment. this podcast will kill you this podcast will kill you ep 221 electroconvulsive therapy part 2: a current conversation psychiatry electroconvulsive therapy brain science treatment-resistant depression neuroimmunology medical misconceptions what actually happens if you or i get ect if you or i were to receive ect, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. the next morning, in the hospital or an outpatient clinic, an iv line is placed along with two blood pressure cuffs (arm and right leg), and ekg, eeg and emg leads are connected. after the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, even half a second). the goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the eeg. erin allman-updike electrode placement, and why the right side comes first there are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. right unilateral is used for most people because it produces fewer cognitive side effects. why consider the right side first? because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. but right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. during a course of treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is not working well, switch to bilateral. erin allman-updike seizure threshold and the effective dose the seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. there is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then probe upward from a low dose until a seizure appears. but treatment does not stop at merely reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. with bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. the dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. if in one session a patient's seizure does not occur or does not last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer. erin allman-updike we still do not know exactly how ect works why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? frankly: we still do not fully understand. there are several main hypotheses. one is neurotransmitter change: after ect, serotonin, dopamine and gaba (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. the rise in gaba is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. two, large fluctuations in hormones such as acth, prolactin and tsh are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. three, ect promotes neurogenesis, with bdnf (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. but how these changes directly h: a child hitting, biting or kicking isn't misbehaving — he's reclaiming his bodily autonomy stop asking how to make the hitting stop. a three- or four-year-old's hitting, biting and kicking is often the only tool left to shout "i have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything his body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks. most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that precedes the behavior. this episode treats aggression as a need signal, and shows the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers. parents whose child just started preschool and who keep getting calls home about incidents; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. so when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say did this child have over his own life before this, and what bit of it can be handed back now. jen kindergarten readiness is really obedience training teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit down when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. but what the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what i need right now." teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, to keep children safe, to save effort, even to enjoy a taste of power; many went into education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over kind of relationship. only by seeing both sides' situations is there room to negotiate. jen we grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children if an adult at a party feels overloaded, he arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even wears noise-cancelling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. turn the camera on a child, though, and apart from conventions like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, he'll never survive the real world." the truth is that adults grant themselves far more regulation than they allow children. the source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back into the middle of the loud party — with an adult, you'd instantly see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we look right past it. jen the repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't the knowledge the child is missing. you need a different set of questions: what happened in the few seconds before this bite? what happened earlier that day? is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? a sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down, so let him stand at the front, the back, or outside the line; words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster zone — reservoir decisions cannot carry the blame. why did seagate, which wasn't flooded, also stop? seagate's factory in northern korat was basically fine, but production still halted — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. the typical case was japan's nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and shut down directly after two plants flooded. the hard drive supply chain is interlocking layer by layer: no matter how safe the assembly line, if the motors don't come, the whole line stops. seagate managed to core plant took on water 1.8 meters deep, and quarterly shipments fell 51%. the difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose underlying supply chain could route around the break point faster. zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: western digital announced in march 2011 it would acquire hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later seagate announced it would acquire samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. precisely because there success rate at only about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests. this episode takes apart the success rate of ai-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosafety rhetoric, while own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. this study exploits the moment in 2017 when the us shingles vaccine switched wholesale from zostavax to shingrix: those vaccinated before the policy switch got the old vaccine, those after got the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. it is still not a randomised trial, however — socioeconomic status, smoking, diet and other unmeasured factors could still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment. vincent racaniello weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit how strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? that is what the e-value measures. the e-value for this vaccine study is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a confounder that is not even very strong, one linked to both "which vaccine was received" and concede that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation should not be treated as evidence. brianne barker ai produces a functional viral genome for the first time the researchers took the genomic language models evo1 and evo2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public dna sequence datasets, then they were fine-tuned on phix174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect e. coli — the first time ai has designed a complete genome from scratch that was then proven functional. if the media summarises this as "ai directly made a virus", it misses a key point: the model has only ever seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function. vincent racaniello the origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory the prompt given to the model needed only the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the phix174 genome for the accuracy of the output to rise markedly. the authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across every genome the model generated. it works like a password meaning "i am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be from phage g4. when humans performed the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the ai's evo36 infects normally, because it accumulated 58 additional mutations across h: ion drives: the slow rockets that win space rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. an ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny fraction of the propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics. this episode covers ion propulsion's principles, limits and applications in full — good for anyone who wants a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion is now mainstream for deep space and satellites; those with no taste for engine detail can focus on the thrust and applications segments. space industry professionals, satellite and deep-space mission planners, and engineers and investors interested in electric propulsion system selection and the economics of propellant. isaacarthur isaacarthur ion drives: the slow rockets that win space ion propulsion electric propulsion spaceflight propellant deep space ion propulsion wins on endurance the rocket equation is cruel: to go faster you must throw away more mass, or throw it faster — but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, a tax collector's loop. chemical rockets use high thrust to leave earth quickly, but their exhaust velocity is capped by the energy stored in chemical bonds. ion propulsion takes another route: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate a small number of charged particles to extremely high speeds and throw them out. the thrust is astonishingly small, but it can persist for weeks, months or even years, ultimately accumulating a velocity change chemical rockets struggle to match. specific impulse and thrust can't both be had specific impulse measures how efficiently propellant is used; chemical rockets manage only a few hundred seconds, ion engines reach several thousand. but that efficiency rests on extremely low thrust: an ion engine can never lift off from the surface of earth, the moon or mars — at most it can depart a small asteroid whose gravity an astronaut could jump off. it isn't physically impossible; it trades thrust for efficiency, and time for speed. chemical rockets are sprinters, ion engines are marathoners. two mainstream forms of electric propulsion the classic gridded ion thruster ionises propellant atoms and accelerates them out through charged grids — high efficiency, but the grids are continuously eroded. hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionise and accelerate propellant, with somewhat lower specific impulse but higher thrust, better suited to satellites, and they are the mainstay of modern electric propulsion. there are also micro electric-thruster systems for small satellites, and high-power plasma concepts — the core difference among all of these ultimately comes down to how to get enough electrical power. why xenon is the default propellant propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same accelerating voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum — mass times velocity — so helium looks tempting. yet at the same power, a higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium needs about 590 megajoules to ionise a kilogram, xenon only about 9 megajoules. xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode the engine. it is today's high-end choice for ion propulsion, but costs about a thousand dollars per kilogram. argon is far cheaper and is the industrial choice of the future. slow rockets are the bedrock of space logistics ion propulsion is especially suited to missions already in orbit: spiralling orbits up or down, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. humans are impatient cargo, but supplies — water, metal, parts, propellant — don't care about being shipped slowly. a future mars programme or lunar base could move people fast with chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion while ion engines deliver the cargo ahead of time, slowly. machines do the boring work; the history of civilisation is written in freighters, ships, railways, trucks and shipping containers. longevity is the core requirement, not a bonus an ion thruster must run continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, power processing units have to survive years of operation. a chemical engine burns for minutes, an ion engine for years — this isn't easier, it's a different direction in which things get hard. it also struggles to exploit the oberth effect: a chemical rocket can burn hard and briefly at orbital perigee for a huge gain in orbital energy, while an ion engine's thrust is spread over months and loses that advantage for nothing. propellant isn't fuel, it's money propellant isn't just fuel; it is mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred and protected. every kilogram of propellant saved is another kilogram of instruments, shielding, cargo and lifetime. the key question of the early space age was whether you could reach space at all; a kernel is the implementation that lands that definition on specific hardware. the same add goes through webgpu / wgsl in the browser, and corresponds to a cuda or metal kernel in other ecosystems. the two are often conflated, but the speed difference comes precisely from the latter: only when the underlying kernel is fast can the whole inference graph be fast. this also explains why it is worth repeatedly polishing a kernel for a simple operation, rather than vaguely tuning a ‘general math library’. what ships is jinja templates, not hardcoded kernels the difference in approach is worth noting: the repository does not hold hardcoded wgsl files one by one, but a number of jinja templates with if/else branches describing different devices. at execution time, the library validates the template, picks the appropriate data type and workgroup size, then renders it into the wgsl best suited to the current gpu adapter and runs it. for example, the same addition function: on the left the data type is narrow and the workgroup small; on the right, because the device supports a wider data type and a larger workgroup, the same add runs faster. the official release lists 200-plus kernel entries, but what is actually delivered is the ability to make kernels on the fly for the hardware. attention in the browser takes only about 20 lines of js the demo brings the abstraction back to practice: running a small piece of attention in the browser took only about 20 lines of javascript. the flow is text→token→vector, but a token's vector cannot be viewed independently — you have to look at how other tokens in the context affect it. what the code does is merely pull four kernels — matmul, softmax, add, layer normalization — from the hub; the rest of the scheduling and gpu data exchange is hidden by the hugging face kernels library. the heavy lifting is all at the kernel layer, which is why the barrier to ‘doing local inference in the browser’ has come down. the whole wave animation is really just one matrix multiplication the same demo gives an intuitive contrast: 128 waves crossing a 1024×1024 matrix, where the color of every cell is an rgba computed by a matrix multiplication. the animation of more than a million pixels on screen runs at about 60fps under webgpu — 60 is not the compute ceiling, it is just requestanimationframe locking rendering at 60; the kernel itself can compute at about 400fps. running the same logic in plain javascript leaves the frame rate at roughly 6.75fps. the gap is not in the math but in whether someone wrote it as an implementation hugging this gpu — which is exactly what that batch of kernels is doing. fleet turns user devices into a tuning data source via benchmarks fleet looks on the surface like a benchmark page: anyone can run their own gpu and see how it compares. but the project team says it plainly: the team only has the few devices on hand, while the real world has thousands upon thousands of webgpu devices, and there may be edge cases they never thought of — some kernel performs poorly on your machine, or even fails outright. fleet collects runtime data from real devices back for further optimization, and the optimized kernels return to all users thanks to open source. when you click run benchmark once, you are not just looking at a score — you are running a round of real-environment adaptation testing for the project. the kernel is the implementation that can actually run the operation. we don't ship wgsl files. we do ship jinja files, so jinja templates. we basically have implemented an attention mechanism in pure javascript. we only need one kernel. we only need the matrix multiplication. all of that data is so valuable for us. number of webgpu kernels released 200+ encoding units in the opening animation about 8000 lines of js needed to implement attention about 20 matrix size of the wave animation 1024

any other software category he tracks. the host adds the data's boundary: it excludes players like microsoft and the big banks, but it is still representative of the overall state of ai industry spending. in other words, what actually props up the enterprise revenue of the two leading model makers is not a broad mass market, but a small handful of extremely free-spending customers. ed zitron the big ai spenders are funded by vc, not revenue this spending structure holds up largely because ai startups are kept burning money on vc transfusions. the common play is to sell subscriptions but subsidise tokens: a user on a $20-a-month subscription can burn $30, $40 or even $100 worth of tokens, with the gap covered by capital. that is, the money openai and anthropic receive from these customers depends on those customers being able to keep raising. the host admits this is his intuition: the loudest voices on ai twitter are basically vc-backed startups, and the tokens they burn internally writing code may far exceed what outside customers pay for. so-called real demand is, at least in large part, actually propped up by ‘the ability to raise’. ed zitron the only ones willing to pay big for ai are tech itself lay this data out and the conclusion is more awkward than most people want to admit: ai has occupied every media outlet and every meeting room for three straight years, almost every company has tried it, plenty have approved big ai budgets, but the ones actually willing to spend big turn out to be, it seems, only the tech industry itself. industries outside tech and ai barely pay high prices for large models, and there is no sign of any reversal. worse, this small set of leading customers is itself unstable — they could easily switch to cheaper self-built open-source models, or eventually move to on-device models. the host points out that this customer structure is the real underlying exposure of openai and anthropic. ed zitron cloud vendors have staked their fortunes on two model companies the risk does not stop at the two labs themselves. the compute purchase commitments on openai and anthropic exceed $1.1 trillion, and they are take-or-pay contracts — no matter how much is actually used or earned, the agreed amount must be paid. the compute revenue of microsoft, google, amazon, oracle and coreweave is all betting that these two can pay. the figures the host cites: openai contributes about 70% of microsoft's fy26 ai revenue; ubs estimates openai and anthropic will account for 48% of google cloud's total revenue next year, corresponding to roughly $84 billion to $100 billion; barclays also gives 2027 forecasts of about $40 billion for aws and at least $50 billion for azure. and both companies are still losing billions of dollars a year. ed zitron the compute bill hits a reset wall in 2027 why hasn't the bubble burst yet? because the mortgage-style structure hasn't reached its repayment peak. these compute contracts usually start with a small prepayment, the data centre capacity isn't online yet, and the real payment obligation gets heavier month by month starting next year. the host cites an analogy from a groundbreaker article: it's like a mortgage's low teaser rate expiring — the rate was extremely low at signing, and after the reset the monthly payment balloons to something unsustainable; borrowers all assumed at signing that house prices would keep rising and that they could refinance or sell, but when everyone tries to run at the same time, no one can get out. openai's and anthropic's enormous compute commitments are the subprime of the ai

h: ai designing chips is real; verification is still the number one bottleneck ai can already write rtl on its own, but the real chokepoint in the entire chip pipeline is verification: it eats more than half of development time, yet ai cannot answer "what should be tested." openai's twenty-person team can shorten the front end, but the back end still has to be left to humans. the author uses what he has seen firsthand and the words of frontline engineers to pull "ai builds chips" out of clickbait: which parts are prototypes, which can go into production, and where the moat actually is. semiconductor investors trying to judge whether "ai designs chips" is a real inflection point or fundraising talk, chip company decision-makers, and engineers watching ai adoption. asianometry asianometry ai edas: is it real? ai chip design eda verification openai agents semiconductors k3 has only a front end, no back end the original material behind "ai tapes out in 48 hours" is a small inference accelerator called nano kpu that kimi announced: 238,000 parameters, about 1.46 million standard cells, 0.277mb sram, claimed to close timing at 100 mhz within 4 square millimeters with decode throughput of 8,700 tokens/s. but the host looked closely: this batch of rtl only had functional verification, with no cell placement, routing, physical verification, or sign-off; the so-called "timing closure" relies on estimates, 100 mhz is not impressive in a 45nm open-source library either, since by hand with the same library you can hit 20-450 mhz, and commercial processes can reach 1-3 ghz. k3's goal is not to build a good chip, but to prove an agent can autonomously reach functional completeness. ai writing rtl is not news at all many people think ai writing chips only started with k3, but back in 2020 at nyu someone used gpt-2 to generate beginner-level rtl, with reports claiming 94.8% accuracy; the now-defunct efabless ran an ai design competition, and a design will salcedo generated with gpt-4 actually went to tapeout, one of the earliest llm-designed tapeouts the host knows of. "ai writes rtl" is not itself the innovation; what actually changed is that an agent can run unattended from start to functional completeness, distilling out process autonomy. the agent's future is being wrapped around the toolchain while fully autonomous design is still nowhere in sight, the real product form is wrapping an llm around the eda toolchain: the llm directs deterministic eda tools through interfaces like mcp and apis, just as claude code lets a model call computer tools. the long-term goal of synopsys, cadence, and siemens is to open up their own stacks and hand data feedback and control to agents that can run for hours or even overnight. siemens played a demo at semicon taiwan: letting an agent drop hundreds of standard cells one by one into a simulator to measure load, speed, and power for later designs to look up. redoing this tedious work for every process node change is exactly the kind of thing to hand to ai before leaving the office. even the best results cannot do without a human in the loop the post by former xai engineer christina lee is, in the host's eyes, the most convincing breakdown. her meta-harness has an inner and outer layer: the inner layer lets the model call eda tools to write rtl, synthesize, place and route, and verify; the outer layer lets the model review what was right and wrong in the previous round, propose improvements, and run again. the first stage only did a mac multiply-accumulate array, pushing through multiple rounds of iteration to 900 mhz to 1 ghz; the second stage connected the mac to sram and other modules, and complexity immediately rose. note that the human always holds the steering wheel: the so-called goal strings were likely provided as reference by the outer model, but the filtering and final confirmation power is in human hands. ai is not the boss, it is the co-pilot. what is truly scary about jalapeno is the 20-person team openai's jalapeno demo had many people fixating on "only 9 months from rtl to tapeout." the host reminds us: synopsys had previously said on an unrelated occasion that using their tools, without ai, also takes about 9 to 12 months; the chip itself is not complex, and the starting point is unclear too, since the architecture concept only began in october 2024. what really stands out is the team size: only 20 to 30 people stood up when the talk ended. and this group's token consumption has long ranked near the top of openai's internal leaderboard, with rtl still being changed the day before freeze. if such a small team can pull it off, future chip roles will need an order of magnitude fewer people, which may be exactly why they did not emphasize it in the slides. verification is the real chokepoint in ai chip design the whole industry talks up the front-end rtl while glossing over the back end: openai's launch slides dwell a lot on spec and rtl, and the host guesses the back end was pr

h: microsoft's former ceo tried to route around the nba salary cap — and lost: a star got $48m for doing nothing what really sinks steve ballmer isn't the $48 million funneled to kawhi — it's that the money bought no real deliverable. the clause about getting paid for doing nothing is what made the endorsements collapse under investigation. the first few minutes sound like sports gossip, but what follows is a complete financial-audit model: four companies, fake job titles, payments with no deliverables — and how to see through a billionaire's carefully built network of sham contracts. founders and investors tracking regulatory arbitrage, financial investigations and specimens of billionaire behavior; also readers who treat top sports owners as business case studies. pure ai-technical listeners can take it as a top-tier billionaire flameout documentary. tbpn tbpn pablo torre explains the steve ballmer & kawhi leonard scandal nba salary cap sports business financial investigation billionaires sham contracts in the nba, rich people's money can't buy everything to understand why ballmer went to such lengths, first accept the counterintuitive fact of sports: no matter how rich you are, you can't just buy a top player. nba rules cap total league payroll, meant to keep big and small markets superficially balanced. pablo calls it ‘sports is a funny mix of socialism and capitalism’ — and that mix is usually convenient for owners, because every time an owner reads the news he finds himself richer. the problem is ballmer wanted kawhi in his prime; if he only went through team salary, he couldn't just throw money at him. so his only path was to keep it off the team's books and have outside companies funnel benefits to the player, routing around the salary cap. pablo torre not crossing the line once, but making the same mistake four times what surprised pablo in the investigation wasn't that ballmer crossed a line — it's that he made the same mistake four times. according to the nba's investigation and pablo's own reporting, besides aspiration (the tree-planting/carbon-credit company), there was also scoreboard maker daktronics, locked in insurance (which did insurance for intuit dome), and boingo wireless (which provided wi-fi to the clippers) — all used to pay kawhi leonard. in every case, kawhi didn't have to shoot an ad or attend a meeting. the result was four sets of documents, four batches of employees, four sets of money flows. pablo says this is exactly what's most damning — once the number piles up, the ‘i didn't know anything’ defense stops working, because all four companies were carrying the same inexplicable task: paying a star who did nothing. pablo torre rich people make mistakes too, because desperation comes from not being able to buy something many people's first reaction is: ballmer is such a shrewd businessman, he can't be this stupid. pablo says that's precisely the most dangerous assumption. in investigating financial violations he's seen too many ‘extremely successful people’ who, desperate for something money can't directly buy, do things they think will never be discovered. in this case, what ballmer couldn't buy wasn't the player himself — it was that the rules wouldn't let him poach kawhi directly from another team; the lakers were also chasing him, and toronto might not let go either. ballmer's wealth lets him win in almost every market, except in front of salary-cap rules. so he believed the four-company, multi-layer structure was hidden enough. the problem is he trusted people he shouldn't have, and every step left a paper trail. being smart and being crazy aren't mutually exclusive. pablo torre kawhi's insistence on doing nothing is exactly the sham contract's fatal flaw the truth of the whole arrangement can be seen from kawhi's own attitude. pablo recounts that kawhi was very clear externally: for this off-the-books money, he didn't plan to do anything; he wouldn't work for the payer, but he wanted the money. ballmer's answer was: no problem, we'll handle it. there's no business deliverable here that could be defended as an ‘endorsement fee’ — no ads, no appearances, no social content, not even a formally announced contract. when a real audit chases money, the first question it asks is: what did you buy with this payment? the moment the answer is written as ‘nothing needs to be done’, the whole multi-layer company structure collapses. a payment with no deliverable is always the most glaring item in the paper evidence. pablo torre the heaviest owner fine ever, designed to close off arbitration the nba's punishment of ballmer is the heaviest ever at the owner level: 5 first-round picks, a $30 million fine, plus $50 million to cover the league's legal fees, and a one-year ban from entering the intuit dome he built for $2 billion — a arena he was so hands-on with that he personally measured the bathrooms. to ballmer the numbers are just ‘rounding errors’; the real design is procedural: the nba
