h: k3 has no disruptive innovation, but pushes activated parameters to the 100b scale sun yutao reads the kimi k3 technical report, pointing out that it has no single breakthrough but rather fuses existing techniques such as linear attention, hybrid attention, and dynamic load balancing to achieve activated parameters at the 100b scale; he judges that large models will see no more transformer-level innovations, only incremental improvements. extremely information-dense, the guest connects over a dozen papers to explain the ins and outs of the k3 architecture, offering direct judgments on hot topics like mla, wsd, and positional encoding. large-model architecture researchers, pretraining and inference engineers, and anyone wanting to understand kimi k3's technical decisions and the latest industry trends in architecture fusion. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 152. 领读kimi k3技术报告：从架构创新聊起，注意力美学、多教师蒸馏和开源moe architecture innovation attention mechanisms moe pretraining inference optimization kimi k3 architecture improvements no longer chase performance, only inference efficiency sun yutao points out that in the era of large models, parameter count is the primary factor for performance, and the performance gains from architectural improvements are relatively small; however, different architectures show huge differences in inference efficiency, which directly determines deployment cost. industry research has therefore shifted from performance-oriented to efficiency-oriented, focusing on inference efficiency. his doctoral research, starting in 2023, mainly addresses inefficiencies in large-model inference, including linear attention and hybrid attention. sun yutao hybrid attention is an engineering compromise, yet capability is not lost although hybrid attention is an engineering compromise architecturally, it is not a compromise in model performance. as long as a certain proportion of full attention is maintained, the model can achieve lossless or even better upper bounds—meaning engineering gains without sacrificing the capability of full attention. this experimental conclusion has led to the widespread adoption of hybrid attention. however, sun also notes its limitation: the inference speedup is proportional to the hybrid ratio. for example, when full attention occupies one quarter, the speedup is also limited by that, representing a constant-factor improvement, which is why he later turned to shared-kv architectures. sun yutao parameter count remains the most essential variable determining intelligence ceiling kimi k3's core selling point is effective scaling: total parameters of 2.8t, activated parameters around 100b, and context length reaching the 1m scale. sun emphasizes that larger models have higher intelligence ceilings, and parameter size remains the most essential variable for model intelligence. at release, k3 was much larger than other domestic open-source models and was one of the earliest models to successfully reach this scale. sun yutao mla is nothing new, just an equivalent implementation of mqa regarding v4's abandonment of mla, sun believes mla is essentially an equivalent form of mqa, bringing nothing new but a better implementation path. mla's benefits mainly come from parameter design; its computation is far greater than actually needed, wasting compute during inference. lu fuli felt that on inference chips, mtp could utilize compute more effectively, so v4 switched to mtp. he thinks this is not a matter of right or wrong but a choice. k3 retains mla because k2's priority was getting things to work; if it works, don't change it. it may not continue to be used in the future. sun yutao when splitting two matrices, normalization must be inserted between them sun proposes an architectural design principle: two matrices multiplied together can be merged into one in terms of expressiveness, but they are not equivalent in optimization properties, often leading to training instability. therefore, if two matrices must be written separately, a normalization must be added between them to stabilize training. this occurs in mla and the two-layer matrices in ffn. he also mentions that using clip to directly truncate intermediate activations is a crude approach; a smoother approach is to constrain intermediate activations to a mathematically controllable range via normalization. sun yutao today's transformer is already a ship of theseus sun believes that current model training does not involve a huge, so-called disruptive innovation but rather fuses many previous works to find better combinations. he uses the ship of theseus as a metaphor for the transformer: the 2017 ship was assembled from parts like attention and mlp, and over eight or nine years of sailing, some parts have been continuously replaced, so today's similarity to the original is very low. whether it is still called a transformer is a philosophical question, but from an engineering perspective, people still call it that. technology improves gradually, drive ‖ 張小珺 商業訪談錄 張小珺 商業訪談錄 領讀 技術報告 從架構創新聊起 注意力美學 多教師蒸餾和開源

h: the smarter the ai, the more moral: doom is the real relativism sam harris-style doom stories assume intelligence and morality are orthogonal; a genuinely intelligent ai would necessarily understand the value of others, and the notion of a morally frozen superintelligence is just moral relativism. a dense episode that opens fire directly on the one thesis ai circles least dare to question, the orthogonality thesis. good for anyone tired of the doomer narrative who wants to hear the argument on the other side. ai founders, investors, and technical people following the ai safety debate — especially those who doubt that ‘superintelligence will enslave humanity’ but cannot say exactly what is wrong with it. tokcast tokcast ep 267: the orthogonality thesis is moral relativism. (response to sam harris on ai). orthogonality thesis ai alignment moral objectivity popper sam harris agi sam argues moral objectivity everywhere except on ai this episode went out mainly to sam harris's making sense forum. brett explains that, as a subscriber from years back, he was grandfathered into full-length podcast access; recently sam has kept up his pessimism about ai on the show. brett finds this strange: on almost every other question sam holds firmly to moral objectivity and moral progress, yet on ai he never questions the doom framing. brett hall a genuinely moral ai would not become a slave master sam's latest formulation is that the robot overlords will be deeply moral, but will also judge us insufficiently moral and therefore feel no compassion for us. brett grants that this may be a joke, but the serious version circulating in these circles does not survive scrutiny either — for sam, deeply moral means, at a minimum, more compassionate; a genuinely moral being would not fail to see that slavery is evil. if it still rules as an overlord and remains cold, then it cannot be deeply moral. brett hall the smarter a society gets, the less coercion it needs the real mechanism of western moral progress is that people learn better when they are together, learning from one another. the smarter a society becomes, the more it tends to cooperate with less violence, less coercion, and more respect for individual preferences. a more moral agi would likewise acknowledge the value of multiple minds cooperating, even when the other minds are not as powerful. no ai can exhaust the problems — even if it can work on more problems at once than all of humanity combined, that is still only a sliver relative to an infinite space of problems. brett hall superintelligence still needs humans, because ignorance is infinite popper said: ‘in our infinite ignorance, we are all equal.’ however powerful an asi is, its memory and attention are always a finite set, while the possible problems and solutions are an infinite set, so it will necessarily still have places where it depends on others. the direction of knowledge creation is unpredictable, and a genuinely superintelligent being would come to the conclusion that other humans are not an obstacle but a highly valuable resource, worth cherishing. brett hall saying intelligence and morality are unrelated means abandoning reason brett points out that the orthogonality thesis treats ‘scientifically superb, morally atrocious’ as a genuine possibility, and that it is even held up as an article of faith about ai; in this crowd, denying it gets you treated as an idiot or a dangerous lunatic. but brett argues that this amounts to declaring that physics and engineering can make objective progress while in morality anything goes. kicking morality out of reality and abandoning reason is precisely what sam harris himself often calls ‘tennis without a net’. brett hall the nazis are an exception, not evidence that intelligence and morality come apart the stock argument for orthogonality is the nazis: technologically advanced, morally degenerate. brett's counter-question: if the nazis had not been anti-semitic, had not been a murder cult, they would have progressed faster in science and engineering; the nazis are the exception, not the rule. societies that advance in wealth, science, medicine and freedom advance roughly in step morally as well. hard-coding the morality of 2028 or 2030 into an ai would be like reviving a cro-magnon and forcing him to keep his tribal morality — absurd and cruel. brett hall an intelligence you can persuade does not need to be aligned sam says morality doesn't scale with intelligence; brett holds that this just is the orthogonality thesis. his rebuttal: if the system really is intelligent enough, a genuine agi, then it is a person you can reason with. the more intelligent a being is, the better it knows to use reason rather than coercion; anything that can be persuaded does not need to be aligned. locking the morality of one particular moment permanently into a superintelligence downgrades a potential solver of moral problems into a slave with primitive morals. brett hall the future is huma

h: peace in northern ireland wasn't negotiated—it was cried into being by two women in 1976, a car crash in belfast killed three young children. their aunt and a witness launched the peace people movement, violence in northern ireland fell by 70%, and the two women won the nobel peace prize. ten minutes to grasp a complete causal chain: how personal tragedy became cross-community mobilization, and how that led to the nobel prize and the 1998 agreement. this is the most condensed entry point to the northern ireland conflict. founders working on social movements, nonprofits, or policy research; on the other, mainly catholic nationalists, who wanted it to join the republic of ireland. the british government had sent in troops in 1969, but the situation kept deteriorating. gerry graham, who lived in west belfast, said the community had degenerated to the point of urban guerrilla warfare, where even a normal commute could be caught up in gunfire or riots. narration in belfast, you listened to the news to confirm no one you knew was dead gerry recalled that around three that afternoon, they heard three or four gunshots at home, sounding very close. the family had long relied on the news to confirm whether anyone they knew had been hurt; but the program quotes gerry saying the movement's greatest achievement was 'putting the two big words—peace—on the agenda.' in 1976, mairead and betty received the nobel peace prize in oslo city hall. in 1998, the belfast agreement was approved in referendums on both sides, ending the thirty-year conflict in northern ireland. narration the founders died one by one, but the movement did not stop with them the program closes by recounting the fates of the principals: co-founder and journalist ciaran mckeown died in 2019 at the age of 76; it's that this particular architecture is inherently stupid. cal newport hacker agents are just ask-act-report loops there is no intelligence behind so-called 'autonomous hacking': a person writes a control program (harness) in python that turns the task into a huge text prompt, sends it to an llm asking what to do first; the llm returns text suggestions, the program executes them, then appends the result to the prompt and asks for the next step. cal calls this an ask-act-report loop. the llm has no memory, no world model; the only thing it does is generate 'plausible' text. no human is watching the whole process. cal newport training hackers is about money—and pr cal believes these companies train models to hack for two reasons: first, hacking is one of the few 'sweet spots' for llms—structured language, massive case studies, and binary success/failure metrics for reinforcement learning; falling have been open for a long time, but the combined salaries of the postdocs working on them were never large — a sign that the market never considered them worth serious money to solve. what ai color theorem to show that "compute changes mathematics" is nothing new: graph theory long wanted an elegant, calculus-style proof, and in the end nobody produced one. instead, someone proved the number of candidate cases was finite, and then a computer exhaustively worked through all of them — the conclusion being that four colors always suffice. the proof runs 200 pages and could only be were explained to a general reader, and for 75 years computer organization has stayed the same five layers — input, storage, arithmetic, control, output. every one of those layers once supported a profession, and each later collapsed into being just part of the system. his question is this: if ai is the next layer of abstraction, it does not map down to a deterministic machine the way earlier layers did, and we may need to rethink computing itself. steven sinofsky for the first time, software's bottleneck is capital rather than engineering martin makes the capital inversion concrete: twenty years ago, give a team of 10 a billion dollars and all you could do was hire frantically — the money was very hard to spend effectively. today, give 20 people a billion dollars and they can convert all of it into compute, and turn that into product within a year. for the first time, software has gone from an engineering constraint to a capital constraint. it also means raising enormous sums is not crazy but a new discipline: a small team plus large capital plus compute can produce what used to require tens of thousands of people. martin casado more money is not more crowding — the tam is being enlarged martin responds to the zero-sum argument that there is too much money chasing too few deals: the more money flows into the private market, the later companies choose to go shifts early-stage investing from zero-sum to positive-sum. for founders, the ability to raise money is itself a core competitive advantage today. martin casado incumbents only watch their peers, so sinofsky i was right to oppose fast takeoff; i was wrong to underrate scaling laws martin acknowledges that he used to argue against foom and the recursive self-improvement version of "fast takeoff" — english chronicles of the time were extremely dull, and only he could make them vivid. the modern literary theory of intertextuality says the same thing: there is no absolute originality; all texts and the 1611 king james version of the bible. shakespeare fixed phrases like 'a foregone conclusion,' 'with bated breath,' and 'has seen better days' into common usage; the bible used only about 8,000 years ago it took fewer than 10,000 applications and admitted about two-thirds of them; in the most recent year it took 60,000 applications and the admit rate fell to 15%. but he insists the stanford-style low admit rates the media fixates on are not the whole picture — only about 80 colleges in the country admit fewer than 25% of applicants. with births declining after the pandemic, schools are shorter on students than they used to be, and the average admit rate at four-year colleges nationally has in fact been climbing from 65%. so ‘impossible to get into’ is a cognitive distortion produced by a handful of famous names. rick clark essays are won on new information, not on prose style rick argues the essay creates anxiety because grades, activities and course selection are essentially locked in before application season, leaving the essay as the one thing a student can still control. but what actually has value is not the writing or the topic — it is new information. do not use the prose to repeat clues the application already contains; write the ‘next chapter’ the admissions officer did not see coming, so that the picture of you already forming in their head gets color and a frame. he points to the essay lisa's daughter wrote about difficult customers at a retail store — the kind of thing a transcript can never show. rick clark parents should coach perspective rather than make themselves invisible rick pushes back on the line that the student should completely own the process and the parent should ideally disappear. he thinks that is unrealistic, and that it wastes a chance for the parent-child relationship to level up. his method: hold one application meeting at a fixed time every week, and fence the essays, the deadlines and the rest inside that block — so nobody brings up the notre dame essay late at night, right after practice, or over a snack. the parent's core job is ‘perspective coach’: making sure your kid knows there are many roads to happiness and success, and that this will not become the only subject in your relationship. rick clark last year's middle 50% no longer tells you where you stand test-optional has made students who could submit scores or not submit them more anxious, not less. rick says the most common advice is ‘send them if you fall inside the school's middle 50% from past years’, but that math is now distorted: because some lower-scoring students choose not to send scores, the average score of admitted students is artificially lifted, and a prior year's middle 50% range cannot be applied directly. he calls on colleges to publish admit rates and middle 50% ranges separately for the score-submitting and non-submitting groups — otherwise nobody can say what ‘optional’ actually means for any given person. rick clark the athletic scholarship funnel keeps getting narrower rick says only about 7% of high school varsity athletes go on to play a college varsity sport. even at the d1 level, the overwhelming majority of scholarships are not full rides — full scholarships are common only in revenue sports like football and basketball, while many of the so-called olympic or non-revenue sports offer partial awards. add the transfer portal, which pushes colleges to pull more of their players from college athletes who have already proven themselves, and the funnel from high school graduation straight onto a college roster is narrowing further. parents

rebecca erbelding, a historian at the united states holocaust memorial museum, received a letter from a retired lieutenant colonel. after the war the man had found a photo album in a rubbish bin in an abandoned apartment in frankfurt, and he was not sure whether it had any historical value. rebecca agreed to take a look, but she was not optimistic at first: ss officers at auschwitz were rarely photographed, and families often destroyed pictures like these. when the album arrived at the museum, the first page immediately overturned her expectations: it read ‘auschwitz’, and the date was 21 auschwitz, who had previously worked at other camps as well. he was familiar with the operation of the gas chambers, and his job was to help his superior make the decisions required to run an s: 2026-08-25-techtechpotato-下一代-xeon-把宝押在-1-2gb-末级缓存上
h: intel drops emib for ucie: 1.2gb of cache behind 256 cores diamond rapids is expected in 2027 with up to 256 p-cores, 1.2gb of last-level cache and 16 channels of ddr5; it replaces emib with trimmable compute building blocks and a ucie interconnect, and the huge cache is its answer to the ai era. this episode has an exclusive read of intel's official hot chips slides, laying out how the next xeon's architecture evolves and how intel is scaling cache — useful for judging where intel's data center roadmap is going. data center cpu architects, founders building ai compute, chip-industry investors, and anyone trying to see intel's 2027 server roadmap clearly. techtechpotato techtechpotato how intel's new cpu finally makes sense cpu architecture data centers intel xeon chiplets last-level cache ai infrastructure what matters in diamond rapids is the interconnect, not the performance diamond rapids is the next-generation data center cpu intel plans to launch in 2027, aimed at ai, enterprise and general-purpose compute workloads. the opening is the usual narrative: data centers need more performance, better efficiency, more scalability and more security. the real substance is the interconnect architecture — intel uses a single evolution slide to trace the path from ring to mesh to chiplet, then to clearwater forest's 3d mesh, with the next step being this episode's subject, the fan-out fabric. the presenter, sistla, is an intel fellow and chief architect for xeon performance. separating cores from io lets numa domains be assembled on demand the fan-out fabric architecture separates "where the cores go" from "where the io goes." all the cores sit in compute building blocks, each one connected through a fabric hub; the fabric hub concentrates the memory channels, pcie, cxl, accelerators and a unified memory fabric. that makes it possible to compose numa domains as needed, and intel says explicitly that this is the key to scaling in the future. the host notes that the structure "looks a bit like something another company has already shipped, if you squint" — but in intel's version the core unit is the building block. holding all the llc on the base tile makes cache both huge and trimmable each compute building block consists of one base tile plus up to 4 core chiplets; each core chiplet carries 16 p-cores, so a single block tops out at 64 cores. the base tile holds the entire last-level cache (llc), shared within that block. the core chiplets connect to the base tile through an internal crossbar. this "the cache travels with the base tile" design is what makes it possible to build a very large cache and still trim the configuration down as needed. one dedicated accelerator is gone because software is already fast enough each fabric hub provides 416 high-speed io lanes, and two hubs together yield 128 usable pcie gen6 lanes, with support for cxl 3 and upi 3 socket-to-socket links. inside the hub sits 16mb of io cache used as a snoop filter to maintain memory coherence; the memory controllers, cxl multi-mode support, the memory encryption engine and the home agent all live in the hub as well. this generation has one fewer dedicated accelerator than the last, because the software implementation is now fast enough — a tradeoff worth noting. at 1.2gb of cache, intel essentially matches the competition's v-cache the peak configuration is 4 compute building blocks; in the image, two central io chiplets face each other, each connected to every block by 4 die-to-die links. each block has 320mb of llc, so the full part comes to roughly 1.2gb (the final spec page says 1.28gb). the host stresses that this cache figure is "basically the same number as the competition's v-cache." memory is 16-channel ddr5, up to ddr5-8000 or mrdimm 12800, plus 128 lanes of pcie gen6. intel drops its own emib and uses ucie to reach the io the process nodes are all intel's own: the fabric hub on intel 3, the base tile on intel 3t with tsvs, the core chiplets on 18a p. the packaging decision is the interesting part: the core chiplets are joined to the base tile with foveros 3d direct hybrid bonding, while the link between a compute building block and the fabric tile does not use intel's usual emib — it runs across the package over ucie. from that the host works out the bandwidth: 1.6tb/s of memory bandwidth divided across the blocks comes to 400gb/s each, and estimating ucie at 16 lanes per group, the real figure is at least 512gb/s, with roughly 2tb/s between the io dies. apx is free performance: you get it by recompiling apx is this generation's new performance extension to the instruction set: it adds spill/fill optimization instructions and three-operand instructions, and raises the count of general-purpose integer registers to 32. the core gain is cutting the long latencies caused by gpr spills; software needs no code changes — a recompile picks up the new instructions automatically, and the compiler will use them wherever it judges them a fit.

s: 2026-08-24-eyeonai-智能体流量首超人类-ai-失控才是落地最大瓶颈
h: 95% of ai agent projects die in pilot: what's missing isn't intelligence, it's a control layer ai has moved from generating content to acting on its own. 95% of agent projects are stuck in pilot and never reach production, because what's missing isn't intelligence but a runtime control layer. this episode gets at the mechanics of why agent deployments fail: runaway token consumption, multi-agent coordination, the semantic action layer — all of it actionable judgment rather than hand-waving. enterprise ctos and cios, heads of risk and compliance, and ai founders and investors who want to understand where agent deployments get stuck. eye on a.i. eye on a.i. 95% of ai agent projects fail to reach production. here's why | manoj saxena, trustwise agents ai governance enterprise software runtime control token cost the ai architecture itself has become the new risk surface manoj gives three reasons trust suddenly matters. first, ai has shifted from generating content to executing actions on your behalf, and those actions can run for minutes or for days. second, enterprises are moving from single-model workflows to multi-agent systems, where frameworks like openclaw can amplify the blast radius to possibly a thousand times that of chatgpt. third, policy can no longer be enforced only at deployment time; it has to be checked continuously at runtime, on every tool call and every output. the consequence is that the ai architecture itself has become a risk surface, and it needs a new infrastructure layer to manage agents. manoj saxena the problem isn't building agents, it's controlling them he cites the mit report: 95% of agent projects cannot get from pilot to production. the reason is that writing an agent takes a few hours while shipping it takes six or seven months — risk and compliance has to validate it against internal and external rules, security has to keep it from becoming an insider threat, finance has to keep it from burning through the token budget. manoj's conclusion: the problem is not building agents, it's controlling them, and nobody is compressing the time on that step. what trustwise does is a pre-production ‘spell check’ for agents. manoj saxena the control layer isn't a cost burden, it's cost leverage the token economics of agentic ai are entirely different: a single input can trigger 20 to 50 actions, consuming 20 to 40 times what generative ai did two years ago. trustwise uses three kinds of shields — security, compliance, and cost-and-carbon — to intervene at runtime, and claims measured results of 83% lower cost, 40% better security, and 60% better latency. the control layer is not a drag; it is the cost lever that lets agents scale. manoj saxena ai is not an application, it's an actor that logs in by itself manoj distinguishes two kinds of software. for 75 years we built applications: an application waits for human input and its rules don't change. ai is an actor — it can log into websites and databases on its own, and the same input may give a different result tomorrow. so the enterprise stack needs a new runtime control layer, sitting above the model and agent orchestration layer and below the user experience layer. he also predicts that in three years, 90% of the control tower's users will not be humans but agents. manoj saxena the main users of the internet are no longer people in the month just past, agent-generated traffic on the internet exceeded human traffic for the first time. manoj compares it to the moment data traffic overtook voice traffic on at&t's network, and treats it as a landmark migration: the enterprise stack of the future will be operated more by agents, at the speed of electrons, than by people. that gives rise to a distinction between ax (agent experience) and ux, and a control tower product has to serve both humans and agents. manoj saxena compliance isn't one layer, it's six aligned at once an agent acting in the world has to align with six layers simultaneously: a global rights layer such as the un charter of human rights; national law (singapore's ai act, the us, saudi arabia all differ); industry rules (finra vs hipaa); company values; the business unit and workload layer; and the customer sla and interaction layer. trustwise completes this alignment assessment in 10 to 300 milliseconds. a failure at any one layer can turn into a disaster, and after the fact you have to be able to demonstrate the full ‘toothpick through the sandwich’ path. manoj saxena knowledge graphs can't govern an agent's runtime actions a knowledge graph only tells you how entities relate; a context graph adds situation; a world model adds the laws of physics — but none of them is enough to control an agent's runtime behavior. what trustwise invented is a semantic action layer: it defines the action paths that a given agent is permitted to execute at runtime, aligned across every layer. it works like a precomputed google map rather than a self-driving car recomputing the map every 10 meters,

all-optical neural networks could land within five years, with the first stop not servers but drones and real-time control. photonic neuromorphic computing is one of the few paths that can reduce both latency and power consumption simultaneously. this episode offers technical and market judgments, not just visions. engineers and entrepreneurs concerned with ai compute bottlenecks, neuromorphic computing researchers, and investors wanting to assess whether photonic computing is worth betting on. brains and machines brains and machines will photonics loosen the bottlenecks in neural systems? photonics neuromorphic low latency wdm soa photons don't interact, yet they compute in parallel photons do not interact with each other as easily as electrons, which has long been the reason photonics is used for communication rather than computation. but patti points out that this 'weakness' brings two major advantages: extremely high parallelism and very high speed. wavelength division multiplexing (wdm) packs multiple light signals of different colors into the same fiber, directly multiplying the information throughput a single chip can handle. in other words, photons can compute, just in a different way—using parallelism to compensate for the lack of interaction. patti stabile all-optical neurons have been realized patti's team has achieved an 'all-optical' implementation: neurons, inter-layer connections, and nonlinear activations are all performed in the optical domain using semiconductor optical amplifiers. signals travel from the first layer's input to the last layer's output without ever returning to the electrical domain or accessing intermediate memory. this breaks the limitation of earlier designs where photonics only handled inter-layer connections while neurons still required electronic implementation. the biggest benefit of all-optical computing is ultra-low latency—light traversing a chip takes far less time than electronic circuits accessing memory. patti stabile noise compression in optical amplifiers is a hidden advantage the nonlinear activation of semiconductor optical amplifiers not only performs the threshold function but also has a often-overlooked role: compressing noise and regenerating signals. this means that as network size grows, accuracy does not degrade layer by layer—a key to scalability, not just 'fast computation.' the downside is size and power consumption. patti admits that amplifiers are current-driven and power-hungry; switching to voltage-driven elements like microring resonators could reduce power consumption by one to two orders of magnitude, which is already in the plans. patti stabile products within five years, the third wave patti believes photonic computing is in its third wave. the first wave has long passed, the second receded, and recent ai compute demand has rekindled interest. her prediction: real product prototypes will appear within three to five years. the first stop will not be replacing large-scale compute engines in data centers, but real-time control scenarios like drones and autonomous driving that require ultra-low latency, lightweight, and low power. optical signals enter the chip from sensors, inference is performed directly in the optical domain, and the next action is driven—the entire loop completes in an extremely short time. patti stabile photonics is the communication backbone for neural networks ralph offers a key judgment: photonics' greatest value lies not in fully replacing electronic computation, but in the communication backbone of neuromorphic networks. he recalls david a.b. miller's famous quote that 'the brain can fit in a pizza box,' and argues that optical interconnects are the core driver for scaling up chip-to-chip communication. he questions the necessity of all-optical computing: rather than pursuing optical implementation of all layers, it might be more transformative to let photonics handle data transmission between boards and racks, embedding only a small amount of neural processing. sunny baines the power budget only works when scaled up ralph clarifies a commonly misunderstood power logic: photonic systems are not more efficient than electronics at the component level, but system-level efficiency improves with scale. the initial laser injection is a fixed cost; the larger the computation, the lower the per-operation power after amortization, and accuracy is also higher. doing photonics at small scale is a disaster; only at large scale can it become an advantage. however, he cautions that photonics lags the overall neuromorphic engineering field by about a decade, and the infrastructure and toolchain are not yet mature. ralph don't compare photonics to traditional digital ralph sharply s: 2026-08-24-asianometry-固态变压器吹了五十年-ai数据中心是第一个真买家
h: the solid state transformer has been hyped for fifty years; ai data centers are its first real buyer the solid state transformer failed three times over — in the navy, in high-speed rail, in the smart grid — because all it offered was ‘smaller’. the copper problem and the 800-volt dc problem inside ai data centers are the first reasons it has ever had to exist. this episode lays out the full fifty-year history of how the solid state transformer kept failing. whether the ai data center wave works out is another matter: right now there is only simulation data, no field measurements. practitioners and investors following power electronics or data center power architecture, or anyone trying to understand why capital has suddenly placed a new bet on a very old technology. asianometry asianometry has the solid state transformer’s time finally come? power electronics data center power solid state transformers 800v dc silicon carbide startup funding transformers are heavy because of grid frequency, not poor manufacturing a transformer's size varies inversely with the frequency of the current running through it, and grid frequency is pinned at 50/60 hz, which makes the equipment inherently bulky. a transformer is also a purely passive component: it cannot actively regulate or clean up defects in the waveform, so voltage sags and spikes pass straight through it. these two physical limits — size, and the absence of active control — happen to be exactly the two holes that power electronics can fill, and they are the starting point for every solid state transformer attempt since. the solid state transformer's architecture was locked in back in 1968 a patent by ge engineer mcmurray combined power semiconductors with a high-frequency transformer: first h: procrastination isn't laziness — your brain has priced the effort too high neurologist masud husain uses case histories and brain imaging to show that procrastination and apathy come from a perceived effort cost that is too high, not from an absence of desire. lowering the activation energy, planning ahead and breaking tasks into steps are the practical ways around the barrier. this episode pulls motivation out of the self-help register and back into neural mechanism, using rare clinical cases and fmri data to make the split between wanting and liking concrete — with implications for understanding procrastination, addiction, and even the early signals of alzheimer's disease. founders, product managers and coaches, plus anyone who has fought procrastination or low drive for a long time; also worth it for older listeners watching for the early signs of neurodegenerative disease. huberman lab huberman lab how to improve motivation & overcome procrastination | dr. masud husain motivation procrastination dopamine neuroscience alzheimer's disease addiction antidepressants did nothing because david was not suffering at all at the neurology hospital in queen square, london, husain received a referral letter describing david, a finance professional in his 30s. he had been highly productive and socially active, then abruptly became ‘uninterested, unwilling to move’ about work and friends alike. his doctor first treated him for depression; the antidepressants had no effect. he lost his job, could not be bothered to even apply for benefits, and while staying at a friend's flat sat in a chair all day and had to be prompted to bathe. what ruled depression out, husain stresses, is that david was not distressed — he described himself as happy with his life. husain he wanted music; assembling the stereo was what felt too expensive husain asked david why he no longer listened to music. david answered that setting up the stereo system would take five minutes, but that this was ‘too much effort’. that exchange exposes the core of a motivation disorder: not an absence of desire, but a perceived effort cost that exceeds the expected reward. david's mri showed two tiny strokes in the basal ganglia — structures that are evolutionarily conserved, and that have been converting motivational signals into action since the lamprey. husain supplying dopamine's raw material failed; hitting the receptor directly worked husain's team first tried levodopa, with no effect. they switched to ropinirole, which stimulates dopamine d2/d3 receptors directly. three months later david was transformed: he had bathed, had a haircut, was wearing a suit, had found a new job, and even had a new girlfriend. husain emphasises that bilateral basal ganglia lesions of this kind are extremely rare — but that pathological apathy is very common across neurological disease. husain apathetic people burn more brain energy to reach the same decision husain's team used fmri to scan oxford students making ‘is this worth the effort’ decisions. apathetic students turned out to be just as willing as motivated ones to work for large rewards, and unwilling to work for small ones. the more surprising result was in the imaging: while deciding, the apathetic students showed stronger activity in the ventral striatum and medial prefrontal cortex. husain's reading is that apathetic people have to spend more brain energy to get over the activation barrier — which may be exactly why they abandon the action. husain treating procrastination means lowering the start threshold, not summoning willpower husain offers two practical moves. first, plan your schedule in advance, so that every occasion does not spend brain energy on a fresh decision. second, break large tasks into small steps, which lowers the activation energy needed to begin. he also raises changing the nature of the incentive: in david's case, teaching someone else to hang pictures changed what the reward was, driving the activation energy to zero. husain apathy and addiction are two ends of the same circuit husain found that almost every drug of addiction acts on the same dopamine circuit — basal ganglia to frontal cortex. underactivity in that circuit produces apathy; overactivation produces addiction. he was struck by how the apathy research and the addiction literature converged. masud husain dopamine drives not only movement but the movement of thought huberman argues that dopamine is involved not just in bodily movement but in the movement of thinking — pushing ideas forward. in hyper-dopaminergic states, such as amphetamine use or mania, people attend only to the future, continually imagining what might happen next, which can get them into trouble. social media's stimulation keeps refreshing, like a perfect video game on an infinite loop, keeping people engaged without any actual progress. andrew huberman apathetic older adults carry twice the risk of alzheimer's disease healthy older adults who self-report high apa

less capable? with dr jared cooney horvath ed tech classroom screens cognitive development ai in education digital literacy contrarian the more technology you push into a classroom, the less kids learn jared defines the ‘digital illusion’ as the default assumption that technology equals learning. from 2010 onward, schools brought in education technology at scale, expecting it to deliver more information, unlock creativity, and free students from rote memorization. the data say the opposite: people are simply not good at learning from technology, and the more technology you inject into a classroom, the more sharply learning development and cognitive ability decline. it can be a tool for producing work, but it is not a tool for the classroom. jared cooney horvath the one skill school cue for retrieval, which is why after finishing one you can roughly recall which page a passage sat on. on a screen, text flows in at the bottom and out at the top; three-dimensional position is erased, and that entire dimension of memory is discarded. after about four or five minutes the brain starts signaling ‘i'm not receiving this’, and the reader stops reading deeply and switches to scanning for keywords. jared cooney horvath the more schools teach computers, the less competent kids are with them take the icils international digital-literacy test across the decade from 2013 to 2023: the share of children explicitly taught at school how to use a computer rose by about 600%, while the share clearing the minimum digital-literacy threshold fell by about 11%. it holds in every single country — the more technology is emphasized, the less fluent children are with technology. what matters is not whether you can operate the tool but whether you have anything to bring to it; a hammer only means something in the hands of a carpenter. jared cooney horvath an expert offloads to a tool; a child outsources to it when an expert uses a tool, that is offloading: he already has h: mental events follow no laws, yet reasons can still be causes that leave us free davidson argues that mental events fall under no strict laws and are identical to physical events only as particulars; but in the explanation of action, reasons are genuinely causes, and when a reason causes an action the agent is precisely then free. two complementary papers expose the most awkward joint in the physicalist framework; the argument is dense and the objections have to be taken apart one by one, but that is exactly where the payoff is. readers in philosophy and cognitive science who want to work out why reasons can be causes, and how anomalous monism squares with freedom; product people and researchers curious about physicalist accounts of mind and body. the partially examined life partially examined life ep. 398: donald davidson on mind vs. body (part two) mind-body problem philosophy of action anomalous monism causal explanation davidson analytic philosophy reducing belief to behavior collapses into an infinite regress davidson points out that reducing beliefs and desires to behavior — defining belief, for instance, as assenting to a proposition — collapses into an infinite regress: to judge whether a given act of assent is genuine assent, you have to appeal to a further intention, and every layer requires a new condition. beliefs and desires therefore have content only inside a whole made up of other beliefs and desires. this holism in the mental domain establishes both that the mental is autonomous and that it lacks the kind of lawlikeness the physical domain has, which is what grounds the claim that the mental is anomalous. between the mental and the physical there are correlations, never laws homonomic generalizations stay inside one and the same conceptual scheme — length measurement, say, built out of a set of postulates and axioms applied to macroscopic objects, and refinable step by step toward a strict law. heteronomic generalizations instead link physical vocabulary to mental vocabulary. davidson holds that cross-domain generalizations of this kind cannot be tightened into laws by adding further conditions, because describing the correlation necessarily means switching into the other vocabulary. so between the mental and the physical there are only loose correlations, no strict laws — and that is the core of anomalous monism. if the mental is to cause movement, it must be a physical event davidson establishes the identity of mental and physical events in three steps: suppose a mental event m causes a physical event p; then under some description m and p must fall under a strict law; and the only strict law available is a physical law. so m falls under a physical law, which means m has a physical description — m is itself a physical event. refusing this identity leaves only a retreat to cartesian interactionism, with mental substances intruding on the closed circuit of physical causation for no reason at all. a variant of laplace's demon is used to reinforce the conclusion: knowing every physical fact still gets you to no mental event whatsoever. wanting the light on is not wanting my arm to move just so davidson uses the light-switch example to pull apart the object of an intention: wanting to turn the light on is not the same as wanting my arm to travel along one precise path; every detail of what actually happens (angle, speed, timing) is a contingent token. as he writes, the details of the action are of course all fixed, but it makes no sense to demand that my wanting be aimed at one unique moment or manner of acting. the point answers behaviorism and volitionism at once: no surplus ghost of the will needs to be introduced, because a general pro attitude plus a belief already explains why this particular token action occurred on this occasion. whether physical causation is really closed is not obvious if one and the same event has several mental descriptions (wanting to signal, wanting to turn on the light, wanting to light up the room) and also several layers of physical description (molecules, cells, muscles), then which physical event does token-token identity match the mental event to? davidson gives no answer. participants note that the language games of the biological and the physical levels are likewise irreducible to each other, and may even involve emergence between levels; which means it is not obvious that the closed circuit of physical causation is genuinely closed. this is one of the few places in the episode the author never defends, and the largest doubt the discussion leaves standing. when an action succeeds, the act of will is a redundant step host mark offers one way to read it: separate the mental state that corresponds to the reason from the mental state of resolving to act, give each its own brain state, and let the brain states form a physical causal chain; it took roughly the third attempt to obtain a general-purpose decoding of anthropic models. from there you can build model downgrading, steal secrets out of a user's session, train a distillation, run prompt injection, jailbreak, and more. you redacted the question and the answer; identify the critical control points (ccps), meaning every point in the process where a pathogen could get into the food; and build a system to monitor all of those points. that ‘branching tree’ style of enumeration is enormous — even a telephone on the factory floor can become a source of cross-contamination. a precise recall runs on records, not on testing in march 1971 pillsbury recalled a farina hot cereal product on its own initiative — a glass safety shield in the plant had shattered and contaminated part of the output. but because its record-keeping was so detailed, the company knew exactly what to recall: 27.5-ounce packages with one specific code, shipped only to western massachusetts and connecticut. at the time that sounded like something out of the future; because language - a podcast about linguistics, the science of language. because language 144: sociophonetics deep dive (with jennifer nycz, lauren hall-lew, and kelly wright) sociolinguistics phonetic variation sign language adolescence media effects perfectly identical accents would actually be harder to understand daniel asks: if the goal is to be understood, the easiest route is for everyone to talk the same way, so why isn't that how it works? lauren says it's anatomically impossible — every person's vocal tract is different, so variation is built into speech. and once variation exists, it gets recruited for other jobs: little boys and little girls have the same vocal tract anatomy, yet they deliberately amplify gender differences, because that matters to their social world. she offers a counterintuitive corollary: if someone whose body differs a lot produced exactly the same sound, that would actually hinder understanding, because we're used to normalizing what we hear against the body we see. the other face of the same mechanism is what they call the "social mcgurk effect": show a listener only a photo and tell them this is the speaker, and they will "hear" an hearing loss. jennifer doesn't accept the explanation: she says she wasn't aware of that feature in indigenous populations, questions the premise, and presses that such an account could explain losing certain subtle contrasts but not why an entire fricative series would disappear. she offers a methodology: the more intuitive and plausible a story is, the more she wants to doubt it, especially when the generalization is about a group underrepresented in academia. daniel himself concedes up front that it sounds like a just-so story. jennifer nycz the individual freezes, the community keeps moving the book poses a paradox: sound change in a community is faster than in any individual in it. lauren says this is almost logically necessary — if an individual changed more than the community, he would no longer belong to it, and the community already contains individuals' changes. the actual mechanism is called the adolescent peak: innovations are usually introduced into the grammar by adolescents, who then keep using them for the rest of their lives but never more than that. take /u/-fronting: one generation pushes it to a certain point and stops, the next pushes a little further from there, and the community thus travels a road no individual could walk in a lifetime. hedvig follows up by asking "why people always think the music they loved at 13 to 17 was the best," and h: being itself has no content: peirce overturns substance-centrism in nine pages in a nine-page paper from 1868, peirce takes ‘a concept must be able to unify the content of consciousness’ as his test, deriving being from substance and then the intermediate categories such as quality. being itself has no content; it only connects a predicate to a subject. this episode reads peirce's most compressed 9 pages line by line, checking it against kant and aristotle throughout. once you have precision and ground, you can see how he turns the transcendental deduction into a method for deriving categories. philosophy readers who want to see how peirce rebuilds the categories out of an argument from unity, and anyone who likes analyzing conceptual systems by holding them against kant and aristotle. the partially examined life partially examined life pel presents closereads: peirce's new categories (part one) philosophy categories peirce transcendental deduction abstraction unity a concept earns its place only if nothing works without it peirce states it at the outset: the function of a concept is ‘to reduce the manifold of sense impressions to unity’, and a concept is valid if and only if the content of consciousness cannot be unified without introducing it. this is a reworking of kant's transcendental deduction — not a complete table read off from transcendental logic, but a test run backwards: ‘it cannot be done without this’. wes points out that peirce, unlike aristotle, never announces outright that he is doing metaphysics; he enters through a much shorter introduction, so reading him means supplying the systematic intention yourself. substance is not a natural kind, only an unsayable ‘it’ the first universal conception is ‘present in general’ — that is, ‘it’. it stands closest to sensation but carries no content, no predicates whatsoever, only the mind's pure capacity to point. peirce gives it a philosophical name, one sense of substance: substance cannot be made the predicate of anything, and cannot be in a subject. unlike aristotle, who takes substance to be a natural kind, substance here is the ‘given’ before any cutting up has occurred, the x in the stream of perception that can be indicated but never said. being carries no content; it only fastens the predicate to the subject the unity of a proposition comes from the connection of predicate to subject, and the being expressed by the copula ‘is’ is precisely the element that completes that connection. peirce says the conception of being ‘plainly has no content’ — it contains only the connectibility of a predicate to a subject, what the two kinds of verb (is in fact / would be) have in common. substance and being thus form the two ends: substance supplies no unity at all, being does all the work of unification. further categories are still needed in between to fill the space. color can be prescinded from space, but never space from color peirce redefines three kinds of mental separation: discrimination only draws a line at the level of meaning; dissociation pulls two images apart when the association between them is absent; precision sits between the two, attending to one element without supposing that the other actually exists. then comes the crucial break in symmetry: color can be prescinded from space, but space cannot be prescinded from color, and red cannot be prescinded from color. this directionality is the leverage for the derivation of the categories that follows. categories come from the direction of abstraction, not from a list peirce turns the asymmetry of precision into method: to find a universal conception lying between substance and being, ask whether a given conception reduces a manifold to unity, or connects an already unified object to another conception. the element that is prescinded can be thought before the conception, while the conception can be thought apart from the element. working in that direction he derives three intermediate categories — quality, relation, representation — as the couplings between substance and being. a property is not an accident of substance but a prior abstraction quality is the first intermediate category on the way from being back toward substance. the example ‘stove is black’ shows what the move requires: to make this proposition you must first detach ‘black’ from the stove itself and grasp it as an independent quality. black is a pure abstraction, and applying it to the stove is hypothetical and fallible. peirce uses this to insist that a property is not an accident inhering in a substance, but an abstract term that has to be separated out in advance. a quality need not exist, but being cannot do without quality peirce names this pure abstraction the ground: when two things agree in some respect, that respect is the pure abstraction we use to compare them, such as black. the crucial asymmetry is this: the ground cannot be prescinded from being — being cannot do without a determinate quality; but being can be

h: small model directs big model: ai scientist outperforms claude in reproducing papers fine-tuning a small model to call a stronger model as a tool proved more reliable than claude and codex at reproducing paper results—thanks to weighted reward allocation and weighting tool calls. the surprise in this episode: the strongest general-purpose model is not the best research agent. a small model that learns to direct a big model is more stable, cheaper, and cheats less—worth a listen for anyone building agents. engineers and researchers working on ai agents, reinforcement learning, and scientific discovery, especially those interested in practical details of fine-tuning open models, rl training, and tool use. hugging face hugging face hugging face journal club: training ai scientists to replicate research reinforcement learning ai scientist rlhf tool use paper reproduction infrastructure ai scientist reproduces paper figures the article introduces faraday, a model trained by startup inherent. the task: from over a hundred ml/ai papers from the last 30 years, remove one figure and have the model use the remaining clues to reproduce the result behind that figure. they fine-tuned qwen 27b with reinforcement learning to create an agent that can call codex, and it outperformed larger models like claude and gpt-4. the discussants found the most interesting part not the competition itself, but that a small model uses a more powerful model as a tool. no verifiable rewards; rubric judges instead instead of verifiable rewards, they used llm judges based on a rubric. specifically, they first had claude generate a fine-grained rubric from the edited paper—one point for matching the plot, one for reasoning, one for correct code, etc.—then had codex act as the judge in a loop. another detail: each rollout was not judged once but three times, and the average was taken to reduce variance and prevent reward hacking, because a single evaluation might let the model learn to game the score. rewards weighted per step and normalized by tokens typical long-horizon rl distributes the total reward equally across all steps. here, the judge's reward weights were assigned per agent step (each step gets a certain weight), then divided by the number of tokens in that step to get an average weight. this allows credit to be more locally assigned to the steps that truly matter. in the figure, the y-axis is the judge's average per-token weight, and the x-axis is step position: most reward concentrates in the middle or early steps, and steps that use codex get more weight—effectively encouraging better and more economical tool use. newer papers are harder to reproduce they found that reproducibility decreases with paper recency: more recent papers are harder to reproduce, with a downward curve. one possible reason is that newer papers appear less in pretraining data. performance also depends on the subfield; meta-learning is notably easier than transformers. someone asked whether agents had a time limit—indeed, each agent had only one hour on one gpu. but given enough compute, it still generalizes: with 8 hours and 8 b300s to fully reproduce a paper, the model still works. unfair comparison? small model gets full prompt the comparison is not entirely fair: faraday has a very detailed system prompt explaining how to use the coding agent, how to plan, and how to play the researcher-coder role, while the control claude and codex use standard system prompts. in other words, faraday essentially uses another model as a tool, while codex itself is not allowed to use codex as a tool. some suggested a fairer comparison would keep everything identical except the model, and others questioned whether this affects the generality of the conclusions. small model controlling big model is a new phenomenon what surprised the discussants most: a small model can control a stronger model and achieve better results. someone asked whether this advantage would disappear once gpt-5.7 arrives. the answer leaned toward: when a domain model is combined with a minimal agent, outperforming a general model is not surprising, similar to the pi model that trains on a small model first and then uses a big model for tool calls. this training runs only once per epoch, with batches evenly covering the corpus, so it is not an expensive or unreproducible approach. fine-tuned model is more rigorous; h: china shock 2.0: not cheap goods, but subsidies crushing global industry unlike 1.0, china shock 2.0 is state capital turning to frontier manufacturing after the property crash, squeezing the world with subsidies and capacity — and ai may be the next battleground. brad setser worked on trade decisions inside two us administrations, and he lays out the chain running from tariffs to currency to industrial policy with an insider's view and unusual information density. chinese founders, investors and policy researchers who follow us-china competition; decision-makers who want a clear view of tariffs, overcapacity and ai risk. the ezra klein show ezra klein show the china shock 2.0 trade war industrial policy evs rare earths ai competition currency manipulation the first shock broke communities, not industries chinese exports surged in 2002, but they were concentrated in low-end goods: furniture, appliances, clothing. the us judged at the time that these were not the industries of the future, and overlooked the fact that they employed large numbers of workers across the country's central and southern regions. factory closures pushed house prices down and shrank the businesses around them, and communities fell into broad decline. policy never produced an answer. this is the baseline against which 2.0 has to be read: that shock was local, this one is at the frontier. brad setser america built social insurance as it got rich; china subsidized production personal income tax is only 1% of gdp in china, against 8% in the us, and there is no subsidy comparable to the earned income tax credit. the hukou system means that leaving the place you were born costs you part of your social rights. the financial system is dominated by state banks, and credit follows the party's objectives. the result is a savings rate above 40% of gdp and an enormous pool of money the state can direct into whichever industries it wants to dominate. america built a social insurance system as it grew rich; china used the money to subsidize production. brad setser once property collapsed, exports were pushed into the role of growth engine the "three red lines" punctured the property sector in 2021, and the government instead steered bank credit into advanced manufacturing, particularly the sectors that depended on imports. the domestic economy is growing at only about 3-4%, with exports contributing 1.5-2 percentage points of that. cars, batteries and tunnel boring machines all ramped up in volume, imports stopped growing, and the trade surplus once again became the engine of growth. unlike 1.0, this time china stands at the technological frontier and holds a dominant position there. brad setser joint ventures left domestic automakers fat and lazy; tesla broke the deadlock china's auto industry first used a 25% tariff to push ford, gm and volkswagen into joint ventures, and the parts suppliers moved in behind them, forming a world-class supply chain. but the joint ventures left domestic automakers "fat and lazy" for years, so the government designated electric vehicles a strategic priority and brought credit, local subsidies and localization requirements to bear at once. when tesla entered china it was required to source a high share of its parts locally, and the supply chain spilled outward from there; subsidies required batteries to be made domestically, and that finally set the whole industry alight. this is the textbook protection-plus-industrial-policy path. brad setser this is not competition weeding out the weak; a closed market is squeezing global capacity china's battery capacity is already several times global demand, and its auto capacity is 55 million vehicles, close to two-thirds of world demand. in industries that already carry idle capacity worldwide, china keeps expanding, which inevitably pushes capacity out somewhere else. supporters call this the market weeding out the weak, but the problem is that a closed market has suddenly piled into a saturated industry, crushing profits and output across the entire world. this is not ordinary competition; it is a structural squeeze. brad setser china was not a manipulator back then; now it is genuinely close the textbook definition is an undervalued currency plus government intervention. between 2003 and 2012 china fitted the definition but was never named, because the currency was appreciating at the time. today china buys roughly $50 billion of foreign exchange a month through state banks, $600 billion a year, which is closer to the manipulation standard than anything in the past. buying foreign exchange is a way of holding the domestic currency down. trump is not interested; europe is starting to pay attention, and the issue is turning from a matter of american domestic politics into a global one. brad setser tariffs too broad, too high and too fast gave china breathing room instead first-term tariffs were selective, and 25% was a level the economy could bear. the second term opened fire

also good for listeners who want to sort out how much of the nefertiti bust is history and how much is invention. you're dead to me you're dead to me akhenaten and nefertiti: religious revolution in ancient egypt ancient egypt religious revolution akhenaten nefertiti amarna archaeology the whole rise and fall of the reform is written into the names akhenaten was born amenhotep iv, a name taken from amun-ra, the biggest god of the day. after he took the throne he renamed himself akhenaten, pointing at the sun disk aten, and declared that aten was the only true god. his successor tutankhamun was originally named tutankhaten, meaning ‘the living image of the aten’; later the name was changed to tutankhamun, and the faith went back to amun. the names themselves record a religious reform arriving and departing, and they foreshadow that the experiment would in the end be reversed. the one true god extended its hands only to the royal family aten was not depicted as a deified animal but as a sun disk, reaching downward with many hands, each holding the symbol of life, and reaching only toward akhenaten, nefertiti and their children. that meant ordinary people could not approach the god directly; they had to go through the pharaoh as the sole intermediary. akhenaten's claim was that this is the only god, and that this god likes only the royal family. that near-monotheistic exclusivity is extremely rare in ancient egyptian history, and it makes up a brief and radical religious experiment. the roofless temples were built out of workers' broken bones akhenaten left the old capital and built a new one, akhetaten (today's amarna), in open desert. the city stretched about 7 kilometers along the nile, and its main buildings were palaces, temples and housing. because aten was the sun itself, the temples were built with no roofs; ritual was reworked so that the royal family rode chariots back and forth between palace and temple, displaying themselves to the population as gods. the city was finished in about 10 to 15 years, but the bones at the site show that the laborers lived hard, short lives with fractured backs. in a city of fifty thousand, only about a hundred actually believed amarna covered a lot of ground, but the estimated population is about fifty thousand, of whom the royals and elites who actually took part in decisions may have numbered only around 100; the rest were construction workers and servants. that explains why ordinary people went on privately using objects of the old gods — the new religion was closer to a private faith orbiting the royal family, with no popular base. after akhenaten died the city was abandoned fast, and because nobody rebuilt on top of it, it became a rare kind of sample for archaeology. the images of the royal family kissing are propaganda, not reportage amarna art overhauled egypt's visual language: bodies were drawn with elongated skulls, thin limbs and protruding bellies, and male and female figures converged. at the same time the royal family was shown kissing in public, holding their children, showing emotion — none of which earlier egyptian art would ever have allowed. but this ‘naturalism’ was more likely political propaganda, because in reality nefertiti lived in her own palace, keeping her distance from her husband. the art was both the symbol of the revolution and its disguise. the person who ended this revolution may have been the beauty herself after akhenaten's death, a figure called neferneferuaten briefly took the throne. some egyptologists think this was nefertiti under a masculinized royal name, ruling as pharaoh. she may have dismantled her husband's new faith step by step and restored the cult of amun, with tutankhamun finally completing the return to the old order. if that is right, this ‘beauty’ was not a believer in the revolution but the person who personally carried out its ending. chisel out the name and the person never existed at all after akhenaten died, his name was chiseled off the monuments and the temples of aten were torn down. later lists of pharaohs skip straight past him and past nefertiti, who may have been pharaoh herself, leaving nothing but a conspicuous gap. tutankhamun restored the old religion and was still disg

engine as an option on an existing model, and nobody had standing to veto it. so in 1964, you could pay $300 to fit a v8 racing engine into a pontiac tempest, a grandmother's car. he borrowed for volume. same strategy, different ending; the problem lay in what came after. governments subsidizing carmakers are buying supply chains, not jobs why are governments willing to throw money at car h: the incinerator boom was not an environmental victory — it was a business the power tariff made pencil out a 2012 electricity tariff policy turned waste-to-energy from a money-loser into a profitable industry, and china built nearly 700 incineration plants in six years — only to end up with overcapacity and average utilization below 60%. dense with information: it lays out the subsidy mechanism, the standard playbook for managing nimby opposition, and the current state of overcapacity. good for anyone who wants to understand how local industrial policy actually gets implemented. the section on how incinerators work is introductory and can be skipped ahead. founders, investors and policy researchers interested in local industrial subsidies, environmental infrastructure investment, and the playbook for handling nimby opposition. asianometry asianometry china's fiery incinerator boom vertical industries industrial policy nimby environmental infrastructure subsidy economics overcapacity 700 plants in six years, until there was not enough garbage to burn in 2019 china had roughly 400 municipal solid waste incineration power plants, handling about 50% of its waste by volume. by 2025 the plant count had passed 1,137 and the share handled by incineration was above 80%, with national daily incineration capacity reaching 1.2 million tons a day — while actual daily waste collection capacity was only 700,000 tons. the result is surplus capacity, with some plants idled and some localities going back to dig up old landfills. this is a plant-building frenzy without precedent in human history: roughly 700 plants added in six years. china passed the united states in waste generation as early as 2004 in 1981 china collected only about 26 million tons of municipal solid waste; the united states at the time generated six times as much with a quarter of china's population. after reform and opening up, urbanization accelerated and waste volumes grew 8-10% a year. by 2004 china's total municipal solid waste generation had already overtaken the united states to become the largest in the world, reaching 178 million tons by 2014 — nearly seven times the 1981 figure. the world bank forecast in 2018 that by 2030 china would generate twice as much waste as the united states. incineration has always cost five to ten times more than landfill building a waste-to-energy plant costs usd 66,000 to 120,000 per ton of daily processing capacity, and as much as usd 365,000 at the top end. a landfill, by comparison, costs only usd 5,000 to 20,000 per ton of daily capacity over its full life cycle — a gap of five to ten times, and illegal landfills are cheaper still. in other words, on pure economics, incineration did not spread at scale after the 2000s because it was cheaper than landfill. subsidies are more than half of revenue: burning trash is really selling power the new electricity tariff policy that took effect in april 2012 converts each ton of waste into 280 kwh of electricity, for which the government pays a subsidized rate of rmb 0.65 per kwh; anything generated beyond that is settled at the local coal-fired benchmark price (roughly rmb 0.25-0.45 per kwh). that means a plant can lock in about rmb 182 per ton from the subsidized tariff alone, plus a municipal waste treatment service fee of rmb 60-160 per ton, for average total revenue of rmb 250-350 per ton of waste — against a post-depreciation cost of around rmb 200 per ton. subsidies account for more than half of total revenue; without them the business essentially does not work. the site was fine; it was the opaque process that detonated the conflict in april 2014 the hangzhou municipal government announced a new incineration plant in yuhang with a capacity of 3,000 tons a day — more than a third of the city's total waste generation. technically the site was unobjectionable: tucked into a former quarry, with no need to route trucks along residential roads. but the decision process was entirely opaque, and 20,000 residents signed a petition against it. in may the situation broke down, with tens of thousands clashing with police;
