h: saving hard when you're young is robbing your poor self to pay your rich self the most popular iron rules of personal finance—save hard while young, dividends drive 40% of returns, index funds only give you average, bonds and cash are safer—mostly get the causality backwards. what actually determines the outcome isn't the rule, it's whether you can hold on. high information density, breaking down the most widely circulated personal finance myths one by one; suited to anyone who wants to correct their intuition in one go. but it's an opinion conversation, not a data report. engineers and founders who want to correct their financial intuition in one go; people currently agonizing over whether to save more, whether to buy dividend etfs, or whether to time the market because valuations are high. the rational reminder podcast rational reminder the biggest myths in personal finance | rational reminder 423 personal finance index funds asset allocation dividends behavioral finance extreme saving when young is robbing yourself ‘save hard while young and let compounding work’ is treated as an iron rule, but mechanically it's backwards: when you're young your income is at its lifetime low, and each dollar has the highest marginal utility for improving your life—$5,000 at 25 might mean a safer neighborhood, better food, a more reliable car; the same money at 45, even counting the investment growth in between, does far less for your standard of living. so extreme saving when young sacrifices the things that matter most at the time you can least afford it. pwl writer nick summed it up: you're effectively taking money from the poor person (your low-income present self) and giving it to the rich person (your high-income future self). benjamin felix people who save all their lives can't spend later dan offers a counterintuitive observation from the advisor's chair: people who won't spend because they want to build wealth may end up with a lot of wealth but lose the ability to spend it—even when the wealth far exceeds anything they could need, they still can't spend it, because the mindset has hardened. he says this is a chronic problem wealth advisors see commonly; the client base is itself wealthier, so it doesn't represent the whole population, but it's precisely people who saved aggressively and invested well who end up here: they arrive where they wanted to arrive but can't enjoy it. felix adds the mechanism: cultivating a habit for a lifetime and expecting to flip a switch one day and become a spender is naive. dan bortolotti why spending and saving arguments get so heated the topic is a minefield because the decisions are irreversible: someone who saved all their life can't go back and re-experience, and someone who spent on experiences can't go back and re-save. you're facing people who have already made irreversible decisions, and telling them ‘you should have spent more’ or ‘you should have saved more’ feels like a personal attack, because it was a decision they made and can never undo—and thanks to compounding, undoing gets harder over time. dan adds: as long as the choice was thought through, you shouldn't moralize about others' choices; saying ‘you should save’ easily sounds like judgment, and people get defensive. benjamin felix the stock market isn't the economy; growth is already priced ‘economic growth is good for stock returns’ is wrong, because the stock market isn't the economy. stock prices represent real companies' expected future cash flows, and by the time you read the economic news and hear about a market or sector's growth potential, those growth expectations are probably already in the price. historically this holds at both the industry and country level: industries can grow massively while stock returns are poor, and shrinking industries like railroads have delivered great returns; at the country level, the countries with the highest economic growth often produce lower average stock returns—though felix explicitly says this isn't a statistically significant result, only that there's no relationship between the two. dan's version: everyone knows a good company, the market will pay a higher price for it, so ‘good but not as good as imagined’ stocks move opposite to what most people expect. benjamin felix dividends describe returns, they don't explain them ‘dividends explain 40% of historical stock returns’ is often used by dividend investors to argue dividends matter, but felix thinks it gets causality backwards. when a company pays a dividend, your return doesn't increase; it just converts capital into income: the dividend you receive roughly one-for-one reduces the capital value of the shares you hold, and what changes is the character of what you own, not your return. so dividends at most describe returns, not explain them. he offers a comparison: dividend etfs and buyback etfs have similar factor exposures (both tilt value, profitability, conservative investment), but buyback etfs have lower div

h: the maya ballgame was ritual, not sport: the sacrificed-winner story is invented the mesoamerican ballgame is humanity's earliest rubber-ball team sport, but it was religious ritual first: the court re-staged the creation myth, and the people who could be killed were captives who lost a ritual re-enactment. the idea that the winners were sacrificed was made up later. the episode uses first-hand archaeological evidence to dismantle two myths about the ballgame: that it was mere entertainment, and that winning or losing decided who lived. along the way it explains how the balls were made, and how betting could destroy a man. anyone curious about the maya and mesoamerica, from archaeology buffs to sports historians, and anyone who wants myths like "the winners were sacrificed" overturned. the ancients the ancients the maya ballgame maya civilization mesoamerica ballgame religious ritual archaeology sports history the rubber-ball team sport did not start in greece or china ed says team sports in general may well be older, but the ancestor of rubber-ball team sports is very likely the mesoamerican ballgame. the greek olympics had no ball games at all; china and persia did have ball sports, but they can only be traced back to 500 bc, and the maya ballgame predates them by at least a thousand years. the current evidence points earlier still: rubber balls from 1600-1700 bc have turned up at olmec sites, and the oldest ball court dates to roughly 1650 bc. ed barnhart the ballgame was never uniquely maya; all mesoamerica played it the game was not a maya invention but a shared element of every mesoamerican culture. the maya heartland sits in modern guatemala, extending north into the yucatan peninsula and into chiapas and tabasco in mexico, and south into about half of honduras; further west lie cultures such as the zapotec and the mixtec. the classic peak runs roughly ad 400 to 800, with each city-state politically independent but sharing religion, calendar, writing and the ballgame. ed barnhart hips, knees, shoulders and chest only: the hip swing is the signature shot according to the aztec rules the spanish wrote down, players could not use hands or feet; they struck the ball with hips, knees, shoulders and chest, and the classic shot was a swing of the hip. the ball was a solid rubber "super bouncy ball" about six inches across, and taking one on the body hurt. the court had a centre line and end lines: sending the ball past the opponent's end line scored, and putting it through the stone ring set high on the side wall ended the match instantly. teams had forwards and defenders, much like modern football. ed barnhart a ball court is a mythic stage first, a playing field second ed flatly rejects separating maya religion from maya sport. the large stone courts at the centre of maya cities are ritual spaces first: in the creation myth, the hero twins play a ballgame against the lords of the underworld, which makes the court a place to re-enact the moment of creation. the court at chichen itza is so vast it hardly looks playable, with stone rings some 30 feet up; dancing, sacrifice and symbolic re-enactment are the more plausible explanation. courts were often built at the lowest point of a city, mimicking the underworld. ed barnhart the game could kill you, and gambling could cost you your family the ball was more dangerous than it sounds: a spanish priest watched a player take one in the abdomen, in the gap between his pads, cough blood and die within the hour, probably from ruptured organs. balls were made from natural rubber cured with sulphur, and the maya very likely drew that sulphur from morning glory sap; ed made one himself by the old method and it is still going twenty years later. the betting was just as extreme: a player could stake himself, and a losing run could cost him his money, his house, even his whole family into slavery to a noble. if a noble tried to slip away after a match without throwing gifts, the players had the right to bring him down and take his things. ed barnhart the sacrificed-winner story was invented eight years ago by one man ed debunks it outright: the claim that the winning players were sacrificed comes from an old man at chichen itza who admitted eight years ago that he made it up, because people loved hearing it. logically, if winning meant death, nobody would play properly. the people who really could be sacrificed were war captives, cast as the lords of the underworld in a ritual re-enactment and killed after they lost. ed himself dug a headless body out of the centre line of a modest court in belize, with a turtle shell placed where the skull should have been — a direct echo of the hero twins' decapitation story. ed barnhart a city of 100,000 with no ball court means archaeologists missed it teotihuacan, another great mesoamerican city, may have peaked at 100,000 people, yet no confirmed ball court has been found there, even though its murals show people passing a ball; often leveled at openclaw is poor memory: once the context is compressed it forgets things easily, and its behavior turns erratic. after switching to hermes, huang dongxu found that it does not solve the memory problem itself but sidesteps it cleverly. its agent loop includes a mechanism that continuously summarizes successful experience and hardens it into reusable skills, so the longer you use h: jensen huang turned down the tsmc ceo job twice: i already have a job in 2013 morris chang seriously considered handing the tsmc he founded 26 years earlier to jensen huang. huang answered with five words — ‘i already have a job’ — and said the same thing both times. tsmc's market cap then was 10 times nvidia's. the first half is 30 years of partnership between the two companies, at medium information density; the real value is in the second half: the succession offer, the 40nm compensation negotiation, and how cowos packaging became the ai bottleneck. founders and investors watching the semiconductor supply chain, ai compute bottlenecks and long-term founder relationships; anyone who wants to know why tsmc is hard to replace and why nvidia cannot do without it. 科技这碗饭 科技这碗饭 黄仁勋x张忠谋：一生有你——英伟达和台积电的激荡30年 semiconductors tsmc nvidia supply chain ai compute founder relationships no money to tape out, so build the chip in a computer first nvidia's first two chips both failed, and by the end of 1996 the company had been cut down to just over thirty people. the normal process in the chip industry is tape out, test, fix the design, go again — two or three rounds is common — but huang only had enough money on his books to tape out once. he took a third of his cash, about one million dollars, and bought a machine that could simulate an entire chip inside a computer, to find as many errors as possible before going into a real fab, and then decided the first version would go straight to mass production. a manager asked him how he knew he would get it right in one pass. he answered: i know it has to be right, because if it isn't, the company is gone. in august 1997 the third chip shipped, and in its first four months it moved more than 1 million units. betting the whole lifeline on one fab with no contract in hand from 1998 huang put almost every nvidia chip on tsmc alone. at the time most fabless chip companies worked with two or three fabs at once, playing them off on price while keeping a fallback, and nvidia took that path thoroughly enough. more important, huang made this bet without a long-term contract in hand — around 1997 the two sides discussed a formal manufacturing arrangement, but day-to-day orders were still placed one at a time, and tsmc never promised to reserve any particular capacity long term. only two things held up the bet: morris chang's verbal commitment, and huang's line that sounded almost like bragging. when tsmc makes a mistake, it is nvidia that goes bankrupt in 1998 a chemical step at the end of a tsmc production line went wrong, causing large-scale breaks across a whole batch of wafers, and more than half the chips in that nvidia lot were scrapped. because it was hard to tell by ordinary sampling which ones were usable, nvidia threw up a temporary test line and hired a large crew to sort them one chip at a time, and tsmc sent two production planners from hsinchu to california for a full month. that quarter nvidia's revenue fell from more than 28 million dollars to less than half, the net loss came close to 10 million dollars, and in the end it had to sell part of its equity to several downstream companies for cash. this is the fundamental risk of the design-only model: the fab belongs to someone else, the mistake was someone else's, but the money lost, the undelivered goods and the walk to the edge of bankruptcy can only be yours. a customer diverting a little business has to be written into risk factors in 2002 tsmc's most advanced process generation could not get its yields up, nvidia's new flagship shipped half a year late, and once it launched review sites nicknamed it the hair dryer for its power draw and heat; rival ati used the opening to overtake it with new products. in march 2003 nvidia announced an alliance with ibm, handing its next-generation flagship to ibm's new fab in new york state, in a contract estimated at more than 100 million dollars. the same day the two companies jointly issued a press release reaffirming the partnership, but three months later tsmc filed its annual report with the sec and for the first time put the matter into risk factors, writing that it could not guarantee it would not lose nvidia's business in the future. the previous year nvidia had still contributed about a fifth of tsmc's revenue; that year its share fell from two tenths to one and a half tenths. in the end ibm could not get its yields up either, and in the summer of 2004 nvidia's consumer chips came back to tsmc, with the flagship following in 2005. after the pizza dinner, a 48-hour ultimatum after the 40nm yield failure nvidia demanded compensation, and then-ceo rick tsai insisted tsmc was not at fault and would not pay a cent; huang said that if they could not agree, they would go to arbitration. after morris chang returned in 2009 he spent half his time on this matter, talking for dozens of hours with everyone involved, then shut himself in with his staff to study it for a full three weeks. ‖ 科技這碗飯 科技這碗飯 黃仁勳 張忠謀 一生有你 英偉達和臺積電的激盪 年

they reached burntollet bridge, around 400 loyalists ambushed them — with off-duty b specials among the attackers — while the ruc stood by on the scene and did nothing. the episode showed something more clearly than the derry demonstration had: the armed force of the northern ireland state and loyalist violence were one and the same thing, and the marchers were both beaten and humiliated. h: looking for a co-founder is how you end up with the wrong one treat a co-founder as a precondition for starting up, and you usually end up settling for a ‘co-founder of convenience’. four solo founders explain from experience: run on your own first, and the right person shows up along the way. four solo founders' honest post-mortems — no methodology packaging, just the mistakes they made and the specific numbers. for founders currently agonising over whether to find a co-founder. founders agonising over whether to find a co-founder, and founders who have already started solo and want to compare notes with their own kind. solo founders 单人创始人 searching for a co-founder is how you get a bad one | 4 vc-backed solo founders solo founders co-founders retention startups sfp treat a co-founder as a precondition and you will settle julian says it plainly on the show: many people believe ‘you must have a co-founder to start’, so they treat finding one as a precondition for starting up — and that makes them more likely to end up with a bad co-founder. sfp's position is not anti-co-founder; quite the opposite, they think a good co-founder is fantastic. the problem is the order: having an idea first and then going to find someone to fill the slot, versus running first and meeting the right person, produce completely different outcomes. aldo is the latter — he worked through four different ideas before he met his current co-founder. julian a co-founder need not be a ceo and a cto aldo's current company is about ‘turning any computer into a data centre’. his co-founder was originally his angel investor, then volunteered to be his founding engineer, and only later was upgraded to co-founder. the two define the relationship unusually: they don't see themselves as ceo and cto but as ‘artist, producer’, switching roles whenever the company needs it. the detail shows the shape of a co-founder relationship can be custom-built — there is no need to force it into a standard template. aldo retention is growth, not an optimisation after growth the line aldo repeats is ‘retention is growth’. chai says aldo taught him which numbers to look at and what a smile curve is, lessons he still uses every day. more important is aldo's criticism of ‘growth is good so retention can wait’: when growth is good you feel you can ignore retention, but the moment growth stops you regret not having watched it. many founders, while growth is good, just pour on more spend and leave everything else to luck — and once luck is not on your side, you fall as fast as you rose. aldo pull on the thread, don't stop at the second-best answer chai first chose between two directions: travel and software reliability. because travel had an existing audience and distribution, he built an ai email client for travel first, and quickly found the direction extremely hard to scale. the second idea came from watching user sessions to find pain points, and that too proved hard to scale. he still isn't sure whether those ideas were ‘bad ideas’ — only that he didn't want to do them. eventually he went back to software reliability and made one key flip: instead of guessing top-down how customers will use your software, he has the software simulate every possible customer action and production scenario, turning reliability into a compute problem. chai tell real feedback apart from fake heat signals nemanja says the most important thing he learned at sfp was distinguishing which feedback is worth iterating on and which is just a misleading heat signal. his example is concrete: a twitter post getting hundreds or thousands of likes doesn't mean you should pay attention to it. if you have free users and free heat but no conversion to paying customers, you are running a free trend, not a business. every piece of feedback aldo gave him was the same question: what would make someone pay you 10x more? how do you make it worth 10x to a large enterprise? nemanja a co-founder failure can destroy everything nemanja saw a counter-example: that company had an excellent idea, a huge market, money from top investors, marquee customers — every condition was perfect — and it collapsed entirely because the co-founder was wrong, and the company shut down. much of the conversation he heard was ‘these things should have been talked through before starting the company’. that is what made him decide not to force a co-founder search. aldo's two experiences confirm it: at his first company his co-founder was his dad, he was 17, and the power dynamic was very strange; the second was with a close university friend who spoke at his wedding, but being too close made hard conversations hard, and the co-founders eventually split. nemanja you don't have to wait until you start to find people aldo's current co-founder is 20 years older than him and was originally his first employee. aldo says what excites him most is that someone far more experienced, who could have done it alone, chose to trust his vision. his  ‖ 單人創始人

h: ai is devaluing code; an engineer's moat is taste and accountability addy osmani, who leads chrome devtools, argues that ai has devalued writing code and that an engineer's real edge is taste and accountability — and warns against cognitive surrender, treating the ai's answer as your own. the methodology in the back half is worth a lot: cognitive surrender, loop engineering, and taste as a moat. frontend engineers, engineering leads, ai product managers, and any developer worried about being replaced by ai. the pragmatic engineer the pragmatic engineer from chrome devtools to ai engineering, with addy osmani chrome devtools ai engineering cognitive surrender taste as moat career change frontend the hard part of a closing keynote is not what to say but whom not to repeat addy ran multiple agents to gather every talk, summary and social post he could find from the preceding days of the ai world fair, and used that to sculpt his own closing keynote so it would not repeat points other speakers had already covered in depth. he says this kind of thing used to be nearly impossible, or would have taken an enormous amount of time; now it is entirely within reach. he describes running large parts of his daily life through agents as a coexistence of «fun and chaos». addy every framework claims to be simpler; only the same app can settle it in the era when angular, backbone and yui were all emerging at once, addy noticed that every framework claimed to make development simpler, yet there was no way to compare them directly. so he built the same to-do application, implemented it in each framework with a standardized feature set — that is todo mvc. the project quickly picked up thousands of stars and became the default example in many framework tutorials. later, apple's safari/webkit team reached out and they jointly developed speedometer, which today is the responsiveness and web-application benchmark maintained collectively by all the browser vendors. addy page load is not one metric but three moments for the user the chrome team broke «page load» out of its vague form and into key moments in the user's journey: is it happening, is it useful, is it usable — mapping respectively to metrics like lcp, fid/inp and cls. these metrics were not pulled out of thin air: they started from user research, then went through repeated validation with the standards community and with developers to confirm they really do correspond to how people judge a page's value. addy osmani treating the ai's answer as your own answer is cognitive surrender addy distinguishes cognitive debt from cognitive surrender: the former is the erosion of memory and comprehension that comes from long-term ai use; the latter is blindly accepting the ai's answer, treating its answer as your own, and gradually giving up critical thinking. he argues for avoiding that state — otherwise, when the agent gets something wrong, the engineer can only pray. to keep his own understanding intact, he insists on reading the final decision summary, and if there isn't one he asks the model to produce its decision process, while staying alert to the possibility that a model fabricates content when its context window is nearly exhausted. addy osmani an engineer's alpha is taste, and every model release shrinks it addy defines alpha as «edge», and says it decays with every model release. the software engineer's current alpha is taste: judging whether you are building the right thing, where to put your energy, and whether what you built is actually «good». an agent can judge whether something matches a spec, but has a hard time judging «good» — including whether the experience is delightful and whether users want to come back. even if future models close that gap, engineers will still be accountable, the way chromium's owners files make them accountable, for understanding the system and for gating and shipping decisions. addy osmani neatly structured writing may lose to rough, real writing video creator navi (neat code) publicly criticized addy's long piece on loop engineering as «abstract, like it was written by ai». addy acknowledges the piece was a first draft he wrote by hand, edited himself over several rounds, and finally handed to a model for a readability pass. he has always favored structured writing, but he is starting to suspect that what readers actually want may be rawer, imperfect writing that feels real. he also mentions michael novati: the piece that got criticized as «ai-like» was in fact one where he had used ai heavily; association and recombination. this inverts conventional content creation: rather than scripting in advance and having the ai perform the script, you set the situation and let the ai play it live, h: the hardest part of ai in hospitals isn't the model—it's making the hospital's ledger work suchi saria, whose sepsis alert was adopted by 90% of doctors, asserts: the obstacle for ai isn't model performance, but trust and financial accounting under prospective payment systems. why retrospective auc looks good but doesn't mean clinical usability, and how drg payments turn clinical benefits into the cfo's ledger—suchi saria explains it more clearly than most papers. medical ai researchers, entrepreneurs aiming to deploy in hospitals, and hospital cfos and clinical informatics officers deciding on such systems. nejm ai grand rounds nejm ai grand rounds dr. suchi saria on building ai that changes care medical ai sepsis alert healthcare payment ai deployment electronic health records startups publication isn't clinical success she warns this is the step most researchers misjudge. the 2015 science translational medicine sepsis prediction model looked great on retrospective data, but when actually deploying in the ed and wards, they found the data's veracity, completeness, and messiness were different; even the icd-10 coded ground truth used to measure quality was too noisy and could lead the team astray. to fill in ground truth, debiasing, transparency, outcome evaluation, and monitoring after deployment, she later did the equivalent of about 40 papers' worth of innovation, publishing only 20. suchi saria hospitals won't buy because of a good paper saria says there are many layers between a tool and making ai adoption a no-brainer for the healthcare system. first, prove the tool is 10x or 15x better than current practice and explain why; then turn the point solution into a platform covering multiple conditions; then partner with emr vendors to compress it integration to about 80 hours and go live within six weeks; then handle governance, monitoring, tuning, and even plan with the fda; only then do clinical outcomes and financial returns come into play. each step is a 'surprise' and a hill to climb. suchi saria software itself can be a treatment she holds a conviction: medical innovation shouldn't be limited to drugs and devices, but should also include software-only ai-based interventional protocols. these interventions don't assist with documentation but use the full emr's multimodal data to precisely answer 'when, for whom, what to do' and smooth the execution. she says this is a big opportunity to improve care quality because most ai today clusters around pre-visit transcription and post-visit coding, leaving the middle ground of actually 'caring for patients' almost untouched. suchi saria doctors actively use alerts if signals are accurate bayesian's 2022 nature medicine report scale: nearly 750,000 patients, two years, 4,400 clinicians, of which 2,200 were physicians. the key internal number is a 90% physician adoption rate. she says this isn't due to pop-up bombardment but signal quality: many old tools alert 95% of the time after the doctor has already initiated treatment, rendering them valueless; hers is designed with an early warning objective that identifies early, so doctors proactively click, enter assessments, and choose agree or disagree. suchi saria under drg, early rescue equals cost savings under drg bundled payment, a hospital receives a fixed amount for treating a sepsis patient. whether the stay is 20 days or 4 days, the extra 16 days of cost come out of the hospital's profit margin and occupy beds that other patients could use; if sepsis isn't identified at admission and documented as present-on-admission, medicare pays even less. suchi says for a 2,000-bed system, these missed detections accumulate into $30–40 million in financial penalties annually, so ai early identification is like giving money back to the hospital, making it easier for the cfo to say yes. suchi saria the hardest part is clinical trust, not technology asked which medical task ai will master in five years, suchi didn't list new algorithms. she said data quality and veracity are hard, but as an ai researcher, that part is most within her control; what she finds truly difficult is the sociotechnical layer: getting doctors to trust the output, and getting emr vendors like epic to make integration easier. in her view, the pain point in medical ai isn't that models aren't strong enough, but that the systems determining whether models can be used are never in the data scientist's hands. suchi saria clinical multimodal data remains a research blue ocean she says there is still a vast open field in academic research. she cites fda-funded translational safety research and the work of several phd students: the emr is not text plus images, but thousands of modalities, each with different missingness patterns, bias patterns, and interaction patterns; how to design architectures for this and how to validate generalization are unfinished problems. foundation model companies are pressured to do well on benchmarks, focusing on q&a over i

h: the illuminati died of infighting; the conspiracy theory was invented later the illuminati was an anti-clerical order founded in 1776 by a professor and five students, peaking at roughly two to three thousand members; it died of infighting and narcissism, and today's conspiratorial image comes from later books and hoaxes. the episode separates the real history from the conspiracy theory, and the second half traces the chain by which the illuminati myth spread — from robison's book to principia discordia to the letters column of playboy. worth hearing to the end. people working in media who want to understand how a conspiracy theory actually gets manufactured, and founders and investors attentive to recruitment mechanics and power structures. stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class adam weishaupt and the bavarian illuminati secret societies conspiracy theories the enlightenment illuminati organizational management information spread a school run by priests produced the man who turned on the church weishaupt was born in ingolstadt in 1748; both his father and his uncle fought the church's control over university teaching materials. after his father died, his uncle became his guardian — and sent him to a jesuit school. in his uncle's library he read french enlightenment philosophy, which laid down the intellectual base coat of his life: reason against dogma. he took a law degree at 20, became a professor at 22, and was dean of the law faculty at 27, the first non-jesuit to hold the chair in canon law in nearly a century — which he owed to his uncle's connections, not to his own credentials. he did not want to abolish the church; he wanted to replace it the historian stauffer's verdict on weishaupt is sharp: his motives were half credible and half not. his feeling for liberty and progress was genuine, but the appetite for power was in his nature, and the order he built was itself despotic. he broke with his uncle, quarreled with colleagues, meddled in other departments' affairs, and cast himself as a martyr for free speech. when he founded the illuminati, his real aim was not to overthrow the church's will but to substitute his own for it. that explains why the organization was later riven by infighting. from day one the illuminati was a recruitment scheme on may 1, 1776, weishaupt and five students founded the covenant of perfectibility, later renamed the illuminati. he had been unable to join the freemasons — he could not afford the dues and found the rituals ridiculous — yet he copied the masons in designing three ranks: novice, minerval, illuminated minerval. recruitment criteria included ‘wealth’. members had to hand over a list of the books they owned, a family tree, a list of their enemies, and a self-analysis, write monthly reports, and advance by bringing in new recruits — in essence an mlm-style secret society. the nobleman who saved the illuminati also brought the schism in 1777 adolf von knigge — nobleman, writer, freemason — joined, bringing social connections and a capacity for governance. he rebuilt the chaotic original structure into three broad classes and 13 grades, introduced promotion tests, rituals, and code names (weishaupt's was spartacus), and shifted recruitment from boys aged 15-20 toward mature, experienced men. by the mid-1780s membership is estimated at two to three thousand. but expansion also brought division and money trouble — the order had deliberately collected no dues to avoid exposure, and was later forced to charge them. one informer's letter made joining a capital crime utzschneider, who quit in 1783, wrote to the electress of bavaria accusing the illuminati of conspiring with austria to overthrow bavaria, and embellished the account by inventing dangerous beliefs for them. the elector first banned all unapproved societies, then in 1785 banned the illuminati by name. weishaupt was dismissed from the university, members were arrested, and material seized in their homes was treated as evidence of crime; rumors even had them involved in atheism, abortion, and rebellion. a third edict in 1787 made membership in the illuminati punishable by death. weishaupt fled to gotha, sheltered by a duke who had himself been a member. the conspiracy theory came out of a joke publication and a letters column in 1798 the scottish scientist john robison published proofs of a conspiracy, charging that the illuminati and the freemasons had plotted the french revolution. in 1963 kerry thornley and greg hill's principia discordia circulated as five photocopies, recasting the illuminati as a comic organization that charged for membership. in the 1970s robert anton wilson and others planted letters in playboy's reader mail column and answered themselves, painting the illuminati as an elite controlling the world and tying it to the kennedy assassination, hitler, and more. today's conspiracy narrative traces back to satire and rumor manufactured on purpose. an order that ca

h: orbit scores a one, recovery scores a zero: no middle state zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) reached orbit on its first flight but failed to recover the booster. deputy chief designer dong kai (董凯) argues a rocket launch has only success or failure, never a middle state: orbit gets a one, recovery gets a zero. what actually sets the pace of catching up is recovery-zone downrange distance, engine redundancy, and building a hundred engines a year. an exclusive post-mortem recorded immediately after the failed recovery, with the deputy chief designer walking through the recovery sequence, the point of failure, the production-capacity logic and the timeline for catching up. dense with information. people working in commercial spaceflight, rocket investors and engineers following reusable technology — anyone who wants the real engineering detail on zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) and a practitioner's read on the industry. what's next｜科技早知道 科技早知道 【重听】朱雀三号副总师：火箭回收只有成与败，没有中间态| s9e41 commercial spaceflight rocket recovery zhuque-3 methalox reusable rockets us-china space the first flight flew a stripped-down zhuque-3, not the full vehicle dong kai (董凯) describes zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) as a liquid oxygen-methane medium-to-large liquid rocket developed in-house by landspace (蓝箭航天). the full vehicle is 76 metres tall, with stainless-steel propellant tanks running 80% of the body's length, nine engines on the first stage and one on the second. the vehicle that flew was a ‘lite version’(青春版), shortened by roughly 10 metres, using the tianque-12a (天阙12a) with 83 tonnes of liftoff thrust; the full vehicle will use the tianqu-12b (天去12b), with thrust above 100 tonnes. on payload it can approach long march 5 (长征五号) while also covering the medium-lift class below it. recovery downrange distance was set at 390 kilometres for the first flight; at full payload it should be 550 to 600 kilometres. dong kai ‘china's falcon 9’ is high praise, but five years to surpass it is too optimistic on netizens calling zhuque-3 ‘china's falcon 9’, dong kai says that is very high praise. falcon 9 is the only reusable rocket in the world in operational service and it is extremely reliable: 150 launches, including one booster reused 32 times. but when musk said zhuque-3 would surpass falcon 9 within five years, dong kai will not be that optimistic. chinese spaceflight as a whole, across every vehicle type, runs about 80 launches a year; falcon 9 alone flies 150 in a year, which works out to three launches a week. he does not think one company, landspace, can get there on its own — the remark is more encouragement and a spur than a forecast. dong kai orbit is graded on three levels; recovery has only success and failure before zhuque-3's first flight, the flight plan graded orbital insertion and recovery separately. insertion was graded by perigee altitude into complete success, success and failure: perigee above 170 kilometres was a complete success, 130 kilometres was a success. recovery had a binary standard only — stand on the landing pad for one minute without falling over and it is a success; short of that it is a failure. the overall mission grade had four levels: only both orbit and recovery succeeding, with perigee meeting the target, counted as a complete success; succeeding at just one of the two counted as a basic success. in the end the first flight hit the orbital target and did not recover, so the launch director declared the launch a complete success (as to orbit) and the mission a basic success. dong kai holding recovery range down to 390 km throws away 2 to 3 tonnes of payload the downrange distance to the recovery zone directly determines the rocket's payload. after stage separation, the first stage coasts ballistically toward the recovery zone; fix the downrange distance and you have fixed the separation altitude. the full zhuque-3 corresponds to a 600-kilometre recovery range; for the first flight the range was cut to 390 kilometres for safety, dropping separation altitude from 76 kilometres to 66 kilometres — 10 kilometres less flying. every additional 10 kilometres of recovery range adds close to 150 kilograms of payload; pulling the range from 390 to 600 kilometres would raise payload by 2 to 3 tonnes. the first flight came down carrying 10 tonnes of propellant, which is exactly the price paid for safety. dong kai five engines at landing ignition are for braking, not for thrift the recovery sequence: after stage separation, the first stage coasts up past 130 kilometres, then turns tail-down. first ignition comes at 80 kilometres altitude, three engines firing together for about 40 seconds, to slow down and keep dynamic pressure from getting too high on entry into the dense atmosphere. engines shut down at 40 kilometres, ending the braking burn, and the vehicle enters aerodynamic control, using grid fins and strakes for trim. the final landing ignition happens at 4 kilometres. unlike falcon 9, zhuque-3 is configured with five engines here, capable of multiple rest ‖ 朱雀三號 董凱 朱雀三號 科技早知道 科技早知道 重聽 朱雀三號副總師 火箭回收只有成與敗 沒有中間態

h: north korea is not a nation-state, it's a religious society kim il-sung was not a stalinist but a third-generation christian steeped in 19th-century american evangelicalism; after overhearing a peasant believe he could walk on water, he decided to play along with the legend. the author spent 12 years writing a narrative history of north korea's origins, putting kim il-sung back into the context of missionaries, revival movements and a mother's dream. dense with information, but it demands patience. readers interested in north korea's origins, the relationship between religion and politics, or 20th-century east asian history; the author's own phrase is "the las vegas of korea": the best taverns, the best gisaeng, and street brawls — hundreds of men splitting into two sides and throwing stones at each other, deaths were common, and spectators came to watch. the missionaries said the locals' enthusiasm for this lethal sport was like our enthusiasm for baseball. it turned out to be the flashpoint. they prayed for revival and got collective loss of control presbyterians were famously strait-laced, nicknamed "the frozen chosen", and certainly never wanted this kind of emotional christianity. the 1907 "pyongyang revival" is one of the most famous christian revivals of the 20th century, but the missionaries had not expected to get this — the author says you could call it mass hysteria, and the missionaries themselves described it that way at the time. new converts who had believed for only two or three years rushed the pulpit and smashed their heads on the ground, confessing in public from murder and adultery to theft, confessing nearly every sin in the ten commandments. the wave swept from pyongyang across the whole korean peninsula and burned all the way to manchuria, with western church leaders flocking to watch. the missionaries eventually gave up trying to suppress it, saying it was probably god's will. the japanese didn't smash the churches, because they had to perform for the west when korean nationalism arose, its vehicle was the christian church. the reason is counter-intuitive: elsewhere christianity came with the gunboats, because the imperialist powers were basically western christian nations; h: cerebras hits 4400 tok/s on a single chip: inference speed is the moat cerebras pushes wse 3.5 to 4400 tok/s per chip, and the cs4 rack packs three wafers into a 120kw cabinet. the core argument: inference has to be split into prefill and decode, and speed is the moat. cerebras rarely opens up its system design to this level of detail. this episode gives hard numbers on rack power, interconnect latency and component reduction — useful for anyone trying to verify whether the sram inference approach actually holds up. founders tracking generational roadmaps in ai inference silicon, engineers making infra selection decisions, and investors following the openai supply chain. techtechpotato techtechpotato gpt-5.6 sol ultrafast.... just got ultrafaster (cerebras 4th gen) inference chips cerebras wafer-scale computing sram openai compute doubling performance did not wait for a new process node — they just cranked the clock rather than waiting for a new process node, cerebras clocked wse3 aggressively: frequency is close to double, so power is close to double as well. the company stresses this is not simple binning, but design optimization for voltage and frequency done with tsmc on the same n5 node. the previous generation's 125 petlops of sparse fp16 goes to 250 petlops, while the core count stays at 900,000 and sram stays at 44gb. physical yield remains close to 100% thanks to dynamically routing around defective cores, but parametric yield has always been the point outside observers question. three wafers in one rack turns the oddity into a standard form factor the old design was a 16u complete system with its own power delivery and liquid cooling for the single chip, leaving the data center side to do air cooling only. cs4 moves to rack scale: fans and power supplies on the front panel, and behind them a module called the backpack, with liquid cooling piped in from the top to the wafer chips mounted vertically. one rack holds three wafers; the author estimates from the number of power supplies roughly 40kw per wafer and roughly 120kw for the full rack, which sounds like the same class as nvidia's nvl72. this is not a spec flex — it is about fitting wafer-scale into a standard data center form factor. making io a swappable module means what they sell is really a rack platform networking per chip doubles from the previous generation to 2.4tbps, and the io modules are designed to be replaceable: if 800g/200g/100g or other interconnect standards need supporting later, you swap the module instead of redoing the system. the backpack is also compatible with future wafer sizes, because the wafer is already at its physical limit and the power and liquid cooling interfaces are broadly similar. the author's read is that cerebras is effectively building a rack-scale platform, which is why they can say cs5 will follow in the second half of 2027. the bulk of the openai revenue comes from chips that do not exist yet wse3 runs at roughly 2300 tok/s on models that fit entirely on a single chip; wse 3.5 reaches 4400 tok/s. gpt-5.6 sol currently runs at 750 tok/s, and close to 1500 tok/s on the new chip. ceo andrew feldman says explicitly that while deals like the openai agreement do include near-term supply, the bulk of the revenue comes from future chip generations — which makes a platform product like cs4 the key to fulfilling those orders. the previously announced openai partnership corresponds to roughly $20 billion in revenue, and that was the growth story told at ipo. capacity is constrained by custom machined parts, not by the wafer itself the first-generation wafer-scale system used a large number of custom machined parts because volumes were small, pushing infrastructure costs far past any reasonable level. cs4 cuts component count by half, possibly by 60%, and automates heavily so the production line can ramp — capacity has been a recurring question on earnings calls. the line the author was given: the new-generation system will cost more than the previous one, but they would not say how much more; s: 2026-08-19-witness-加拿大三万人大搬迁-最好的事与最糟的事
h: thirty thousand canadians moved: the young were saved, the old lost everything from 1954, nearly thirty thousand people in newfoundland, canada, were moved from remote fishing villages to towns. the younger generation gained education and a way out; the old and the inuit lost their homes, scattered until there was no way left to reach one another. resettlement has no single verdict. nine minutes of oral history, with both the concrete detail of people who lived it and archival recordings of the premier. the information density is not low — good for anyone who wants to understand quickly what «modernization by relocation» costs. policy researchers and local officials working on urbanization, regional development compensation and indigenous resettlement, plus anyone running community rebuilding projects. witness history witness history canada's controversial resettlement programme urbanization resettlement newfoundland oral history regional policy community collapse a village that cannot support a school and a hospital should be emptied out from 1954 the canadian government launched a large-scale resettlement programme, aiming to move nearly thirty thousand people from several hundred coastal communities (outports) in newfoundland and labrador into designated growth centres. the official logic was modernization: these remote settlements could not sustain modern education and health care, and only concentrated settlement would bring roads, schools and electric light. the episode makes clear at the outset that the process would run for more than two decades and would completely transform a way of life that had lasted for centuries. katherine harvey no power and no road meant, in the government's eyes, no modern life don white, who lived through it, grew up in port nelson on newfoundland's east coast. the early life he describes sounds like another era: one grocery store for the whole village, no electricity, people living off moose, rabbit and seabirds and off salmon and lobster fishing; his grandfather had a schooner that crossed the bay each year to bring in vegetables for the winter. the nearest hospital was an hour away by boat, and the road system consisted of footpaths. these details are not nostalgia — they are the premise for understanding the motive behind resettlement: in the government's view, this kind of life could not supply the basic conditions a modern citizen needed. don white four children rowing themselves to school forced the decision to move don white's schooling was the most direct catalyst for moving: the family lived on the south side of the harbour and the school was on the north, so four children had to row an open boat across the harbour themselves, with no adult along; in winter the harbour froze over and the only option was an hour's walk around it. the whole school was a single classroom, with at most 22 pupils across all grades, and it closed after grade six. he says plainly that the family decided to move precisely so the next generation could get a decent education and decent opportunities. that chain of reasoning turns «resettlement» from an administrative order back into a family choice. don white industrialize or perish — but the government decided where you could go the chief architect of the plan was joseph r. smallwood, the premier at the time. in his own words: newfoundland had to industrialize or it would perish; and on an island where even elementary education was hard to guarantee, people could not possibly acquire the skills industry required. in a private recording he also stressed that resettlement was not a way of shedding a burden — the government set a condition: it would help you move, but the destination had to be approved, because it absolutely did not want people jumping «out of the frying pan into the fire». that double framing shows resettlement was both an idealistic theory of development and a form of conditional control. joseph r. smallwood six hundred dollars could move a house, not a fresh start resettlement was not free of charge. the government gave each departing household a grant of 300 dollars, later raised in steps to 400, 500 and 600 dollars. to save money, islanders invented their own way of moving: they fitted their houses with runners and hauled them by rope and cable all the way to the water's edge, even rolling an entire house — stove, table, curtains and furniture included — onto a raft and floating it along the coast to the new home, with no machinery, all by human muscle. the other side of that ledger: many people found no way forward once they reached town, and instead crowded into cramped quarters and faced unemployment. the subsidy could cover the move, but it could not cover the risk of starting over. resettlement saved the young and ruined those who only knew fishing not everyone benefited. one interviewee in the documentary (edward) called it the worst thing he had been through: he had no skill other than fishing, and was reduced t

h: ai giants' earnings look like enron: the compute bubble backed by nvidia ai executives no longer talk tech, only money and gigawatts. nvidia props up customer revenue with investments and guarantees, playing financial engineering like enron—but not yet illegal. two hardware veterans dissect nvidia's and openai's financial maneuvers using the enron analogy, dense with information, ideal for those wanting to see inside the ai bubble. investors, tech journalists, and hardware enthusiasts focused on the ai bubble and semiconductor financial engineering. better offline better offline the ai clown car w/ gamersnexus ai bubble nvidia enron financial engineering data centers compute executives no longer talk tech, only money steve burke points out that jensen, lisa su, sam altman, and other executives now rarely discuss any technical details on podcasts and tv—it's all tens of billions, hundreds of billions, trillions in tam and gigawatt numbers. previously, they appeared only at major keynotes and then vanished for six months; now they show up frequently but only talk finance. ed adds that even lisa su, once considered pragmatic and not given to marketing stunts, now sounds like she's huffing paint when she speaks. steve burke compute pricing is far below cost steve reveals that oracle rents h100 gpus for about $4 per hour, but according to oracle insiders he's spoken with, just the operating cost (opex) to run an h100 is over $6 per hour, not even counting depreciation. long-term contracts are cheaper: oracle's h100/h200 contract price for openai is just over $2 per hour. at that price, even at full utilization, it would take ten years to break even, with a gross margin of only 30%—worse than running an airline. steve burke nvidia's financial engineering resembles enron steve breaks down nvidia's financial maneuvers: it never borrows money itself but instead invests in customers or guarantees their debt. for example, it invested $1.5 billion in sb energy and guaranteed the data center's value at $10.8 billion once built. if openai can't lease out capacity, nvidia covers the difference. it also helps coreweave secure revenue by committing to purchase compute from them, while jensen's foundation rents compute from coreweave. these moves stay within legal bounds, but they resemble enron's spvs to offload bad debt—except nvidia is smarter, never becoming a direct creditor. steve burke jensen dodges the bubble question when axios asked jensen whether this is a bubble, he paused noticeably and chose his words carefully, saying a bubble will come someday, but not now—rather in five to ten years. he used a word starting with b; ed thought he was going to say 'bubble,' but he said 'build out.' steve also notes jensen said compute should become an investable asset class, even traded like a commodity. ed sarcastically remarks that's like treating gpus in a warehouse as a separate asset class for tax purposes. ed zitron the pr scam of data centers generating their own power ed mentions the trump administration's push for data centers to generate their own power, ostensibly to prevent residential electricity rates from rising, but trump said at a meeting that 'data centers need good pr right now.' steve points out that energy is a hazardous material and cannot be deregulated, and that ai practitioners severely underestimate the difficulty of power. he also notes that gas turbines, meant for emergency backup, are now being run around the clock as primary power for data centers, causing them to wear out prematurely. steve burke openai's surveillance dream ed contrasts microsoft's recall feature, shelved due to strong user backlash, with openai's high-profile launch of a similar feature, with sam altman saying ai can watch everything you do. steve adds that smart tv manufacturers are collecting massive amounts of data, even using acr technology to capture screenshots of users' screens, currently analyzed by humans but eventually intended for llm automation. this kind of surveillance use is exactly the ideal customer for openai and anthropic, but steve doubts that if such an efficient surveillance tool existed, someone would have already bought it. ed zitron the absurdity of mandatory ai use in companies ed shares a friend's experience at a major game company: internal policy makes ai use part of the job, and not using ai counts as dereliction of duty. management requires employees to figure out how to make ai help them do their work and then report back to h: chinese laborers shaped the us customs: modern border control originated from the chinese exclusion act customs, visas, and passport systems were not inventions of europe and america but were born in the late 19th century when chinese immigrants flooded into the united states, prompting the need to screen and exclude. the paradox that legal immigration is hard while illegal immigration is easy persists to this day. this episode uses a historian's work to overturn the common sense that 'immigration control originated in the west,' and through cases such as the chinese exclusion act, indentured labor, and the natal model, it explains the mechanisms of institutions and power. for chinese-speaking listeners interested in immigration, customs systems, global history, and foucault's theories, especially those concerned with how modern states control populations through documents and permits. 忽左忽右 忽左忽右 493 追忆历史学家亚当·麦基翁：华人移民与现代边境制度的形成 mckeown immigration history chinese exclusion act global history foucault customs system chinese immigrants shaped the us customs system in 'the melancholy order,' mckeown argues that the global modern customs and immigration control system was not established by white european immigrants, but developed in the late 19th century when a large number of chinese immigrants poured into the united states, as the us needed to determine who could enter and by what standards to classify them. in a striking phrase, it was chinese immigrants who shaped the us customs. this system then spread globally, so chinese immigrants played a key role in the formation of modern border control, thereby also refuting eurocentrism in immigration history. cheng yanliang foucault's concept of power runs through the immigration system mckeown is deeply influenced by foucault: power is not top-down and concentrated in the state, but exists in everyday details and operates in a network. when immigrants apply for visas, they are required to provide various certificates and materials; this disciplinary mechanism and knowledge discourse precisely reflect the operation of power. yang bin points out that the immigration system is full of absurdities and paradoxes. for example, when applying for a student visa, regardless of whether you actually intend to return to your home country after graduation, you must check the box stating that you will return; otherwise, the visa officer will directly reject you. the system appears to operate between legal and illegal, but it is actually riddled with paradoxes created by power. cheng yanliang the chinese exclusion act established national immigration sovereignty mckeown analyzes the chinese exclusion act of 1882, pointing out that its most important aspect was establishing the unilateral jurisdiction of the receiving country. previously, the authority of the sending and receiving countries was unclear; the chinese exclusion act placed the decision-making power in the hands of the united states, thus giving rise to the distinction between passports and visas today: a passport is an identity document provided by the home country, while a visa is decided by the receiving country whether to accept. in the modern international system, the decision-making power over immigration control ultimately rests with the receiving country—this is the key conclusion drawn from the chinese exclusion act. cheng yanliang illegal immigration is easy, legal immigration is hard the us immigration system has a paradoxical outcome: about 10 million low-educated illegal immigrants make up 5% of the us labor force and have long been able to stay due to lax enforcement; conversely, highly educated non-immigrant talents often have to wait years in line to apply for a us green card. the system ostensibly encourages free immigration, but in reality it is centered on screening and obstruction. this absurdity, contrast, and paradox is what mckeown calls the 'melancholy order.' so-called free immigration is merely an invention and imagination of the modern state; immigration has always been defined, classified, and filtered by the state. cheng yanliang indentured labor replaced black slavery in the mid-to-late 19th century, as the abolitionist movement surged in the western world, a labor vacuum appeared on the plantations of the new world. contracted chinese laborers emerged as substitutes for black slaves, known as 'selling piglets.' chinese laborers in the us typically earned about $30 per month, and after deducting living expenses, could send home $80-100 per year; at that time, the average annual income of chinese farmers was only $8-10, a difference of about tenfold. it was this economic drive that fueled the wave of emigration from south china in the late qing dynasty. a case in point is sun yat-sen's elder brother, sun mei, who started as an indentured laborer and later became a large rancher owning 6,500 acres. cheng yanliang passports came before id cards after the united states and the west establish ‖ 忽左忽右 忽左忽右 追憶歷史學家亞當 麥基翁 華人移民與現代邊境制度的形成

h: you can't make a kid want to work: structure and consequences beat enthusiasm building a work ethic doesn't run on making a kid enjoy the work. it runs on three things: rules that structure the household, privileges tied to responsibilities, and the sense that someone is counting on him — plus, when needed, letting him take his own fall at school. an encore episode with moderate information density, but two judgments are worth taking away: a kid will not come to want the work just because you want him to do it; and extrinsic motivation and letting your kid fall on his face are both entirely legitimate. parents with a 10-15 year old at home who are stuck on a kid who won't get started on chores or homework; also educators who want to understand how a work ethic actually forms. ask lisa: the psychology of raising tweens & teens ask lisa 285: encore: how do i help my kid develop a work ethic? parenting teen psychology intrinsic motivation responsibility family structure you cannot make a kid want to work, only make him do it rena's near-reflex on hearing the letter was "this kid is only 11" — though she also admits that at 11 she hated being asked to do things just as much. lisa's verdict on this parent is that she's half right: the instinct that the kid should be doing more is sound, but "we can't make them want to do it." she then breaks a work ethic into three sources. some people care intensely whether the adults are pleased — in the research that's more often girls than boys. some do the work because the work itself suits them. the boy in this letter has neither going for him: he isn't bothered by his parents being annoyed, and his interests run entirely to reading and screens. so stop fighting on the ground of getting him to want it, and work on the ground of him having to do it anyway. lisa damour interest cannot be assigned; a kid has to collide with it where does intrinsic motivation come from? lisa offers two known routes. choice: when a kid gets to pick, motivation runs high. and interest, which cannot be required — only encountered. she describes a type she sees often in clinical work: a kid who coasts through school with his parents feeling like they have a foot on his neck, then hits one class in 11th grade that lights him up, and from that point can throw himself at it completely. she likens the encounter to a chemistry problem — the kid has to run into the thing that matches him. so this book-loving boy is not short on intrinsic motivation; his motivation simply has nothing to do with chores right now. rather than pushing him to fall in love with cleaning the chicken coop, start by accepting that he won't. lisa damour if you can only have one, structure beats warmth lisa cites the baseline finding from family research: kids do best when both warmth and structure are high. but when researchers compared the configurations 14 different ways, structure won the trade-off — kids in homes with structure and no warmth turn out "okay," and better than kids in homes with warmth and no structure. in daily terms: a kid looking thoroughly unhappy because he's been told to do something is a perfectly acceptable outcome. what matters is that the parent holds high expectations, stays predictable, and follows through. lisa puts it bluntly: it's fine for your kid to be mad at you, as long as what you're doing is fair — "our expectations are high and we're going to hold you to them." that runs directly against the parental instinct to wonder whether you've done something wrong. lisa damour lock in homework habits while the work is still easy fifth and sixth grade, when the coursework is still light, is precisely the window for establishing homework habits. lisa's advice is a fixed time and a fixed place, and her reasoning is practical: by the time the work gets hard, you want the routine to already be automatic. when a kid dashes something off, a parent doesn't have to demand a polish job, but should hold out for a decent job — so he first learns what it feels like to do work well. practicing on the easy things is what makes it possible to carry that into the hard things later. she even concedes that some families get through the middle school years on exactly the foot-on-the-neck approach. that isn't a parenting failure; but as he saw it, fort dufferin was nothing more than a hornets' nest, and he was not prepared to spend the lives of large numbers of his soldiers on a fort that could only be taken by frontal assault. so for the next two days the 19th indian division worked forward step by step through the wrecked houses of the city, while night patrols kept probing the walls for weak points. the tactics shifted here from assault to siege, and what followed proved the choice a sound one. douglas claverdon the siege did not go smoothly: the boat crossing the moat sank parked under trees at the roadside, the bbc van recorded an infantry company advancing under enemy fire while it waited for another company to work around from the left. the recordist says he spent most of the time lying underneath the van, wishing he had a steel helmet. on the night of 16 march the 15th punjab tried to cross the moat by boat and get into the fort, but one boat sank, drowning the leading troops of the second wave; h: the sultan came to her: tétouan's woman governor was no pirate sayyida al-hurra governed tétouan for more than twenty years, built shipyards and worked with ottoman privateers against spain and portugal; european sources call her a pirate, while recent scholarship treats her as an example of early decolonial practice. the middle stretch untangles pirate from privateer, and shows how the standpoint of the surviving sources shapes the history — a payoff beyond the biography. the listener mail at the end is skippable. content writers working on north african and mediterranean trade, or interested in case studies of women governing; if you are short on time, listen only to the middle section on privateering and skip the mail at the end. stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class sayyida al-hurra, moroccan queen morocco pirates and privateers ottoman empire women rulers maritime history her title meant noble, powerful, independent — not pirate the episode opens with its most important judgment: european sources compress sayyida al-hurra's whole life into the word "pirate," but the label cannot account for the full picture. sayyida al-hurra is an honorific, literally carrying senses like "noble, powerful, independent," and it was used for other muslim women as well, among them the twelfth-century yemeni ruler arwa al-sulaihi. she was probably born somewhere between 1485 and 1495; her father was ali ibn rashid, a prince of sharifian descent, and she grew up in the multiethnic community of chefchaouen, fluent in arabic, spanish and portuguese. tracy v. wilson the city she governed was a fortification and a refugee camp at once chefchaouen was built in the rif mountains, roughly 60 kilometers from the coast, precisely to defend against portuguese incursion after portugal took ceuta in 1415. in the same era, spain conquered granada in 1492, ending the reconquista, and issued the alhambra decree that same year expelling jews; muslims were then required to convert or leave in 1502 and 1526. chefchaouen and tétouan consequently filled with muslims, jews and converted muslims (moriscos) fleeing the iberian peninsula, forming refugee communities that were diverse but not entirely equal. tracy v. wilson her governorship came from her brother's appointment, not from inheritance in 1510 she married mulay al-mandri, the governor of tétouan — a political marriage joining two families and two parts of the region, chefchaouen and tétouan. because she was educated, she was able to assist her husband in governing from the start, and when he traveled her share of the rule was gradually formalized. her husband died around 1519 and his brother wanted to seize power, but her own brother ibrahim, serving as vizier in fez, named her the successor. it was not common for a woman to hold that kind of power, yet she appears to have won the trust of the population and was accepted as governor. tracy v. wilson her ships guarded the coast and also captured spanish and portuguese vessels facing continuous pressure from portugal and spain, and a moroccan economy in decline as european shipping routed around africa, she worked with the ottoman privateers oruç reis and hızır reis (often lumped together as "the barbarossa brothers"). the two were sons of a potter from lesbos, first served a sultan's son, later were hired by algiers, and ultimately served the ottoman empire. she built shipyards where the ottomans could construct and berth ships, and she also expanded her late husband's fleet; those ships both defended morocco and attacked and captured spanish and portuguese ships, with captives held at tétouan awaiting ransom. tracy v. wilson if holding captives for ransom counts, elizabeth i was a pirate too holding captives and demanding ransom from their home country cannot on its own be the line that makes her a pirate, because the practice was fairly common at the time. the episode notes that oruç was once captured by a knightly order and freed when his brother hızır paid the ransom; spain and portugal were also kidnapping and enslaving people in africa. the scholar jason idris sparks goes further in his paper and draws an analogy between her and elizabeth i: elizabeth likewise employed the privateer francis drake and eventually knighted him. for these rulers and for the barbarossa brothers, the motive was largely to defend muslim territory and to strike back at the attacks on muslims on the iberian peninsula. tracy v. wilson she would not go to fez, so the sultan came to marry her in 1541 the sultan of fez, ahmad al-wattasi, proposed marriage to her. by convention a sultan's bride would travel to fez for the wedding and remain in the capital, but sayyida al-hurra refused to leave tétouan; the sultan had to go to tétouan himself for the wedding, and afterward she stayed on as ruler. as the show puts it, "this was not at all how it was usually done." the marriage was political, comparable to ferdinand and isabella unitin

h: science is not a warehouse of answers but a structured inquiry into ‘what we don't know’ science is not a warehouse of facts but a structured interrogation of what we do not know; failure is the normal condition and uncertainty is the hallmark. what the public really needs to learn is how to ask a good question. the opening small talk runs long, but the second half — on uncertainty as the mark of real expertise, and on the bind that assessment puts science education in — is worth the time for working scientists and educators. research administrators, science educators and technology investors — anyone who has to judge whether a high-risk direction deserves a bet; and scientists who get pressed by students and the public on what science actually rests on. sean carroll's mindscape mindscape 364 | stuart firestein on how science relies on ignorance and failure science education scientific method uncertainty pseudoscience philosophy of science pluralism science class teaches the conclusions and never the science itself sean opens with a view he has held for a long time: science education is like an art class that only shows you the masterpieces and never teaches you how to mix paint, or a piano class that plays recordings and never teaches fingering. students get f=ma, rock classification and natural selection drilled into them, and then get examined on how well they remember. but the daily reality of science is failure, surprise and not knowing. the public misreads how science works precisely because school never shows the process, only the results. sean carroll ignorance is not a hole in science, it is the fuel firestein named his two books against intuition: ignorance is what drives science, and failure is the reason science succeeds. at a conference, scientists talk only about what they don't know; nobody stands up to present what is already established. every known fact drags ten new questions in behind it. failure is the normal condition, and because science deliberately gives up authority and demands evidence, infallibility is not part of a scientist's job description. the public, meanwhile, sees science as a stack of answers — the misconception most in need of correcting. stuart firestein the scientific revolution began by deliberately manufacturing ignorance the first move of the scientific revolution was to manufacture a great deal of ignorance on purpose and rebuild from a blank slate. firestein quotes bacon: truth used to come from authority, and from that point on authority came from truth. bacon also invented the experiment — cutting a slice out of nature, controlling the other variables, and putting one small piece of nature to the question. but nobody foresaw that most experiments would fail; failure was written into the genome of the scientific method from the start. stuart firestein the scientific method is after-the-fact rhetoric, not how the work is done the ‘scientific method’ is firestein's main target: no scientist actually works through the hypothetico-deductive checklist, which is just elegant rhetoric applied afterwards. hypotheses are cheap, you use one and throw it away; what matters is imagination and creativity. he also doesn't believe in serendipity — when a nobel laureate calls it an accident, that is false modesty. somebody who was not in that position doing that work would never have stumbled into that discovery; you have to already be hard at work before an accident has any chance of hitting you. stuart firestein intuition is best at producing errors that look correct firestein illustrates counterintuition with a body-disposal trick a magician friend taught him: bury the corpse eight feet down, and bury a dead dog at four feet. police and cadaver dogs dig, hit the dog, and call off the search — intuition says it is just a pet grave. our intuitions manufacture high-quality errors of exactly this kind all day long, and scientists are no exception. being counterintuitive means digging a little deeper, and not letting a result that happens to look beautiful turn into a paper too early. stuart firestein the more certain a claim is, the more likely it is pseudoscience the demarcation problem has never had a precise solution in the history of philosophy. firestein offers a practical test instead: the difference between science and pseudoscience is that science is uncertain and pseudoscience is certain. someone who always has an answer and never changes it is not to be trusted; a real expert concedes uncertainty precisely because they can see the holes, the competing theories and the missing data. pseudoscience, for its part, is happy to borrow ‘scientifically proven’ as a selling point. stuart firestein optimism is an invention of science, not a temperament optimism is not a word about mood but a philosophical position, and it was only coined by voltaire in 1759. firestein argues that science invented this kind of optimism: for the previous 250,000 years human beings could only accep
