h: the boston tea party was not a tax revolt — it was the fallout from a london financial blowup the boston tea party was not a tax revolt sparked by heavy burdens on north america, but a self-rescue in which a london financial crisis was passed on to north america through the leverage of the east india company — one blowup at the imperial center that finally lit the fuse of colonial revolution. a history-of-thought episode that cuts in through a financial-crisis story: it lays out another layer of causation behind the boston tea party, and uses burke's choices on three fronts — north america, india, france — to force you to weigh anew the old binary of radical versus gradual. for managers choosing between radical reform and gradual improvement, and for chinese intellectual readers who treat anglo-american conservatism as a ready-made answer but have never read the original texts. 忽左忽右 忽左忽右 491 埃德蒙·伯克的保守主义与渐进改革思想：从北美、法国到英属印度 history of thought conservatism british history finance and politics radical vs. gradual the boston tea party was not a tax revolt the chain behind the boston tea party lies not in north american tea taxes but in the london financial storm around 1772. some bankers shorted the east india company too early, blew up their own positions and fled, dragging down a large batch of small london financial institutions with them; the east india company's cash flow tightened in turn, with roughly two-thirds of its tea sitting in the warehouses. the solution britain devised was to divert the tea to north america for clearance sales, and on the surface it looked perfectly balanced: it freed the east india company and preserved a symbolic tea tax. but what north americans saw was not the price of tea — it was londoners once again using the colonies to fill in the pit of their own financial crisis. one act of self-rescue at the imperial center thus became the fuse of north american independence. burke lived inside exactly such an empire where everything was tangled together: trouble in far-off india had to be resolved by shipping to north america on the other side of the globe. burke was not a thinker but a commons politician burke was later placed in the history of political thought, but jiang yuan reminds us: he was essentially not a cloistered thinker but an irish-born member of the british house of commons. as a young man he went to london to study law, then switched to politics, served as secretary to the marquess of rockingham, and entered parliament through a rotten borough controlled by the party leader. the burke we read today is overwhelmingly not academic works but parliamentary speeches and letters to his bristol constituency. two great undertakings marked his career: one was promoting anglo-american reconciliation, the other was leading the impeachment of warren hastings, the first governor-general of india. precisely because he was this kind of practical politician, his writing never pushes ideas to extremes and always weighs real difficulties and concessions — this is both why he became a symbol of conservatism for later ages and the filter we should remove when rereading him: he was a man who made judgments, not a prophet who wrote systems. an mp is not a loudspeaker for his constituency the north american colonies insisted they had no representation in the british parliament, but londoners had their own account: the house of commons operates on virtual representation — an mp does not represent the gains and losses of some district or place, but by independent judgment acts for the whole kingdom, colonies included. burke's attitude toward this is honestly embodied in the bristol episode: as the mp elected by the bristol constituency, he voted in favor of a free-trade bill that damaged bristol's port monopoly, and wrote that what benefits britain will ultimately benefit bristol too. in his view, representation is not carrying the constituency's voice into parliament, but representing the whole nation through one's own independent judgment as a gentleman. the people of bristol understood this logic and promptly replaced him at the next election; he then returned to a rotten borough with almost no voters and carried on as an mp. whether this logic counts as democracy is another question, but it at least challenges an intuition — representative government need not be realized only through one-person-one-vote territorial representation. the east india company's double standard was the real institutional evil burke's impeachment of hastings was aimed on the surface at one man, but in fact at the double standard of a system. the east india company was both a company and half a government ruling india: when you ask it to bear governing responsibility for famines and for deaths by the tens of thousands, it says it is only a company and making money for shareholder dividends is enough; but turn around and it has an army, can fight and sign treaties with this time, for her son who is now 13, they signed a "digital citizen" contract a year before the phone, spelling out the risks and benefits and the developmental behaviors required to earn one: come to your parents when you see problematic content, hand it over when asked, no sneaking around. on his 13th birthday the son hadn't met the conditions, and the phone really was delayed a year. lisa distills this into "yes, when" rather than "no": what the child sees is concrete behaviors that lead to permission, not a refusal he can never argue his way out of. nadine burke harris a phone isn't all-or-nothing — just remove the browser when lisa's daughter turned 13, her older sister had just left for college and the two needed a private channel to talk. she gave her daughter an old iphone with no browser, no social apps, and no ability to install apps without permission — a machine that could text, take photos and play music. she notes: the browser is where a lot of the trouble happens; and listening to music is teenagers' number-one way of regulating emotion, so confiscating the phone wholesale confiscates their most important emotional outlet along with it. "phone" is not a singular concept; it can be broken into different combinations of permissions. lisa damour stand beside your kid, not across from your kid lisa stresses that the most common wrong frame is: i'm scared, so i'll stand between my child and technology and become "me vs. my child's craving for tech." the real frame is "kid, you and i together against the harm technology can do." facing an imminent phone ban at a school, she told the students directly: the bad guys are not your interests — it's that technology is designed to be so compelling that it erodes the education you came to school to get; so students and the school fight for education together, rather than the school policing students. that narrative, which puts teenagers and adults on the same side, is more useful than the ban itself. lisa damour rules come third: respect first, then reasons lisa shares her order for setting rules with teenagers: enter with respect first, acknowledging that the device is tempting; then give reasons, laying out your worries and the data; only then set the rule; and finally expect pushback, without taking it personally. kids are allowed to be angry and to express anger, but they are not allowed to emotionally abuse their parents for disagreeing with a rule. she points out that rebellion itself is an opportunity: use the conflict to teach your child "how we treat each other when we disagree." this order turns rules from a power contest into a discussable family matter. lisa damour what

the whole company should vote he turned hiring into a four-step funnel: the first step is not hr screening resumes, but the system selecting seven or eight employees with similar backgrounds from across the company to vote, with options from strong yes to strong no — this avoids any one group becoming a bottleneck and replaces a single person's taste with averaged judgment. the actual funnel: 17% of applicants advance to a phone interview; after the phone interview about half get a take-home; the conversion rate from onsite to offer must stay at least 25%. the phone interview doesn't test specific skills but three things: judgment, horsepower and agency, and he tries to design ai-resistant assignments, such as the gpu kernel minimum-cycle challenge anthropic has used. max hodak annual 360 reviews should become a monthly re-vote the annual 360 review, he thinks, is a low-feedback, high-trauma ritual. the replacement is an internal mechanism called eigenreviews: every four to six weeks, randomly have colleagues answer the same question — "knowing how this person has performed since, would you still vote to hire them today?" weave the answers into a company-wide graph, then recursively weight it after the fashion of eigenvector centrality — people everyone endorses should have their votes count more. to prevent collusive voting, each run drops out a random subset of edges over a thousand rounds; if the scores come out bimodal, that suggests a possible voting clique that needs human investigation. the feedback lag drops from a year to about a month, and the annual hr process goes away with it. max hodak what decides life or death isn't the technology, it's the weekly iteration rate the convergence point of the whole piece is one sentence: iteration rate separates the winners from the losers. if you can accumulate one useful lesson a week while your competitor manages one a month, that competitor will never truly threaten you; h: smashing threshing machines won 252 death sentences, and the workers still lost nineteenth-century english farm laborers smashed threshing machines to protest unemployment, and got 252 death sentences, 481 or 505 people transported to australia, and the limited parliamentary reform of 1832 — the workers' fate unchanged, the political map redrawn. this episode links enclosure, the poor law and machines replacing labor into a single causal chain, and the trial numbers are far more brutal than the usual narrative. high research density, suited to anyone who wants the historical version of "technological unemployment." founders, policy researchers and podcast listeners focused on technological unemployment, modern british history, and "what happens after the machines get smashed." stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class swing riots agricultural revolution technological unemployment british history parliamentary reform machine breaking poor law the threshing machine was only the last straw; enclosure was the root enclosure in england began in the twelfth century and peaked after 1750; between 1770 and 1830 roughly six million acres of common land were enclosed. people who lost grazing rights and the right to cut fodder either went to the cities to find work or lost their livelihood entirely with no compensation, left dependent on the farmers who owned the land. unlike the usual "machines cause unemployment" narrative, the episode lays out the institutional dispossession first: enclosure, a labor surplus after the wars ended, the corn laws, and reform of the poor law. the threshing machine was just the straw that broke the camel's back. one machine took half a winter's income threshing was the autumn and winter farm work of separating grain from the ear, done entirely by hand with a flail before machines appeared. it was not just physical labor; it could account for fifty percent of a farm worker's winter income, and in winter there was almost no other way to earn money. though people tried to build threshing machines as early as the seventeenth century, it was not until the 1710s that water- and horse-powered models became reliable and cost-effective. once a landowner bought one, the hand threshers were out of work. the more efficient the machine, the more directly it hit seasonal unemployment — that was the economic root of the threats and the riots. machine breaking was not a luddite invention machine destruction as a form of protest in britain goes back at least to the seventeenth century. in 1675 london spitalfields weavers smashed new looms that "could do the work of twenty men"; in 1779 three hundred of samuel nead's knitting frames were destroyed. the luddites pushed this pattern to its peak. supporters argued that in the long run machines would lower prices, expand demand and increase employment, but that did not help the people unemployed right then; another often overlooked reason was that machine-made goods were of lower quality. for artisans who depended on the guild system, none of this was abstract economics — it was whether they ate. captain swing on the threatening letters was a signature, not a person the swing riots take their name from the signature on threatening letters, captain swing. unlike ned lud, who was built into a legendary leader during the luddite movement, captain swing had no organizer persona; he was simply the author of the threatening letters. the letters threatened that "if you don't put up your threshing machines, you will have a swing" — swing meaning both the sway of the gallows and the swing of the flail at threshing. the actions were not purely smash-and-grab either: demonstrators would first negotiate with landowners and parsons, and some landowners smashed their own machines or agreed to raise wages and refund tithes to avoid greater losses. the workers' spokesman was a royalist who had opposed reform william cobbett was initially a royalist who denounced the french revolution, opposed democratic reform and supported enclosure. after buying a farm in 1805 and traveling around in person, he saw the destitution of agricultural laborers, admitted his earlier views had been wrong, and turned to vigorously advocating parliamentary reform. but he was not simply a spokesman for laborers: his thinking included racism and antisemitism, and he yearned for a romanticized england that had never actually existed. this contradiction meant that later he condemned arson as an "abominable crime" while insisting the root cause was extreme poverty — the government did not arrest him for nothing. the real violence happened in the courts, not the fields the uprising swept southern and eastern england, with at least three thousand incidents. the government did not wait for the regular assizes but set up special commissions to try people quickly. between december 1830 and january 1831, 252 people were sentenced to death, though only 19 were actually hanged; h: llms are not autocomplete, they're our cognitive cousins llms are not fancy autocomplete but ‘cognitive cousins’ that share core cognitive principles with humans: attention mechanisms recapitulate production systems, prediction is the dominant training signal; sample efficiency is off by three to four orders of magnitude, but an architectural tweak could close the gap. high information density; the main value is putting llms into cognitive-science mechanisms and comparing them item by item, rather than stopping at behavioral comparison; the second half's judgments on consciousness, moral status and education are also directly quotable. researchers working on model mechanisms and alignment, investors trying to judge whether llms have human-like cognition, and founders who care about how ai will rewrite the next generation's education. sean carroll's mindscape mindscape 363 | chandra sripada on how llms and humans are cognitive cousins cognitive science cognitive cousins production systems dual-process theory predictive coding llm mechanisms llms are not autocomplete, they're humans' cognitive cousins sripada offers two competing explanations: llms may just be fancy autocomplete, a statistical approximator; or the prediction training signal may be strong enough to compress the core principles of human cognition into the weights. he clearly leans toward the latter, calling prediction ‘the mother of all training signals.’ this choice determines everything that follows: if it's just autocomplete, behavioral similarity is mere imitation; if it's a cognitive relative, then llms' psychological effects and architectural features are worth studying as evidence about the human mind. chandra sripada human psychological effects emerge spontaneously in llms sripada lists a string of phenomena that reliably show up in human experiments and all appear in llms: the difficulty of center-embedded sentences, garden-path sentences, similarity interference, the recency/primacy/middle-loss effects in serial memory, continuity and temporal asymmetry, and disjunctive vs. conjunctive search in visual search. these effects are not hard-coded through prompt engineering; they emerge spontaneously as the model predicts the next word. he stresses that one cannot stop at counting behavioral similarities—the key is mechanistic analysis, which is exactly the starting point for explaining the transformer with production systems later. chandra sripada system 1 is the weights, system 2 is the context kahneman's dual-process theory splits thinking into two systems: system 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive; system 2 is slow, serial, controlled. sripada argues llms give a clear correspondence: in-weight processing is like system 1, in-context processing plus chain of thought is like system 2. this correspondence turns psychology's fuzzy dichotomy into a hypothesis that can be tested against transformer mechanisms. chandra sripada llms supply the mechanism dual-process theory was missing sripada points out that dual-process theory in cognitive science is often criticized as ‘a list of adjectives’: one is fast, automatic, effortless, the other slow and dependent on working memory, but with no mechanistic content. llms help fill in the mechanism: in-weight and in-context are actually a continuum with clear poles at either end. for a simple prompt like ‘michael jordan plays basketball,’ the weights already contain most of the response and no complex structure needs to be built in activation space; for a prompt like ‘einstein is german, gandhi is indian, so madame curie is?’ the task structure must first be constructed, making it vulnerable to interference. chandra sripada conditional rules model the human mind better than step-by-step instructions compare two ways of programming a robot to make tea: traditional fetch-execute is step-by-step instructions—‘walk into the kitchen, pick up the kettle, fill it with water’—and it collapses when it hits an unwritten situation like ‘someone put ice cubes in the kettle’; a production system is a set of conditional rules—‘if the kettle is empty, fill it; if the water is cold, boil it; if the water is hot, pour the tea’—making judgments based on state representations, and is therefore far more robust. cognitive scientists have long felt production systems model the human mind better than itemized instructions. this setup points directly at the transformer's attention mechanism. chandra sripada the transformer is actually a production system sripada translates the transformer's core mechanisms into production-system language: attention heads are continuous conditional rules—‘if the key matches the query, add the value’; mlp units are similar, where the rows of the first matrix are features and, if they match the residual stream, the features of the second matrix's columns are added. 99% of the computation in a transformer is dot products, i.e. ‘a match scalar times a vector.’ this structure was invented independent

the median professor spends 60% of time on research leave and actually teaches very little; research funding is $1.3 billion, with 80 professors contributing more than 95% of it — 1.5% of the faculty carries the vast majority of the research, while other professors produce nothing and still enjoy research leave. he asks: when research output is concentrated in the hands of a very few, how should a university explain how it spends its money? ben sasse death shatters false idols and forces attention back to real relationships he says the core of his faith is sin, grace and gratitude; the diagnosis did not shake his faith but made him calmer. he describes death as ‘the last enemy, not the final word’ — enemy means it should not be cooperated with, not the final word means it does not hold the last decision. treatment side effects like vomiting and bleeding made him realize that death is a truth injection: it shatters false idols such as workaholism and online flame wars and forces attention back to real relationships. ben sasse he hates pancreatic cancer but would not go back to before the diagnosis he hates pancreatic cancer and would not wish it on anyone; but he would not go back to the stage of not knowing ‘the power of pancreatic cancer prayer.’ for the seven weeks before the diagnosis, he was in severe pain all night, every night, running hot water on his spine in the shower, crying out to god. his prayer practice is not mystified: the family prays aloud daily, and he personally follows a structure of worship, confession, thanksgiving and petition. he says all life carries a terminal diagnosis, and that relationships — with god and with the people you love — are what matter most. ben sasse asked heaven or hell, the right answer is both he defines the present as an economic revolution set off by a technological r

anyone building content, education or political products will see their own position in it. founders and product managers in content, education and political communication: this episode makes clear what you are using to replace long-form reading; investors can reassess the scarcity of attention. the gray area with sean illing the gray area we’re postliterate postliteracy attention economy education political communication media theory walter ong we read more than ever, but can't get through long texts rose distinguishes the literacy crisis from postliteracy: a literacy crisis is a breakdown in fundamentals like decoding words and understanding short sentences, whereas postliteracy is text no longer serving as the primary channel for information, news, entertainment and cultural connection. the problem, she says, is not that people "can't read," but that they read so many short fragments every day that the time once reserved for long, complex texts is squeezed out; retirees, college graduates and women — historically the groups that read the most — are collapsing at the same rate. rose horowitch linear argument is not innate; literacy gave it to us in orality and literacy, walter ong records soviet researchers' tests on uzbek peasants: literate peasants could answer the syllogism about what color polar bears are, while illiterate peasants refused to reason on the grounds that "i have never been to the north." rose notes these experiments have not always replicated since, but ong's larger judgment holds: literate cultures value linear argument with evidence and rebuttal, and that way of thinking does not exist naturally in purely oral societies. rose horowitch reading rates fell for twenty years, and reasoning fell with them the mechanism cognitive science offers is that the brain gets good at whatever you practice over time. the less you read, the less background knowledge you have, the lower your tolerance for long texts, and the more difficult and unpleasant reading feels. rose cites research showing that american adults' ability to solve logic puzzles, analyze patterns and reason has declined over the past twenty years alongside reading rates — the brain is simply adapting to what we no longer ask it to do. rose horowitch schools are personally accelerating the exit of long reading on the education side, surveys of middle and high school teachers show only 0 to 4 books assigned per year, with classrooms increasingly using short informational excerpts to prepare for standardized tests; 80% of elementary school teachers say students receive a school-issued tablet or chromebook before they even start kindergarten. the effect carries into university: professors have to teach students how to read, how to recognize irony and metaphor, before they can teach content. schools are both responding to the trend and personally accelerating the exit of long-form reading. rose horowitch trump will not be the last postliterate president rose says trump is the first postliterate president: he speaks and contradicts himself as if there were no historical record, leans heavily on repetition and emotional language, and introduces people with fixed epithets like "sleepy joe" and "crooked hillary" that are nearly homeric. media theorists long predicted such a figure would appear — short video and social media algorithms reward simple, inflammatory, memorable expression — so trump will not be the last. rose horowitch the brain isn't broken, and attention can be trained back neuroscientists told rose there is no permanent change or damage to the brain; if you want to, you can still retrain sustained focus. she offers one concrete sample: after the dallas, texas school district banned phones on campus, library checkouts were 200,000 books higher than the year before the ban. she also notes that paper books make it easier to reread and remember than ordinary digital devices, because readers have a spatial sense of "which page the content is on." rose horowitch socrates feared writing would destroy memory, and he was right facing the objection that every new technology provokes panic, rose responds with plato's phaedrus: socrates worried that writing would destroy memory, making people "think they know" without truly internalizing anything. her rereading is this: later generations often use this example to prove the worry was overblown, but looking back, socrates and plato were right — no one today can recite the iliad or the odyssey from memory. still, lit

the next day disney stock plunged 10%, fox, time warner and discovery were all sold off, and viacom fell more than 20%. over the following 11 years disney's stock was essentially flat while the s&p 500 rose 3.5x — the market's expectation for disney's future cash flows never grew again. this was the public signal that the pay-tv bundle model had peaked, and the direct motivation for disney's later rushed pivot into streaming. david streaming is a worse business than the cable bundle to fight netflix, disney terminated its content deal with netflix, giving up hundreds of millions of dollars a year in pure profit, and built disney+ itself. ben points out this directly violates disney's "fewer, better" flywheel strategy: streaming requires a constant supply of new content, its cost structure is completely different, and if it fails the disney brand is damaged while the netflix brand isn't — because "the netflix brand is just the button you press when you want to watch something," and audiences hold different expectations of the two. he says flatly that the streaming business is worse than the cable tv bundle: users can cancel anytime, acquisition and retention costs are high, content production is expensive, and there are no second-run windows. ben fox was the worst of the four acquisitions in december 2017 disney announced an all-stock acquisition of fox's entertainment assets for $52 billion; h: a ram bow sinks its own destroyer: the new warship class born of a torpedo boat that cost 1% as much in 1908, a 380-ton destroyer was rammed and sunk by a 10,000-ton cruiser in an exercise, killing 35 men. behind the tragedy: torpedo boats upended naval warfare at 1% of a battleship's cost, and the destroyer was the answer. the analogy ‘torpedo boat = today's drone’ is worth a lot; the engine telegraph evidence in the wreck and the unsolved question of the turn make this episode's military history unusually concrete. naval history enthusiasts, people working on unmanned systems and asymmetric warfare, and anyone with a product or investment lens on how cheap platforms disrupt expensive ones. dan snow's history hit history hit the naval revolution: triumph and disaster naval history destroyers torpedo boats asymmetric warfare shipwreck archaeology unmanned systems one torpedo boat cost enough to sink a battleship the arrival of the torpedo worried the royal navy deeply: a battleship could be sunk without building another battleship. the episode uses today's drones as the analogy for this asymmetric threat — a torpedo boat cost roughly 1% of a battleship and could close on a capital ship at night and fire its torpedoes. this changed the rules of naval war: where sinking a battleship had once required big guns trading broadsides with big guns, now a small platform could do it. britain therefore had to find a new countermeasure in both cost and numbers. the destroyer was a ship type forced into being by the torpedo boat to chase down and intercept torpedo boats, the royal navy put out tenders to shipyards in the 1890s: whoever could build a fast ship making 30 knots would get into the fleet. tiger was a product of this new type, with four normand boilers producing about 6,400 shaft horsepower, 86 tons of coal, and a hull crammed full of weapons and machinery. the type was first called torpedo boat destroyer, later shortened to destroyer, and it became the backbone of the 20th-century fleet — escort, anti-submarine, anti-aircraft — down to today's guided-missile destroyers. the faster a ship ran, the more easily she broke down later tiger had a crew of only 57-58, with extremely cramped living space; she was called a very wet ship, pitching in heat, vibration and bad weather with poor seaworthiness. the bridge was completely open, with no radar, gps or radio; at night navigation relied on compass and dead reckoning. more brutally, there was an inside joke in engineering circles at the time: the faster a ship ran on her speed trials, the more prone she was to breakdowns later, because running at full speed did structural damage to the hull. this was the product of the navy pushing men and equipment to the limit. the 1908 night exercise was preparation for germany the april 1908 exercise was not a show. an ‘attacking force’ of more than ten destroyers set out from portsmouth, slipped through the home fleet in the dark, simulated torpedo launches with flashing signals, and proved it could get close without being detected. it was conducted with all ships darkened and no moonlight, because there was no radar or radio and scouting was entirely by eye; destroyers could also deploy quickly along the coast and take on intelligence gathering. this training was seen as necessary preparation as war drew near — the german fleet was already strong enough. no one knows why she turned to port that night on the night of the accident, tiger was ordered to follow the leading ship, hms recruit, but in the darkness could see only the wake ahead. no one has ever explained why she suddenly turned to port and cut across berwick's track. dave's personal judgement is that they simply never saw berwick — had they seen her, they would not have crossed in front of a giant ship bearing down on them. that night there were many large ships, dense manoeuvring and total darkness, and the accident was almost unavoidable; years earlier tiger had nearly collided in a similar exercise. dave a ram bow built to kill the enemy cut open a friendly ship berwick displaced about 10,000 tons; tiger was 380 tons light and 425 tons full load, a mass difference of 20-25 times. more ironic still, berwick's bow carried a ram designed specifically to sink enemy ships, a ‘weapon of the future’, yet in a peacetime exercise it sliced into a friendly ship like a hot knife through butter. the two sighted each other with only about 100 yards to spare, leaving no time to react in a matter of seconds; court politics, economic warfare and the siege of antwerp all come through clearly. the drawback is that the information density isn't especially high, with the weight concentrated in the middle and later sections. listeners who want to understand elizabethan court politics, how the anglo-spanish cold war turned hot, and where the dutch/belgian border comes from; especially suited to those who like big history told through one person's fate. the rest is history the rest is history 695. elizabeth i vs the catholics: the shadow war (part 5) elizabeth i anglo-spanish war philip sidney dutch revolt economic warfare 16th century the person the queen trusted least was the perfect courtier at the 1581 tournament philip sidney was the star of the field: born into england's most elite web of connections, and already a poet and courtier famous across europe — astrophil and stella is reckoned second only to shakespeare's sonnet sequence. but elizabeth never really trusted him, finding him too well connected, too independent, too aggressively protestant; keeping him at court to entertain the french marriage embassy was closer to an insult. that same year, in a tennis-court quarrel, the earl of oxford called him a puppy, and the queen herself reprimanded sidney for forgetting his station. he was not knighted until 1583, at the age of 29 — for a "perfect courtier," the lateness was itself a snub. the dutch-belgian border was drawn by this war around 1585 parma had recovered most of the southern low countries for spain, with ghent and then brussels falling, and the rebel cause looked about to collapse. four great rivers formed a natural dividing line: the northern provinces eventually held off spain and became the 17th-century dutch republic of protestantism, capitalism and rembrandt; the south returned to the habsburgs and catholicism and, two and a half centuries later, became belgium. this shadow war between england and spain also happened to decide the borders of the low countries on today's map of europe. drake and sidney were both waiting for the war that had to come drake, back from his circumnavigation, bought four grand houses, sat as an mp, served as mayor of plymouth, and even legislated on the cod trade — and was bored out of his mind. sidney had been master of the ordnance since 1583, responsible for england's defensive preparations. both were like churchill in the 1930s, convinced that a life-and-death war with spain was closing in, and both were militant protestants by faith. their mutual admiration was no accident: one wanted a real war, the other wanted a kindred spirit. by 1585 the war had actually arrived. with orange dead, the dutch revolt nearly collapsed on 10 july 1584 william of orange was assassinated at delft, crying out as he died, "god have mercy on me and on this poor people." he was the symbol, the spirit and the military leader of the dutch revolt; with him gone, the rebels nearly fell apart. opposite them stood parma, the most feared commander in europe — both governor of the netherlands and commander of its army, capable in diplomacy and in war. when he took over in 1578 the spanish army was on the verge of collapse; by 1584 he had recovered almost the entire south. france, paralysed by the war of the three henrys, left philip ii finally free to act. antwerp wasn't taken by an army, but by a bridge antwerp was the largest, richest and most strongly protestant city in the low countries. parma began the siege in june 1584, and its core was a floating bridge nearly half a mile long cutting the scheldt. the dutch sent fireships packed with explosives to blow up the bridge; they did destroy a section and kill 800 spanish soldiers, but parma repaired the bridge before the gap could be exploited. when the rebels attacked again in may, the tide swept their own fire ships back onto their own lines. the siege lasted 13 months, and antwerp fell on 17 august 1585, with more than half its inhabitants leaving. elizabeth sent troops for trade, not for protestantism three days after antwerp fell, elizabeth signed the treaty of nonsuch with the dutch rebels, sending 6,350 infantry and 1,000 cavalry and — unusually — agreeing to subsidise the war effort. she had not suddenly turned militant: philip ii had imposed an embargo on english shipping in may 1585, and if antwerp fell into spanish hands the whole trade artery of the low countries would be throttled. she demanded three ports be handed over as cautionary towns garrisoned by english troops, ensuring control of the scheldt es

h: the undersea cable is becoming the world's largest listening network: not spies, physics distributed acoustic sensing (das) turns ordinary fiber into a continuous vibration listener: oil and gas well surveys, earthquake monitoring, whale tracking and anti-submarine ship detection all run on the same technology chain, and the ocean is rapidly losing its privacy. dense with numbers and a complete technology-evolution chain, tracing one line from wellbore to whale to submarine; but it only covers what has been achieved, without working out the business math or economics, so don't expect investment analysis. investors in undersea cables and the ocean-sensing sector, engineers working on earthquake monitoring or underwater target recognition, and policy researchers concerned with maritime security. asianometry asianometry the dark fiber listening network dark fiber distributed acoustic sensing ocean surveillance earthquake monitoring maritime security the scattering that makes the sky blue is also the source of the eavesdropping light attenuation in fiber comes mainly from scattering. brillouin scattering is produced by low-frequency phonons (triggered by temperature or strain), raman scattering comes from molecular vibrations and the latter is often used for temperature measurement; but the most prominent is rayleigh scattering — light reflected back by density fluctuations smaller than its own wavelength. these fluctuations act like tiny mirrors scattered throughout the entire fiber, reflecting a small fraction of the light back the way it came. rayleigh scattering transfers no energy and does not change frequency; it is the reason the sky is blue and the source of every das signal: both the later otdr and das are picking up this reflected light. polarization sensing failed because there were too many causes to attribute in the 1980s otdr was commonly used to find fiber breaks: send out a pulse of light, measure the arrival time of the rayleigh backscatter echo, and thereby locate the break or high-loss point. in 1981 aj rogers of the uk's central electricity research laboratories proposed polarization optical time domain reflectometry, hoping to infer temperature, strain, acoustic waves and other external factors from polarization changes; but in the 1980s this path failed — there were too many causes of polarization change to attribute a specific change to a single factor. the rayleigh signal is the sum of all fluctuations along the entire fiber, the signal is over-averaged, and temperature sensing could not be done either. the industry then turned to raman and brillouin scattering: weak signals, but their stokes/anti-stokes frequency shifts correspond definitively to temperature and acoustic strain. what commercialized das was not the navy, but oil wells three breakthroughs turned rayleigh backscatter from a diagnostic tool into a sensing method: narrower-linewidth lasers (purer light), compute capable of sampling tens of thousands of times per second, and a clear commercial need. the us navy did some early work, still half-classified today; what truly broke das into commercialization was the oil and gas industry — in the mid-1990s oil companies began using fiber to monitor wellbores. downhole temperatures are around 200°c and pressures up to 2,000 bar, a harsh environment where any electronic device wears out; the fiber approach puts all the sensitive equipment on the surface, with only cable downhole. what fiber vsp won was not accuracy, but speed the oil and gas industry first used raman scattering and the anti-stokes signal for distributed temperature sensing (dts), then in the late 2000s applied rayleigh-scattering das to vertical seismic profiling (vsp). traditional vsp relies on a downhole geophone array, stringing about seven geophones at a time and re-deploying after each survey, slow and expensive; the fiber approach has a signal-to-noise ratio slightly below wired geophones but already very close, and the killer application is speed: minutes in some cases, versus 10 hours for the geophone approach. the early challenge was data processing — das can generate up to 10,000 times the data per second of an ordinary temperature sensor. seismic stations are too expensive to deploy; dark fiber is already laid two teams, at berkeley and stanford, applied das to earthquake monitoring in the early 2010s. traditional seismic stations are costly and cannot be deployed at scale; meanwhile telecom and tech companies have laid vast amounts of unused dark fiber, which ajo-franklin of berkeley lab estimates at about 1 million kilometers globally, with another 100,000-200,000 kilometers added each year. these cables float freely underground rather than being fixed, and earthquakes are extremely low-frequency signals that are hard to distinguish from the noise of cars and trains; but they successfully tracked over a hundred small earthquakes both on campus and in the field, some with epicenters as far away as mexico.

h: changing your life isn't swapping beliefs, it's moving out of the casino you built yourself you are not an independent subject standing across from the world; you are a product jointly constituted by your environment, your body, and your symbolic immune system. to change your life, you have to change beliefs, action, and world at once — not just force yourself to "think it through." it upgrades "change your environment to change the person" from aphorism to mechanism, from the womb to the nation-state, with the casino and the algorithm as the same people-making machine. a clear entry point if you don't know heidegger; veteran readers can fast-forward to "co-immunity." founders who want to change themselves by changing environments; product and content people swept along by algorithms and feeds; engineers curious about sloterdijk or heideggerian thinking. philosophize this! philosophize this! episode #251 ... you must change your life, pt. 2 - the worlds that make us sloterdijk environmental shaping symbolic immunity base camp co-immunity you don't look at the world — you are part of the world sloterdijk does not think a person only starts being trained at the moment of birth. in the womb, you and your environment are already shaping each other; birth merely extends this co-constitution outward — climate, neighborhood, family all take part in constituting you. this unsettles modern people's handiest self-understanding: that i am an independent subject standing across from the world, and the world is a neutral object. his claim is: you are not the thing that looks at the world, you are part of the world, and the world is part of you. so there is no pure rational subject who first thinks things through and then decides; you have always lived inside a relational network already saturated with meaning. stephen west heidegger got it right, but he left out space the same casino can be seen two ways. abstractly, it is a space full of neutral objects; the slot machines, the lights, the free drinks are just being used. seen heideggerianly, the moment a person walks in they encounter a practical network already laden with meaning — the slot machine is a "chance to win," the free drinks are "hospitality," the vomit-colored carpet is an "invitation to indulgence." sloterdijk thinks heidegger's step is right but incomplete: heidegger emphasized time, and what he wants to add is space — in his own words, his trilogy should be called "being and space," not "being and time." stephen west a habit you can't quit isn't weak willpower, it's the casino you live in the third view is the most radical: the casino as a whole is a people-making machine. the lights, the sounds, the win-then-lose cycle all train you to stay inside periodic behavior; the casino stays open 24/7 precisely because it doesn't want you to leave. sloterdijk wants you to carry this question to every environment: this room you're in now, the feed you scroll every day, the algorithm you feed, are likewise training you while being trained by you. so "i can't kick the bad habit" is not weak willpower — it's that you've been living in a casino all along. to change, you can't change only beliefs; you must change beliefs, action, and the world you're in at the same time. stephen west symbolic immunity is both armor and an excuse to avoid change as a being exposed to threats, a person has only two kinds of response. one is to strengthen coping capacity: physical strength, health, emotional awareness, professional skill — last episode's anthropotechnics is this route. the other is to build immunity: beyond biological immunity there is symbolic immunity — identity narratives, funeral rites, meditation, religion, aesthetic practices, even humor can serve as "spiritual armor." but the same symbolic immunity is a double-edged sword: it can be a defense system that lets you truly face trauma, or it can be used to block out every shock that might force you to change. the key is how you use it. stephen west humans naturally live in an upward-climbing vertical tension sloterdijk observes that a great many shared practices are arranged vertically: music school from zero foundation to virtuoso, a craft from apprentice to master, taekwondo from white belt to kicking through six boards in one strike. behind this is an anthropological fact: humans naturally organize themselves around the gradient of "better/worse, mastery/incompetence," living in a kind of "vertical tension." this doesn't have to mean running for congressman; h: dna repair is the secret to a long life: bowhead whale repair proteins are already in human trials research shows that in nearly half of hospitalised covid-19 patients, dormant viruses in the body were reactivated, with higher inflammation and cell damage a year later; and what long-lived animals like the bowhead whale have in common is not tumour-suppressor genes but stronger dna repair — drugs for it are already in human trials. both stories challenge the intuition that disease comes from outside invaders: the real enemy may be something asleep inside the body, and repair capacity may matter more than natural gifts. medium information density, worth a listen. researchers focused on the clinical mechanisms of long covid, r&d staff and investors in anti-ageing drug companies, and general readers who want to tell scientific evidence apart from supplement marketing. nature podcast nature podcast briefing chat: is dna repair the secret to a long life? whales and mole-rats offer tantalizing hints long covid dormant viruses dna repair anti-ageing human trials bowhead whale some viruses are never cleared, only held down over a lifetime a person is infected by a great many viruses, but as long as the immune system is healthy, most infections are defeated. some pathogens, however, are never fully cleared — they quietly lie dormant in the body, held in check by a healthy immune system. once immunity is weakened, they resurface; many of the complications seen in people with hiv, for instance, are caused by reactivation of dormant viruses. researchers therefore wondered: could a severe infection like covid-19 also weaken the immune system and wake dormant viruses, becoming a source of long covid? this hypothesis determines what has to be tested next. charmani nearly half of hospitalised patients had old viruses revive, but causation is unsettled the team looked back at covid-19 patients hospitalised in 2020 and 2021, testing blood samples, nasal swabs and lung fluid for reactivation of common viruses. nearly half showed viral reactivation. after a year of follow-up, these people had higher inflammation levels, stronger immune-cell activity and more cell damage. but the study did not directly diagnose long covid, and it is only correlational: covid-19 may induce stress that triggers reactivation, and reactivation may then amplify the inflammation covid-19 caused, forming a loop; or reactivation may simply be another symptom of immune exhaustion rather than a cause of long covid. a phase 2 clinical trial is testing antivirals against herpesviruses, on the reasoning that if the reactivated viruses are themselves harmful, the therapeutic target should shift to those reactivated viruses. charmani dna damage is not just carcinogenic — it is upstream of ageing dna damage can mean a change in a base pair (a, c, g, t), or a change in the chemical structure of the base itself, such as the addition of an oxygen atom. it is not only the cancer-causing mutation people worry about. dna damage is strongly correlated with ageing and is thought to underlie hallmarks of ageing such as inflammation, cellular senescence and mitochondrial dysfunction. conversely, long-lived animals such as naked mole-rats and bowhead whales tend to have outstanding dna repair capacity; bowhead whales live past 200 years and rarely get cancer. so researchers wondered: can we transplant their repair mechanisms to extend human healthspan? charmani the repair protein works when moved into human cells and fruit flies too last year the podcast reported a clue from the bowhead whale: a protein called cold-inducible rna-binding protein (cirbp), linked to extremely strong repair of dna double-strand breaks. double-strand breaks are the most destructive form of dna damage. the bowhead whale's rare cancer seems to stem mainly not from the usual tumour-suppressor genes but from this repair capacity. more importantly, putting the protein into human cells and fruit flies works just as well, showing it does not depend on the whale's special environment. the question thus shifts from ‘why do they live long’ to ‘can we transplant this mechanism’ — and that is the most tantalising part. charmani boosting only one repair system can sometimes make things worse it is far from that simple. enhancing human dna repair is an old problem, and the difficulty is that there are too many systems: about six major repair systems, which interact, overlap, and sometimes one system needs the product of another. when only one of them was boosted in the past, the effects seen were very limited, and sometimes it made things worse. so you cannot simply say ‘just switch the repair genes on’. we are still at the stage of figuring out how these species work, and of trying experiments in petri dishes. charmani the hope for longer life is in human trials, not supplements on the shelf the same team moved from bowhead whales to rodents: beavers can live 10 to 12 years, while mice may live only a few.

h: her studio contract locked her weight: gain and you're in breach, diet and you're dead in the 1920s, the actress molly was benched by her studio for gaining weight and ended up on an operating table; in the 1990s, the bride mary died from the diet drug fen-phen. when the body becomes a commercial asset, punishment and shortcuts lead to the same place. the dual narrative uses specific cautionary tales the weight of fame: a hollywood tragedy hollywood body standards diet drugs business ethics contract clauses medical risk the contract locked down her body in 1920s hollywood, the big studios controlled production, distribution and theaters, and treated actors as assets on the balance sheet. molly's contract specified working hours, exclusivity, and one special clause: as long as she wanted to work, she had to keep the same bodily contours forever. when her body changed naturally, the studio invoked the "facial and bodily disfigurement" clause, treated adolescent weight gain as breach of contract and stopped her pay. the contract gave commercial power a legal basis to intervene in the body — that is the foundation of the whole episode's narrative. the ultimatum: slim down or you're out production manager al rockett summoned molly and delivered the ultimatum: you can get as fat as you like, but the studio won't use you until you get down to the "correct size." at the time molly weighed only about 20 pounds more than the average screen actress of her height. she wasn't indulging herself — she was a teenager still growing, and always hungry. but 1920s aesthetics demanded the pencil-thin flapper figure. the punishment cut off her income directly and forced her to comply. a twelve-week deadline to lose weight the studio gave molly twelve weeks to restrict calories and fit back into her old costumes. in the industry of the day, lila lee drank only orange juice and lost eight pounds in under two weeks, and vilma banky had to lose fifteen pounds before she was hired. the press publicly humiliated molly's "solid flesh," even inventing a rumor that she wanted to lose weight by catching influenza. fans wrote letters of protest, but the studio was unmoved. what this shows is systemic pressure: not one person's judgment of her, but an entire industry's standardization. the diet black market: from tapeworms to thyroxine the 1920s "diet craze" spawned a flood of dangerous products: laxative chewing gum, slimming corsets, soaps claiming to dissolve fat. more extreme still were swallowed tapeworms, and rido fat, an over-the-counter drug containing concentrated thyroid extract — in 1926 a dieter who overdosed on it quickly developed heart disease and died at 33. molly tried and still couldn't fit into her costumes, so she turned her gaze to surgery. surgery: ten pounds of fat cut away molly found the star surgeon robert griffith to perform a lipectomy. the doctor made long incisions at her hips and legs, scraped away about ten pounds of fat, then pulled the skin tight and stitched it. anesthesia was primitive, there was no penicillin, and open wounds were highly prone to infection; two years earlier a woman in paris had developed gangrene after similar surgery and had her leg amputated. after the operation molly looked slender, but was so weak she needed crutches. she satisfied the studio, but paid with her health and her comeback. millions of fen-phen prescriptions after lawyer alex macdonald took on mary's case, he discovered millions of fen-phen prescriptions being written every year, meaning millions of people — the vast majority women — were sitting on a medical time bomb without knowing it. mary had taken it for only 23 days, and the damage was already permanent. the mayo clinic later confirmed dozens of cases of a rare heart condition linked to fen-phen, and the fda pulled the drug in september 1997. the companies chose to conceal the risk reports they received in order to protect profits. not vanity — the decisions were rational tim harford's conclusion is that molly's and mary's decisions were not vanity or naivety, but entirely understandable. molly's employer was the source of her income and demanded she get thin; mary's specialist recommended fen-phen to her. they trusted people who seemed to know what they were doing, and ran into a ruthless commercial logic. technological shortcuts persist today: glp-1s have real health benefits, and brazilian butt lifts can kill. we treat body diversity as a bug rather than a feature, rewarding fast visible change regardless of the cost. tim harford molly o'day must hold the same silhoue

policy researchers who want to understand how the us export control toolbox actually works. chinatalk chinatalk the fcc's new robot rules robotics export controls supply chain fcc us-china tech the covered list is not a sanctions list, and the fcc can't change it alone the fcc's covered list is not the same as the ofac sanctions list or the bis entity list: the fcc has no authority to update the list itself. another national security agency or an interagency body must make a determination first, and only then can the fcc update and enforce it. devices on the list cannot get import or marketing authorization. the fcc doesn't just regulate spectrum and broadcasting — nearly every electronic device that emits radio frequency must pass fcc certification before it can be imported, marketed, or sold. that little fcc logo is the tool, and it's also the switch that can cut off new models at the border. adam chan robots are the only bet that hasn't taken shape yet adam sorted the fcc's recent covered list actions into categories: undersea cables, telecom, and drones all have clear industries and demonstrated impact, while mobile robots are still a very early industry. his read is that there are good reasons to see this action as staking out position five years ahead of time. the driver is the lesson from telecom networks in 2019 and 2020 — at the time, us domestic telecom networks depended almost entirely on huawei and zte equipment, forcing a large-scale rip-and-replace. the us government's thinking now is: don't let the same thing happen again in a critical industry like robotics. adam chan a crude rule moves faster than a finely tuned one facing the charge that this is too blunt, adam's response is that simple, even dumb, rules are often the best rules. it avoids two things — naming specific entities, and the whack-a-mole problem that comes with writing complex definitions and long transition periods; at the same time it sends a strong signal to the market, drawing in capital and investment. he also acknowledges the tool will cause collateral damage, but argues it can be patched afterward: the drone definition was initially very broad, and a later determination exempted toy drones; the robot determination also builds in a conditional approval process that lets companies apply for exemptions. adam chan the real risk isn't not being able to buy — it's not being able to build at all the host raises a sharp counterquestion: the choice may not be ‘chinese robots vs. american robots’ but ‘chinese robots vs. an american robot ecosystem that doesn't exist at all.’ adam's answer has two layers: first, the cheapest and easiest moment to fix supply chain dependence is now, and the longer you wait, the more commercial incentives lock the dependence in; second, the covered list generally only affects new models, which amounts to a transition period of several years, not a sudden cutoff. his evidence: after the drone action there has already been more than five billion dollars of investment, over a million square feet of manufacturing capacity, and thousands of jobs; in routers, where there were originally zero domestic us manufacturers, dozens of companies have now committed to expanding production. adam chan research use and teardown practice both get carve-outs the rule builds in several categories of exceptions: imports and sales for us government use are unaffected; small-batch imports for product development can also continue. adam mentions a specific scenario — some us counter-drone companies import foreign drones precisely to practice shooting them down, and as long as they meet other fcc rules and stay under the quantity cap, that's still allowed. he also mentions an exemption on the drone side: any drone or component on the defense department's blue uas list gets a pass, and many of those are actually made overseas or in allied countries, such as ukraine. adam chan to get an exemption, you first have to hand in an onshoring plan the conditional approval process requires companies to submit an onshoring plan explaining how they intend to move production back to the us. adam says the enforcement branch does not intend to hand companies a blank exemption to ‘keep producing overseas,’ even if the company has no obvious risk from an ownership or cybersecurity standpoint. he also giv

s: 2026-08-06-nopriors-三位万亿公司五年内出现-但下一个不会这么快
h: three trillion-dollar companies in five years, but the next one won't come that fast three companies going from zero to a trillion-dollar valuation in five years is a historical anomaly, not a new normal. what's genuinely scarce isn't a big market — it's the speed to reach $50 billion in revenue within five years. sarah and elad give concrete judgments on the number of trillion-dollar companies, whether founders should sell, and how to allocate token budgets; the second half on regulatory capture is worth more than the first. ai founders deciding whether to raise again or sell their company, and early-stage investors who need to recalibrate how many trillion-dollar companies there will be and the pace of exits. no priors no priors chasing trillion-dollar companies, founder ambition, token budgets, and regulatory capture with sarah & elad venture capital founder exits compute regulatory capture rsi three trillion-dollar companies in five years is an anomaly, not a new normal elad points out that over the past five years anthropic, openai and spacex each went from near zero to a trillion-dollar valuation, whereas historically spacex from the early 2000s and google from the 90s followed a 15-to-20-year arc. he thinks many people now assume another batch of trillion-dollar companies will emerge within three to five years, and that this doesn't hold. he can think of "maybe one more" himself, but refuses to say which. sarah pushes back from the other side: what she encounters more often is investors lacking imagination, valuing ai companies on old per-seat, per-lawyer tams, when coding has already proven that consumption and value can grow 100x. elad gil a trillion-dollar market needs $50 billion in revenue, not a big tam elad reframes the question from "is the tam big" to "where is there a revenue stream of $50 to $100 billion for a single company." he mentions a blog post he wrote in 2010 about how hard it is to reach a $10 billion market cap, a number that today is just some neolab's seed round. his judgment: plenty of companies can reach $5 billion or $10 billion in revenue, very few can reach a trillion — that's an order-of-magnitude difference. sarah adds the key distinction — people conflate market size with speed of arrival; what she doubts isn't the size of markets like energy or robotics, but whether physical-goods companies have enough footprint to get there that fast. elad gil the best founders are building small businesses out of fear of the labs sarah observes two things happening at once: in the mid-to-late stage market, investors keep betting on "can reach a trillion" speed, and she doesn't believe that speed exists; meanwhile a cohort of very strong founders is turning to niche markets because there's far less fear of neolabs and far less head-on competition. she names harvey, open evidence, decagon, sierra and cognition as companies that at the time entered large markets that could plausibly appear on a lab's roadmap. elad pushes this further: what worries him isn't the median founder, it's that the best founders are turning timid — a shift in the trend line, and in his view a negative signal. sarah guo every company has a 12-to-18-month window to sell at its best price elad's framework: a tiny handful of companies (he names anthropic and openai) should absolutely not sell anytime soon; but most companies in any era should at least consider selling, and there's usually a 12-to-18-month window in which the company is worth the most it will ever be worth. he cites ben horowitz's practice — a pre-scheduled annual board meeting whose agenda is to ask, unemotionally, "should we consider an exit in the next six months," driven by process rather than by the founder or an investor. sarah adds a new question: are you capturing value on the curve of falling costs and rising capability, or are you on the wrong side of it? if the latter, and you have no plan to get to the other side, you should sell. elad gil raising will get easier; your real cost is your time elad judges that because a few three-trillion-dollar-scale companies rose so fast, a lot of vc capital is flowing back, funds are getting bigger, and the money has to be deployed, so valuations will keep rising over the next year or two and raising will get easier rather than harder. he therefore shifts the decision's center of gravity from "can i raise" to "what is your company's true expected outcome" — don't listen to investors, the media or twitter; sit down and do the math yourself, including future dilution and the number of years it will take. he stresses that the biggest opportunity cost isn't money but time: the cohort of founders from 2020 and 2021 who are still running companies that don't work five years later missed the entire ai shift. sarah cautions that private markets can stay irrational for a long time, and that the ability to raise is equivalent to avoiding a margin call. elad gil rsi arrives every 18 months, and it's been arriving

s: 2026-08-06-rationalreminder-亿万富翁的经济预测-和短视频里的理财建议一样不可信
h: a billionaire's economic forecast is no more trustworthy than financial advice on short video the halo effect makes people treat everything a successful person says as insight, but outside their own field they are just as ignorant; good advice is humble and probabilistic, bad advice is confident and specific. ritholtz compresses decades of mistakes into checklists for spotting bad advice, valuation, concentrated positions and spending — high information density, worth listening to more than once. founders, investors and engineers, especially anyone with a concentrated position or who regularly watches financial short videos. the rational reminder podcast rational reminder barry ritholtz: how not to invest | rational reminder 421 investing behavioral finance concentrated positions indexing media the halo effect makes billionaires' forecasts look credible ritholtz says billionaire economic forecasts have two features: first, like everyone else they talk their book — they hold assets so they are naturally bullish, and that bias cannot be avoided; second, most of them are simply not qualified to make economic forecasts. what is genuinely dangerous is the halo effect — people see someone who is extraordinarily successful in one field and extend the halo to everything he touches. but spoiler alert: they are not successful in other fields, they are just good at the one thing they are good at, and they are just as ignorant about the future. barry ritholtz good advice is humble and probabilistic, bad advice is confident and specific the tells for spotting bad advice: appeals to emotion (scaring you, stoking your greed, pushing fomo), manufactured urgency (‘the market is going to crash in september’ is a huge red flag, not insight). good advice tends to be both humble and probabilistic — ‘i don't know what's going to happen, but here are the various outcomes and their probabilities’. bad advice sounds very confident and very specific. ritholtz also offers the ‘3d’ framework: doubt (people with no self-doubt usually don't know their own blind spots), depth (a long track record backed by a repeatable process), dunning-kruger (not just overconfidence, but the degree to which you understand the boundaries of your own skill). the most expensive sentence for a novice investor is ‘how hard can this be’. barry ritholtz the news is a daily beast that must be fed the media always has column inches to fill, newsletters and columns to write, 24/7 broadcast to air — but that unrelenting demand on your attention is fundamentally incompatible, on a time scale, with the investor's goal of letting a portfolio compound over years and decades. for a long-term investor, following the news isn't merely useless, it's negative — it damages your returns, because the media constantly pushes you to act, and people are born with an action bias; history tells us most financial decisions are not good ones, and the fewer decisions you make the better the outcome tends to be. ritholtz cites new research by henry bessembinder: if you had bought at the inception of the s&p 500 and then done nothing, you would have significantly outperformed all the rebalancing, adding and trimming in between. barry ritholtz the irs had to issue 42 announcements to debunk short-video finance ritholtz says the algorithm rewards the loudest, most extreme views, and this content is ‘financial junk food’. he gives two examples: first, the us irs had to issue a 42-point press release debunking, one by one, 42 things on tiktok and instagram — following them isn't just wrong, some get you fines, some get you clawbacks plus interest, some get you prison. second, mothers' old saying: don't take candy from strangers. you don't know who the person giving you advice is, what their record is, what their method is, or whether they fly off the handle the moment something happens; taking advice from a rando on social media is financially the same as taking candy from a stranger. barry ritholtz gell-mann amnesia: you know a source is wrong and still trust it michael crichton told a story: he read an article about an event he had personally lived through, and the reporter got it completely wrong — but he turned the page and believed what was on the next page. that is gell-mann amnesia — you see that a source is wrong in an area where you have expertise, yet you keep giving that source credit. ritholtz's response is to build a list of sources he has verified over many years, but he stresses ‘that's my list, you have to make your own list’ — don't outsource your thinking. he also says the media on the whole does a good job reporting the news, but you need to be skeptical of exaggerated claims — extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof, and we often don't see that proof. barry ritholtz sturgeon's law: 90% of financial products are crap ritholtz says several of his favourite pieces of investing philosophy come from books. the first is sturgeon's law: when science fiction writer te

s: 2026-08-06-sciencevs-体重循环不毁代谢-健康行为比体重重要
h: yo-yo dieting doesn't wreck your metabolism — healthy habits, not weight swings, decide how long you live weight cycling (yo-yo dieting) does not permanently damage metabolism, and for ordinary people the weight regained rarely means muscle loss; what actually shapes health and lifespan is the healthy habits themselves, not the up-and-down of the scale. it takes the claim that "yo-yo dieting wrecks your body" and tests it along four lines — metabolism, muscle, inflammation, disease — and the conclusion is more reassuring than intuition suggests. suited to anyone worn down by repeated failed diets. people currently dieting or who have regained weight, and anyone scared off from trying again by the idea that yo-yo dieting is harmful; also for science readers who want to tell observational studies apart from randomized controlled trial evidence. science vs science vs weight loss: why won't it stick? weight cycling weight loss metabolism inflammation healthy habits randomized trials failing at weight loss nine times is not a willpower problem research estimates that as many as half of american adults have experienced weight cycling at least once, and among people who weight cycle, the average is 8 times by midlife. drummer john is on his ninth attempt at losing weight; he says he has gained and lost hundreds of pounds on and off over his life, and each regain makes him feel like he "succeeded and then failed," blaming his own self-control. but as the episode goes on to show, the hunger hormones and metabolic mechanisms in his body make it hard to keep the weight off, and they matter far more than willpower. your body claws the calories back below the level of awareness researchers gave one group of subjects a diabetes drug that makes sugar exit in urine; the subjects lost calories and lost weight, and they had no idea. as a result, the drug group felt hungry sooner and ate more than the placebo group. this happened below the level of consciousness, showing the body automatically compensates for a calorie deficit. holding your weight is like keeping a rubber band stretched taut — slack off even slightly and it snaps back. slowed metabolism is an extreme case, not the general rule the biggest loser study had 16 contestants lose about a third of their body weight on average, and six years later their resting metabolic rates were still about 500 calories a day below predicted — the equivalent of a big mac. but university of copenhagen professor faan points out that this group is extreme and the sample is too small. meta-analyses show that for ordinary people metabolic suppression is on average very small, and may even fall within measurement error. so after nine cycles, john's metabolism most likely is not damaged. there is no evidence cycling makes you fatter; the variable is age a north carolina study found that 74% of the weight lost was fat, but 88% of the weight regained was fat, which sounds like muscle is being lost. a german study found no such difference. the key distinction is age: the former's participants were 50-70, the latter's were 20-40. people lose muscle as they age anyway, regardless of whether they weight cycle. almost no studies follow people through more than one full cycle, so "each cycle makes you fatter" has no evidence behind it. mice return to their starting weight, but the immune system remembers fat tissue contains large numbers of immune cells; when visceral fat cells die from lack of oxygen, macrophages come to clean them up, triggering inflammation. alyssa hasty put mice on a high-fat diet for 9 weeks to gain weight, then a low-fat diet to lose it, then high-fat again for 9 weeks. compared with mice that stayed obese throughout, the cycling mice ended up with exactly the same body weight and visceral fat mass — but more t cells, and more "excitable" ones. she says the body remembers the weight swings. still, this comes from mice on extreme diet switches, and the human evidence is murkier. regain it all and your diabetes risk is still lower observational studies show people who weight cycle have higher risks of heart failure and death, but this kind of study cannot prove causation. the answer from randomized controlled trials: even when people in a supervised weight-loss program regained all the weight, their risk of type 2 diabetes was still lower than people who never tried, and their cholesterol and blood pressure were lower too. a survey of 12,000 people found that what actually predicted mortality was healthy habits — fruits and vegetables, exercise, smoking and drinking — not bmi. so regaining the weight is not wasted effort; the healthy behavior itself is protecting you. it is true that weight cycling can mess up your metabolism.not so fast. i am currently on my ninth time trying to lose weight. john so the resting metabolic rate was lower than predicted by about 500 calories per day. faan mattco the t cells were elevated even further in the weight cycled compared to the obese
