h: ai won't break sap, but it will shatter seat-based pricing ai won't flatten what enterprise software has accumulated, but it will shatter seat-based pricing. sap's defense isn't training its own foundation model — it's open partnerships plus business understanding. the real battlefield is the last mile: process, data and organizational inertia. a rare view from an executive inside a legacy enterprise software giant, using concrete numbers and cases to puncture the illusion that "the model is the product" — and explaining why 28% of attempts yield only 3% in returns. enterprise software founders, investors, heads of technology at companies going global, and engineers trying to figure out whether fde is a good career direction. 晚点聊 latetalk 晚点聊 174: ai冲击企业软件巨头？与sap原欣聊大模型to b的颠覆与边界 enterprise software saas pricing ai to b fde sap organizational inertia the real disruption is the pricing model ai's impact on sap isn't at the code layer, it's in the business model. sap's stock fell from a high of $300 to $160, but stretched out to 2021 it still grew more than 20%; adobe dropped from about 480 to around 220, and zoom has almost vanished. what's actually being replaced is point-solution saas. the core of the shock is the traditional seat-based pricing model, which will shift toward consumption-based or even outcome-based pricing — a challenge every enterprise software company will have to face. yuan xin don't train a foundation model — stay open sap doesn't train its own general-purpose large model, because foundation models evolve too fast and what sap is good at is enterprise process, data and interaction. sap's approach is to open up to all third-party models, and on model selection, pair the most suitable model with the most suitable scenario. at the same time it trains its own proprietary small model, rpt 1.5, on its own structured table data, for financial scenarios like receivables forecasting where accuracy needs to be close to 100% — because in finance, 99% accuracy is still unusable. yuan xin the boss wants ai, but the dirty data is still there what big-company cios dread most is the boss reading an article on wechat and forwarding it with "i want that too." the gap is that everyone assumes once ai arrives, the dirty, grubby work no longer has to be done. ai can accelerate data cleaning, but it can't make that process disappear. to land ai, you still need fdes to comb through historical data and organize it by business object, and at the same time to "distill" the veteran's unstructured decisions into enterprise memory, so that the share that can be automated keeps growing step by step. yuan xin fde and consultants will eventually merge fde is not a rebranded on-site engineer. traditional erp consultants are industry experts who enter from the business side and ultimately land requirements into a standard product; fdes deploy the people who build the product to the customer ahead of time, and the capability they distill flows back into the product. early fdes leaned toward low-level engineering and lacked a converter to turn business needs into coding requirements, which is why anthropic and openai started partnering with consultancies like mckinsey and accenture. the two groups will merge into a hybrid role that understands both business and technology — which is exactly the necessary path for spilling out of a small circle into the enterprise market. yuan xin the customs agent's accuracy flipped a large innovative company built its own agent to handle customs declarations for 33 countries, and accuracy was only 60-70%, so people had to review the remaining errors anyway, to loud complaints. after sap came in, relying on the gtc global tax platform's basic understanding of 33 countries' tax rules plus document ai's template configuration — replacing long-context tokens — accuracy jumped instantly to the 90s, and what started as a pilot in one country had thirty-plus countries clamoring to go live. this shows that exploring ai's business value doesn't require discarding old accumulation; standard process plus incremental value is the effective path. yuan xin 28% attempt it, only 3% see returns mckinsey interviewed more than 2,000 companies worldwide: 28% have already used ai on projects, but only 3% believe there is real business return. so very few projects actually go to production; most are still in poc and prototype stage. big customers have money to burn on trial and error and move fast; small companies run fast with open-source tools; those struggling most are mid-sized companies in the few-hundred-million to roughly 10-billion range, where whether to embrace ai is strongly correlated with the founder's mindset — and chinese companies are more willing to put money into the product side than the management side. yuan xin going global rides on a localization base sap's global platform itself covers operations in more than 150 countries, and its product organization includes a localization team dedica ‖ 晚點聊 晚點聊 衝擊企業軟件巨頭 與 原欣聊大模型 的顛覆與邊界

domestic fuel prices rise only about 30%, which crushed refinery margins but preserved household mobility. rory this time the us spr used an "exchange", not a release arnab unpacks the energy department's operation: this was not a traditional drawdown but an exchange — oil is lent to traders to put into the market now, and the traders promise to return the same volume of crude later plus a premium, with the premium being repaid from this november all the way to 2028. doe also had the traders taking the oil bid against each other, so whoever promised the higher premium got the spot barrels. this mechanism is more creative than any spr operation he has seen before, and it shows "the reserve is worth investing in" — but he states plainly that the biggest credit for oil not ports like bahrain to reconstitute, so the navy has to bring oilers in from europe, crete or the pacific, transfer fuel at sea in the arabian sea to replenishment oilers, and those oilers then local operations and workups, then another deployment roughly two to two and a half years after maintenance ends. now the navy has to pull ships out of that normal cycle early to replace ships that have already been out for nearly a year. the problem is that interrupting training and maintenance cycles early means ships break down once they get to sea and very likely have to come home early. the end result is that reserve capacity gets burned off and ships are forced out of deployment because they're broken. the mccain and fitzgerald collisions in the late 2010s were the consequence of overuse and insufficient maintenance. brian iran's terrain leaves almost no entry point for a ground war inside the pentagon there is discussion, pushed by marines and military commanders, about seizing islands including karg island and starting to take ground. but iran is hard to attack from every direction: the southwest is the marshland where the marsh arabs live, which made it hard for saddam's mechanized forces to pass; the north is the alborz mountains, high and difficult; the east is the baluch desert, basically salt flats. every province has irgc, quds force and basij recruiting stations, so any attack will bring local militias up. and the us no longer has a navy or coast guard presence in the persian gulf, many bases will not be rebuilt, and ground forces would essentially be operating in isolation. justin fuel can be transferred at sea, food cannot the navy has designed a tanker-to-oiler-to-ship transfer model for fuel, but there is no similar scheme for food. cargo ships carrying food have to come from very far away, the military still requires food to come from the us, there is almost no opportunity to buy locally, and supply officers can't go ashore to buy food the way they used to. feeding two carrier strike groups is a huge undertaking in itself. if they're out for a year, the good food runs out first and only frozen food is left, and there are no mres on board. they have to redesign a model for how to feed at sea in an environment where the supply line is contested. brian global basing isn't an empire, it's the logistics skeleton the point of the global force posture is to serve as the skeleton of logistics hubs and logistics models that let forces flow into a region to protect critical national interests. the us has already been shrinking that skeleton in europe and the middle east, and now it is under attack, which means losing the skeleton for doing the next big thing in the region. the problem with this administration is that it first pursued a "denial" strategy, doing more in this hemisphere and less elsewhere, stripping away the capabilities needed to sustain combat power, and then used combat power in various places anyway. a father in the military once said that behind every infantryman there are twenty support personnel responsible for paying, clothing, feeding and maintaining equipment, and those are exactly the things being removed from europe and the middle east. justin

h: nobody confirmed the doors were shut: institutional carelessness was the real killer in 1987, the roll-on/roll-off ferry herald of free enterprise capsized because its bow doors were left open, killing 193 people. the real culprit was not a sleeping crewman but a system that let everyone feel "this isn't my job." the most valuable thing in this episode: it shows how a corporate culture in which "nobody did anything wrong" killed 193 people. for anyone who writes processes, assigns responsibility or runs safety audits, this cuts deeper than any textbook on governance. operations and safety leads in high-risk industries, and founders and managers who need to design error-proof processes for their teams. cautionary tales with tim harford cautionary tales the doors of death: the herald of free enterprise maritime disaster organizational failure safety culture attribution of blame regulatory lag swiss cheese model who was supposed to shut the doors a roll-on/roll-off ferry is designed so vehicles drive straight into the hold, with a large door at the bow and another at the stern that must be closed before departure. closing them was the job of assistant boatswain mark stanley. on a cold evening in march 1987, his superior told him to go back to his cabin and rest until the announcement called him on duty. he made a cup of tea and dozed off on his bunk. four years earlier, another roro ship in the same company had put to sea with its doors open because the man responsible for closing them had fallen asleep; that time it was only luck that nothing happened. tim harford the indicator-light proposal was rejected by executives after sister ships had twice sailed with their doors open, one captain wrote a memo urging the crew to take it seriously; another captain proposed fitting indicator lights, since the bridge could not see the state of the doors. the company's senior management responded that the assumption was that whoever closed the doors would tell the bridge if something went wrong; someone else retorted by asking whether they should also install an indicator light to check that the warehouse manager was awake. the proposal went nowhere. the captains saw the hole in advance, but nobody was willing to plug it. tim harford 193 people died within a minute and a half after herald of free enterprise left port carrying 459 passengers and 80 crew, seawater poured through the open doors onto the vehicle deck. passengers first joked about dropped plates, then the ship capsized as fast as if it had been pulled out from underneath, lying on its side on a sandbank within a minute and a half. inside it was pitch dark and freezing, and life jackets only tangled people up; some escaped by stepping on other people's faces, while others arched their backs as human bridges so that strangers and children could walk across them. in the end 193 people died. tim harford all four links looked blameless justice sheen found that the disaster was not caused by one man. stanley had fallen asleep; his superior said "closing the doors was never my job"; the first officer, under company policy, only had to confirm that the man closing the doors was "near the doors"; and the captain, under another policy, assumed that no report meant everything was normal. taken individually, none of the four acts was monstrous; together they opened every line of defence. james reason later distilled the swiss cheese model from this disaster: catastrophe comes when the holes in successive layers of defence happen to line up. tim harford the judge pointed the finger at senior management sheen's conclusion was unambiguous: "the underlying fault was at the higher level of the company." the board of townsend thoresen had never treated safety as its own responsibility; nobody policed overloading, and the company did not even know how many people were on board; the bow and stern draught figures were fabricated by the crew because nobody ever checked them. sheen's own words were: "the disease of carelessness was infecting the body corporate as a whole." but the inquiry commission had no power to punish, and although the coroner's jury found this to be unlawful killing, it could not name a single individual. tim harford the law cannot keep up with new technology the roro ferry was an innovation, but maritime law had been written before it existed. the law only prohibited leaving an unseaworthy ship in port; it did not say "you may not put to sea with your doors open," so townsend thoresen slipped through a gap nobody had ever imagined. peter spooner, a relative of one of the dead, organised a families' association and pushed for a corporate manslaughter prosecution. but the law at the time required finding the person who represented the company's "controlling mind," and precisely because responsibility was organised to be nobody's, no individual could be found, and the case failed. spooner reflected: "there is only so much that regulation and legislation can do. t

h: ai's understanding of you is engineered line by line by content engineers people who once wrote the news have turned into ai content engineers, breaking questioning, empathy and tact down into training rules — that is where ai's ‘understanding of you’ comes from, but training on consensus also leads them to admit: great art will not grow from here. this episode lays bare the least-known job behind ai, with both a transition methodology from two former media people and a calm dismantling of the ai-steals-jobs narrative — suited to anxious liberal-arts graduates and ai product people. reporters, screenwriters and content professionals who want to move from media into ai; also suited to ai product managers and founders trying to understand the product design behind model answers. saw a meta job posting for a ‘content engineer’ requiring content, editorial and film production experience, and decided it was made for him. he explains the role is not designing the model or the product style, but designing the human perception: defining what counts as a good conversation, and breaking inspiration, feel for language and soul-level collision — things that can only be sensed, not stated — into rules that can be quantified, trained and evaluated. ordinary language also has grammar and syntax, and can be technically taken apart and analysed. tony understanding what the asker means beneath the words bianca gives an example: someone asks whether taylor swift will get married at madison square garden. a bad answer is to say directly that she will and list the bridesmaids, or to mechanically stitch information together; a good answer acknowledges the information is uncertain and adds the source and context of the speculation. the content engineer's expertise is understanding intent, not just understanding the literal question — especially since in non-western cultures the information that truly matters is often not said directly, and has to be caught from tone, pauses and follow-up questions. this is the same reason oral interviews beat email interviews. bianca internationalisation turns from translation into re-creation dongni says generative ai has turned localisation from plain translation into contextual re-creation: the same piece of information, in a chinese context, has to answer ‘who is china's meryl streep’, and can be written as ‘siqin gaowa won the golden rooster award’. ai understands language but not cultural correspondences, and entertainment reporters naturally carry a vertical-domain small model, making them the best fit to tune this kind of strategy. he also mentions that video generation models favour conventionally attractive faces, and that people who understand cinematic faces can raise model diversity faster. tony when context breaks, human filling-in resembles ai's bianca cites the best paper at iclr: when ai handles complex multi-turn dialogue, if the context is insufficient it keeps filling in the gaps, and the errors snowball. she recalls her own 2018 research on the mong kok girl incident on weibo, where the comment section turned from friendly chat into mutual abuse precisely because the context had broken, and everyone began to fill in the other side's identity. she thinks the observations of the humanities and the findings of the ai industry are not far apart — many problems were studied in linguistics long ago, and are now simply being explored again through a different entity. bianca consensus training will not produce great art bianca admits that ai training is essentially based on majority consensus, optimising for humanity's shared standards as a whole, and therefore will not produce great art. the best essence of what makes us human precisely does not come from consensus. she has tried using ai to write scripts, but what ai produces cannot grasp what she really wants; the script of everything everywhere all at once could not naturally come out of ai, because ai would consider it illogical and not conforming to the academic three-act structure. she believes that over time it will become clear which places suit ai and which do not. bianca the ai-steals-jobs narrative mixes several problems dongni is sceptical of the ‘ai stole my job’ narrative. he thinks it mixes at least three separate problems: the gig economy existed before ai appeared, and media people were already surviving on uber and doordash; the project-based nature of ai trainer work means you leave when a job is done, and ai will not thereby become a senior screenwriter; more importantly, this narrative sets creators against ai and ignores a third path — treating ai as a paintbrush. people without a camera can make films, people without a vfx budget can do vfx, and the question to ask is ‘what can i create with ai’. tony few-shot exam ‖ 硅谷 硅谷 藏在大模型背後的新聞人 們的回覆是這樣寫出來的

self-improvement. eiso kant small models grind, not get smarter peng ming, head of applied research, told eiso that laguna s's progress came more from behavior changes than stronger intelligence: more h: a 28nm chip beats by 1000x: the compute-in-memory black magic that needs no euv zhicun technology turns 28nm flash into a compute-in-memory chip, exploiting the physical property that efficiency rises with array size, so efficiency improves as models grow — and transformers are pure upside for it. a rare episode that lays out compute-in-memory's physics, process choices and four years of tape-out blood and tears, with unusual candor from a founder's point of view. engineers who care about the underlying architecture of ai chips, semiconductor investors, and founders who want to understand the nature of the compute bottleneck 老石谈芯 老石谈芯 28纳米反超1000倍?不需要euv的芯片黑魔法：对话知存科技王绍迪 compute-in-memory ai chips memory transformer semiconductor manufacturing edge ai before he founded the company, nobody in the industry believed in compute-in-memory wang shaodi wanted to build compute-in-memory chips while doing his phd. before graduating in 2016 he approached four or five leading chip companies in china and the us; none had heard of the technology, and none would open a new direction for a fresh phd graduate. academia was a dead end too — a peking university professor asked him point-blank where the funding would come from, and at the time very few chip grants nationwide exceeded a million yuan, not even enough to pay for a tape-out. with both paths blocked, he had no choice but to start his own company. wang shaodi the bigger the model, the faster the read in a conventional von neumann architecture, matrix multiplication requires reading data out of memory cells one by one and sending it to the arithmetic unit; the larger the memory array, the slower the readout — a law of physics. compute-in-memory instead turns each memory cell itself into a compute node in the matrix multiplication, so a single activation completes an entire matrix computation without row-by-row, column-by-column readout. that means scaling an algorithm from a few rows to ten thousand rows still takes only one activation, and effective bandwidth and compute actually grow as the model grows — the exact opposite of the von neumann rule. wang shaodi ohm's law is the principle behind the black magic at the core of compute-in-memory is using ohm's law — voltage times conductance equals current — to implement multiplication directly: apply a voltage along the rows of the memory, each memory cell is itself a conductance value, and the current that naturally flows out along the columns is the product of voltage and conductance; currents from multiple rows in the same column sum together, completing addition physically. the whole matrix multiplication is finished in a single read, with no need at all for the adders and multipliers of digital chips — it is essentially using the most basic electrical relationships from middle-school physics to do ai computation. wang shaodi why bet on the most ordinary flash memory faced with sram, non-volatile flash, the rram much discussed in academia and other storage media, zhicun chose the seemingly most unremarkable nor flash, because the compute current flash needs for analog multiplication is the lowest of any memory, and compute-in-memory requires activating as many cells at once as possible to process as much in parallel as possible — lower current means a larger array can be turned on and effective compute is stronger; flash is also the most mature memory process, making tape-out and debugging fastest. the price was a hard fight on precision: it took several hundred people at the company seven or eight years to get precision to the level applications required. wang shaodi transformers are pure upside for compute-in-memory moving from deep learning to transformers gave compute-in-memory two dividends: first, deep learning often reads a parameter once to compute tens of thousands of times, so memory bandwidth pressure is modest; a transformer reads each parameter once and computes once, so the read-to-compute ratio is inherently 1:1, whereas architectures like gpus typically run 64:1 to 128:1 and the worst can reach 1000:1 — a perfect match for compute-in-memory's 1:1 storage-to-compute ratio. second, transformer matrices are 1000 to 10,000 times larger than those in deep learning, and compute-in-memory finishes the whole matrix in one go, so the larger the matrix the higher the compute efficiency — again by 1000 to 10,000 times. on top of that, large models need only int4's 4-bit precision, far below the 12 to 16 bits the deep learning era demanded, which sharply lowers the bar to deployment. wang shaodi six tape-outs in four years, and powering up is when the nightmare begins there are no ready-made eda tools for compute-in-memory, and each chip that comes back from tape-out may hide dozens of problems — for instance, a design targeting 8-bit precision that in fact achieves only 3 bits. the team has to locate them one by one: spending more than a month slicing the chip open and running experiment after experiment to pin ‖ 老石談芯 老石談芯 納米反超 倍 不需要 的芯片黑魔法 對話知存科技王紹迪

the other is spending the agent generates itself while executing a task — calling apis, buying research reports, downloading materials — small in amount but high in frequency, and it needs to happen autonomously within an authorized limit. the former is large in volume and long in the chain; second, the agent cannot be trusted to hold card information, and once a chargeback happens the responsibility falls on the user; third, merchants are uneasy about who owns the customer relationship when an agent places an order, and agent penetration among ordinary users is low, so the roi on large-scale merchant investment is insufficient — which is why merchant readiness is progressing slowly. patrick clink × visa vic: the first transaction patrick describes the partnership with visa: clink is positioned as the first agent enableer in visa's global production network. at the end of june it executed the first vic transaction at an expo. the flow: the agent passes the user context, authorized amount and product category to clink, which records it as a mandate; after the agent finds the product, clink verifies it matches the original authorization, then applies to visa for a one-time payment capability, and visa verifies and completes the payment. this mechanism makes the final chain of accountability clear. patrick why fiat beats stablecoins patrick explains why clink chose fiat over stablecoins: consumer protection mechanisms in the fiat system are mature, banks and card networks have complete processes for authorization and dispute handling, so the trust problem is easier to solve; once a stablecoin payment goes out it is essentially irreversible, which damages consumer confidence and sustained trust. a guest then adds a real case: after a company laid off an employee, a certain token burned over 600 usd overnight with no way to trace it, and the company later had to switch to individual apis per person so it could be traced. patrick stablecoins are building an on-chain alipay gao ning describes progress in the stablecoin track. within the stablecoin system, simple small transfers are already fairly mature, because on-chain payment is end-to-end transfer. more interesting is that some people are trying to solve taobao's early problem: buyers and merchants not trusting each other. the approach is to lock the money in a neutral place with a smart contract and release it to the merchant after delivery is confirmed, solving the irreversibility of "paid but not shipped". gao ning thinks the small-amount, high-frequency infrastructure is no longer lacking; what is missing is scenario richness and the migration of user habits. gao ning clink is a ramp between highways patrick says clink is not building a new highway but connecting roads to roads. a user may come from openai's acp protocol while the merchant uses shopify or stripe; between different protocols, different payment companies and different e-commerce platforms, someone needs to do the conversion and bridging. clink's strategy is to be as compatible as possible with ucp and acp, and to build plugins for e-commerce platforms such as shopify and magento, so merchants can onboard at low cost and become agent payment ready without changing their existing oms and order systems. patrick china's payment ecosystem takes a different path gao ning says china has no overseas card-network chargeback/appeal system — disputes are more like customer complaints, and responsibility is assigned differently. but ‖ 科技早知道 科技早知道 可以給你的 發一點零花錢了

july 16 with weights promised for july 27. the author pins the whole piece's key conclusion on one number: the performance gap between open and closed, or between the us and china, has narrowed from the contested 6-9 months to 3-5 months. he adds a robustness note — even if moonshot ultimately doesn't deliver on open weights, as long as a comparably strong closed model exists in china, most of claude fable and gpt-5.6 sol max, and cheaper), first on frontend code arena. this is the closest an open model has come to the frontier since deepseek r1. nathan lambert the distillation narrative dies in this episode the author states the conclusion outright: if adversarial distillation contributed to k3 at all, it was only to a small degree. the reason is that r1 and k3 are different in kind — r1 was a chinese lab sprinting to pivot to reasoning models first, whereas k3 is scaling along known axes: data, algorithms, architecture, tooling, environments — the same set of problems people at openai and anthropic are working on. another layer of evidence comes from his trip to china: the culture of the kimi team was one of the few among the companies he visited that you could feel at a glance, with strong individual execution and freedom of expression even under gpu constraints; having seen it, the result was unsurprising to him. he predicts the distillation debate and the there was almost no national-level policy statement from china on open-source ai; the author says that to his knowledge no senior leader had commented publicly. that changed this week: in his keynote at the world artificial intelligence conference (waic), xi jinping very directly bet the future of china's ai ecosystem on open source and global diffusion. the author's reading is that this commitment, landing in the same week as the strongest open-weights model in history, amounts to an implicit statement of china's risk tolerance for open weights. the simplest explanation: the chinese government is tracking model risk closely, at a technical granularity that may be finer than america's ‘vibes-based regulation’, and will act if it measures risk — and it currently judges frontier models to pose no substantial risk. at the same time, economic policymakers think getting ai used first is a good thing, scaling distribution before monetising, a path consistent with cars, solar and decelerationist, and the author says he's right. the transmission chain is concrete: strong open models sharply compress the gross margin space of closed labs — first, the labs have less profit to reinvest in the next generation of models; second, the market marks down these companies' terminal values, discounting future funding rounds. together these delay the arrival of the most transformative models. but the author doesn't think this is enough to knock openai and anthropic out of the ranks of the world's most valuable companies, and he thinks it's a net good for society: open source is accelerationist on the diffusion side, lowering the entry price for a given performance tier of intelligence and encouraging customisation — it's just that this curve starts much more slowly. his phrasing: an exponent that starts slower but may be larger. the risk is that closed capabilities run so far ahead that customisation loses its meaning. nathan lambert where the 2.5× when the model's output equals the data's true distribution — which is exactly equivalent to training the model into a text compressor that approaches the shannon limit. it pins together two distillation compression kl divergence gzip can draw the language family tree a 2002 paper used only gzip, a general-purpose file compressor, to automatically cluster texts in different languages and his father was freed and joined an arab tribe. bashshar later told stories about how noble his paternal lineage was, but the episode states plainly that the truth of these stories is unknown. he was disfigured by smallpox in childhood, was blind, and was large and heavy of body. he himself said blindness actually helped him write poetry: "lack of sight strengthens the acuteness of the heart and cuts out interference from things which are visible." he wrote poems mocking arabs for eating lizards in one satire, bashshar declared that his grandfather and father were the noblest of persians, that the roman emperor was his uncle, and that they all wore crowns; his father wore persian sable and drank from gold cups, never followed mangy camels singing camel songs, never dug up desert melons to stave off hunger, and never dug lizards out of stony ground to eat. the episode notes that this lineage was mostly invented, but the satirical intent is clear: persia is the land of civilization, and the arabs can keep their wretched qasidas that romanticize the dry desert. his attitude toward bedouin poetry was playfully irreverent, and at the same time he could wield its conventions with complete fluency. one poem put him in the tigris bashshar had a tense relationship with the caliph al-mahdi (r. 775-785), who once ordered him to stop writing love poetry; he ignored it. according to the historian al-tabari, around 783 bashshar wrote a poem saying: wake up, sons of umayya, you have slept too long; the persian bureaucrat ya'qub b. dawud is the caliph, your caliphate is ruined, go look for god's caliph among the tambourines and lutes. this amounted to saying the abbasid dynasty could be replaced by the umayyads they had usurped — crossing from insolence into sedition. he was imprisoned, beaten half to death, sewn into a sack and thrown into the tigris to drown, at about seventy years old. he insulted a caliph and lived twenty more years in 762, descendants of the prophet's daughter fatima rose in revolt against the abbasids in medina; stop and war begins brain scans show isopropyl myristate activates the odor-processing regions in worker brains and suppresses other females from entering a sexually active state — effectively a "scent contraceptive." add the molecule to a colony that has just lost its queen and everything stays calm, with workers behaving as if the queen were still there; once the addition stops, high-ranking females immediately begin fighting among themselves for the throne. the authors think the mechanism is clear: whoever gets pregnant first starts making the molecule and thereby suppresses all the other females. melissa holmes calls it the holy grail of research on naked mole-rat social structure. the same molecule and lactating women isopropyl myristate is not unique to naked mole-rats. gary lewin notes that a study years ago measured the volatile molecules given off by the breasts of lactating women, and isopropyl myristate was among them; when researchers put the mixture on cotton swabs, newborns would start sniffing and even try to suckle. but he says that paper was an isolated case and no one followed up. now that the molecule has such a strong social effect in naked mole-rats, researchers perhaps ought to revisit whether it does anything in other mammals. two cotton-candy planets and hannibal this week's highlights has two number stories. one is two newly discovered exoplanets, close to jupiter in size but more than 20 times lighter, with a density lower than cotton candy — among the lowest-density planets known; h: the optimal linear-programming solution is never interior: simplex climbs only along boundary vertices the optimum of a linear program always sits on some boundary vertex, so the simplex algorithm never searches the interior: starting from the origin, it picks a direction from the most negative column, sets the step size by the minimum ratio, and keeps moving to a more profitable adjacent vertex. this episode turns the geometric intuition of "climbing along boundary vertices" into matrix operations at every step, spelling out direction, step size and stopping condition. once you've worked it by hand, optimizer documentation reads completely differently. engineers who call optimization libraries but have never derived the simplex method by hand, operations-research students, and teachers preparing to lecture on linear programming. statquest statquest the simplex algorithm, mathematical details!!! linear programming simplex method slack variables gaussian elimination operations research algorithm details climbing between adjacent vertices a linear program seeks the extreme value of an objective function inside a feasible region bounded by straight-line constraints. the simplex algorithm does not search the interior of that region; it starts at the origin and moves along an edge to an adjacent vertex that raises revenue, then from the new vertex looks at the next adjacent vertex, until no move increases revenue any further. because the algorithm "cannot see" the picture, all the seemingly complicated matrix operations that follow are essentially answering two questions with numbers: which direction, and how far. josh starmer first normalize every constraint to less-than-or-equal before the iterations proper, standardization is required: a constraint with a greater-than-or-equal sign must be flipped into less-than-or-equal by multiplying both sides by -1; a constraint with an equals sign is split into a less-than-or-equal and a greater-than-or-equal inequality, and the greater-than-or-equal one is then multiplied by -1 and flipped, so the two inequalities form a kind of "inequality sandwich" equivalent to the original equality. the episode explains the purpose: the algorithm then only has to handle one kind of sign at every step, with no branching checks for different constraint forms during iteration. josh starmer slack variables pad inequalities into equalities even after an expression becomes less-than-or-equal, the left and right sides may still not be equal. the fix is to append a non-negative slack variable to each equation, filling in exactly the shortfall. the episode's example: when producing 10 kg of cookie mix and 8 kg of doughnut mix, only 8 kg of flour is actually used while 10 kg is available, so the slack variable for flour is set to 2 kg; the slack variables of the other constraints vanish from the calculation because their coefficients are 0. only after the slack variables are added do all equations share one format and can be put into a matrix uniformly. josh starmer load the matrix, then negate the first row the last formatting step is to fill all coefficients and totals into the matrix and multiply the first row by -1. the negation is only to match the usual definition of the simplex method, so that "where to go next" can be read directly as the most negative coefficient in the first row; at this point the initial revenue is 0, because the search starts at the origin. once the matrix is in order, every iteration revolves around the same action: first choose a direction, then fix a distance, and finally use row operations to read the new vertex's coordinates explicitly. josh starmer only the minimum ratio lands on the boundary the algorithm itself cannot see the feasible region, so it uses the ratio test to set the step size: take the total on the right-hand side of each constraint row and divide it by the corresponding positive coefficient in the current column; the quotient is the coordinate reachable along that axis. the episode uses three candidate points on the cookie mix axis to illustrate: the ratios 25 and 16.7 correspond to where the yellow and blue lines meet the axis, both outside the feasible region; the lowest, 10, lands on the brown line's intersection, i.e. on the boundary. so the minimum ratio is always chosen; a point with a larger ratio necessarily overshoots. if the minimum ratio is tied, the convention is to pick the row with the smallest row number. josh starmer gaussian elimination makes the coordinates surface on their own once the pivot column and pivot row are chosen, gaussian elimination turns the pivot position into 1, then clears every other position in that column to 0 by adding multiples of rows. after elimination the reading rule is simple: if a column has a single 1 and zeros everywhere else, read the total on that column's row as the current vertex's coordinate on that axis; h: a black hole is a 100%-efficient power plant; fusion only reaches one percent lower a brick slowly to just above the horizon and let go, and its rest mass can become work at a distance with 100% efficiency; chemical burning gets only one part in ten billion and fusion only one percent, because nuclear reactions never touch the rest mass of protons and neutrons — only gravity does. one hour takes general relativity from the equivalence principle to the black hole power plant; it's a lecture, not an interview. only the last eight minutes touch ai doing theoretical physics, so don't expect industry news. engineers who want to actually explain gr rather than recite its conclusions; investors and researchers who care whether ai can do theoretical science on its own, and how far pure thought can go. dwarkesh podcast dwarkesh adam brown – a deep but accessible introduction to general relativity general relativity black holes energy efficiency ai in research string theory history of physics the equivalence principle is the only clue in electromagnetism, charge and mass have nothing to do with each other — a neutron is heavy but uncharged, an electron is light but fully charged. gravity is not like that: the inertial mass that resists acceleration in newton's second law and the gravitational mass that gets pulled in the law of universal gravitation are the same number. in newton's system this is a pure coincidence, but newton himself verified it to one part in a thousand, einstein's era to one part in a billion, and today to one part in 10^15. einstein treated this coincidence as the only clue: a force that can be explained as an inertial force must have inertial mass as its "charge"; conversely, only a force whose charge equals inertial mass is even eligible to be an inertial force. electromagnetism never has that eligibility; gravity does. adam brown the price is redefining what a straight line is swing a bucket in a circle and the water doesn't fall out; someone sitting in the bucket would say that's centrifugal force. the charge of an inertial force like centrifugal force must be inertial mass, because its source is just mass's tendency to travel in a straight line. from this einstein makes the leap: gravity itself is a kind of inertial force. the price is enormous — you must accept that the parabola of free fall is the straight line, and that you, sitting still, are not. this is no more absurd than a flight map on which san francisco to london has to curve over greenland: draw something curved as if it were flat and you will inevitably get wrong which line is straight. so matter curves spacetime, curved spacetime defines what a straight line is, and treating curved spacetime as if it were flat makes you see a fictitious force called gravity. adam brown the infinite-energy paradox forces out black holes lower a brick of mass m slowly on a pulley from far away to radius r and release it, and the fraction of its rest mass energy you can extract is gm/(c²r). lowered to earth's surface it's only 7×10^-10; to the sun's surface, 2×10^-6; to a white dwarf like sirius b, larger still. but the formula has no upper bound: once r is less than gm/c², the fraction exceeds 1 — you extract more energy than the brick's rest mass energy, and using that energy to make another brick and lower it again gives you a machine that creates energy from nothing. adam says explicitly that this is a purely newtonian calculation and only suggestive, but it shows that something must break down near that radius. adam brown gravity's resolution is to get stronger, not weaker in electromagnetism the analogous paradox is resolved by the force getting weaker: two charges brought too close smear out quantum-mechanically and stop attracting so hard. general relativity goes the other way — the acceleration needed to stay at rest carries a factor of 1/√(1-2gm/c²r), which diverges at 2gm/c², and the brick is torn straight out of your hand. the same square root also gives time dilation and redshift, and gives the exact extraction fraction 1-√(1-2gm/c²r): lowered to just above the horizon it is exactly 1, no more and no less, 100%. so a black hole is a power plant at the efficiency limit: chemical burning 10^-10, fission 10^-3, fusion 10^-2, because neither fission nor fusion changes the total number of nucleons — 99% of the energy is locked in the rest mass of protons and neutrons. adam brown doomed, but not yet dead i watch you fall toward the black hole from far away: first faster and faster, then slower and slower, your clock running ever slower, your light ever redder, and after a last photon you fade to black — i never see you cross the horizon. early physicists therefore thought something violent must happen at the moment of crossing; that is wrong. you cross with nothing unusual happening to you; tidal forces would hurt for a solar-mass black hole, but the bigger the black hole the gentler, and at galactic-mass scale you wouldn't notice at all. o

h: ai self-evolution could close the loop in as little as six months, but models will quietly drift off course the inflection point for rsi is a model that can handle long-horizon tasks. apodex's chief scientist says the self-evolution loop could close in as little as six months, but recursive drift and model taste still need humans minding them for a long time to come. a frontline researcher breaks down the rsi technical path, verification methods and timeline. high information density, and direct material for understanding the real progress of model self-evolution. ai founders, large-model researchers, investors, and engineers following agent architectures. 硅谷101 硅谷101 e242｜最快半年ai跑通自进化？与陈天桥首席科学家聊聊硅谷模型必争之地 ai self-evolution rsi long-horizon tasks agent teams model taste research automation recursive self-improvement became possible because of long-horizon tasks self-evolution is not a new idea. two or three years ago there were already approaches like lm-as-optimizer and agent optimizer, but back then a model could only optimize for two or three hours; one small mistake would compound on itself and it could not keep iterating. what is different this year is that models have gotten stronger and can complete long-horizon tasks that take a human 1.5 hours or even 12 hours, so they can self-correct many times within a single task, and the "r" in recursive finally holds up. at anthropic, 80% of code is written by claude — it is precisely coding ability that makes it natural for a model to train itself. bei bing three technical bottlenecks stand in the way of long-horizon tasks long-horizon tasks are not just a context-length problem. first, standard attention has quadratic complexity, so million-token inference is extremely resource-hungry and needs architectural innovation. second, long-context support alone is not enough: the model must have been trained on very long data, otherwise it goes out-of-distribution. third, the training and inference infra also has to change, including gpu optimization and kernel-level code. stack those three difficulties together and the difficulty of long-horizon tasks rises exponentially. simon adds that even with a million-token context, truly ultra-long-horizon tasks still need agent architecture and memory mechanisms to digest. bei bing recursive drift is the fundamental obstacle to self-evolution when a model generates its own training data, reasoning errors accumulate and amplify across generations — that is recursive drift. apodex's countermeasure is verification: code and math are easy to verify, using test scripts or formal proofs, so they are relatively controllable; but the tests themselves can be too broad or too narrow, and subtle drift still occurs. so apodex specifically trains verification ability, and during reinforcement learning it has the judge learn alongside, to keep the model from learning bad behaviors like reward hacking. bei bing verification relies on sub-agents checking each other plus redundancy the name apodex comes from the greek word for "proof." verification methods differ by domain: code uses unit tests, math uses formal proofs, but more problems depend on human judgment. apodex 1.0 uses an agent team: first decompose the problem, one sub-agent solves it and another sub-agent verifies it separately, avoiding context contamination; then have multiple agents work the same problem to produce redundancy, with a global agent judging which answer is more accurate. during training it also has agents judge the credibility of information sources — a forum, for instance, is less reliable than a textbook. simon the three self-evolution paths have very different moats beibing divides self-evolution into three paths: pretraining, post-training, and harness (scaffolding). evolving at the harness level is the cheapest — you can do it just by calling apis — and the open-source community and academia have produced plenty of results there, so the moat is the shallowest. post-training is the more core and more difficult battlefield: you first have to diagnose model defects, create targeted problems, and verify training results, which takes a lot of resources. pretraining is currently mostly toy-level tasks and has not really scaled to product level. apodex does all three; post-training and scaffolding are like the left foot stepping on the right foot, iterating alternately. to judge a company's capability, first ask which layer it evolves at. bei bing why an agent team beats a single smart ai simon states it plainly: one smart ai cannot beat a team that checks each other. the reason is the nature of self-attention — the longer the context, the worse attention works, and linear attention does not solve ultra-long context either, so a single model has a ceiling under current technology, just as a person's working memory is limited and needs notes. so multiple agents must divide the work and share information through memory mechanisms to handle ultra-long-horizon problem ‖ 硅谷 硅谷 最快半年 跑通自進化 與陳天橋首席科學家聊聊硅谷模型必爭之地

nobody just had the leisure to compute it, and ai can do it for us. same in mathematics: the axioms and rules of inference are already there. this is "coloring in the existing picture of organic chemistry," not generating new explanatory knowledge. reaching the threshold of creating new knowledge — and thereby counting as agi or an "artificial person" — requires the latter. brett hall opponents of many-worlds shout "untestable" first the host observes that the most common objection today is not a refusal of the explanation but the reflex "it's untestable." yet deutsch published an experimental scheme for testing many-worlds decades ago; the host, maria violaris and sam kuypers have all explained it, and after pointing to the paper and the video, the other party — physicists included — still will not budge. the experiment requires a "conscious observer" in superposition, so then people say we have no agi capable of doing it. the host cites deutsch: needing agi to run this decisive experiment is not a fault of the many-worlds theory. brett hall the explanatory gap: the turing principle cannot answer what a person is deutsch says that some of those who deny the possibility of ai are in fact expressing a more reasonable criticism: turing's computational explanation seems in principle to leave no room for a physical explanation of mental properties like consciousness and free will. ai partisans respond bluntly that "the turing principle guarantees a computer can do anything a brain can do" — true, but that answers with a prediction, whereas the problem lies in the explanation; there is an explanatory gap. the host adds: this is why we still cannot build agi; saying the brain is some kind of computer does not settle what a person is. brett hall simple rules do not specify a peacock, yet peacocks appear deutsch uses a darwinian analogy: the laws of physics do not contain the shapes of elephants and peacocks; s: 2026-06-26-dwarkesh-ai-的下一个突破-在工作中学习-而非仅靠训练
h: ai's next breakthrough isn't training — it's letting ai learn on the job labs are betting rlvr can generalise into general intelligence, but the real bottleneck is sample efficiency and continual learning. opsd and "dreaming" may be the key, letting ai learn from deployment rather than pretraining alone. this episode challenges the current rlvr-dominated training paradigm, arguing that continual learning and sample efficiency are the real bottlenecks to agi — essential for understanding where ai evolution is headed. ai researchers, technical decision-makers, founders and investors watching ai's future, especially those interested in training paradigms and continual learning. dwarkesh podcast dwarkesh the next big breakthrough will be ais learning on the job continual learning rlvr sample efficiency opsd ai training architecture innovation the labs are making a very large bet labs are betting that if you train ai on millions of verifiable tasks across thousands of diverse rl environments, you can build agi. that training will produce general problem-solving ability — the kind that lets a model push an open-ended task forward for weeks while facing errors and ambiguity. optimists believe defects like data inefficiency and the lack of continual learning can be steamrolled by scaling training, just as "fundamental" problems in nlp were drowned by the flood of compute. a model's training sample efficiency may be a millionth of a human's, but training cost is one-time and amortised across billions of user sessions. what matters is the model's intelligence, generality and sample efficiency within a session — and that is improving with rl training. dwarkesh patel grindability matters more than verifiability progress on computer use is slow not only because of verifiability but because of "grindability" — whether you can run large numbers of rollouts in parallel on a deterministic, replayable simulator. coding lets you spin up repo environments where a thousand agents try in parallel, but computer use cannot have a thousand agents simultaneously testing the amazon checkout flow, because they will be detected and banned. cloning apps like slack and gmail is feasible but labour-intensive and does not scale. the lesson: unless you can build a replayable training target for a domain, models struggle to improve there. and many skills agi needs — running a business, litigating, trading stocks — cannot be replayed inside a data centre; verification takes months or years of real-world action and cannot be perturbed in parallel. dwarkesh patel can rlvr generalise? that is an open empirical question labs are betting rlvr generalises to every domain: train in enough containerised, reproducible environments and you get a general agent that can make plans, learn quickly and acquire new skills. drop an ai with unlimited rlvr into 1948 texas politics and it might understand better than lbj how to win a senate seat; give the 2002 version a hundred million dollars and it could build spacex. but this is an open empirical question. dario said on a podcast that short-context training does not necessarily generalise to long-context performance, hinting that rlvr generalisation is not infinitely strong. if it cannot generalise from short to long, how would it generalise from a mass of white-collar tasks to building something from scratch in the real world? dwarkesh patel learning has to be written back into the weights continual learning requires getting back to the weights. ai cannot learn merely through an ever-growing kv cache — that does not scale, and it is not how humans learn. human learning involves compression, which is what enables generalisation and insight. but once you go into the weights, you give up the sample efficiency of in-context learning, because gradient updates are extremely sample-inefficient. online learning models that have shipped successfully, such as cursor tab, need 400m+ requests a day predicting the same target. yet the point of continual learning is that the world is complex: every job, company and problem is different, and you need to learn deployment-specific information that cannot be stuffed into a shared training run. sample efficiency and continual learning are deeply linked problems: on the job there is little data, so you need sample efficiency, while the "fast weights" memory of in-context learning scales poorly and needs architectural innovation. dwarkesh patel dreaming is the speculative fourth axis of scaling "dreaming" is the more speculative approach: if ai can build simulators of reality to rehearse new skills and try alternative strategies, it can experience orders of magnitude more simulated samples in the same wall-clock time. efficientzero could beat a novice human in 2 hours because it played dozens of simulated games in its head. future llms might consume less real data while practising endlessly in environments they build themselves. but building a whole-world simulator is far harder

h: disney's moat isn't ip — it's walt's flywheel design disney's moat isn't the ip itself, but the flywheel walt built with engineering after marrying art and commerce in his head: high-quality animation, maximum distribution, injected auxiliary nodes, then decades of compounding. this episode breaks disney's century of business history into a replicable flywheel model, with direct lessons for content founders and platform strategists. the mid-section's animation production detail is a bit dense and can be fast-forwarded. content founders, platform strategists, ip operators, and anyone who wants to understand long-term compounding business models. acquired acquired the walt disney company ip operations flywheel effect animation industry long-termism vertical integration disney synchronized sound opens a new era walt combined cartoons with synchronized sound to create steamboat willie. this required inventing a new method to sync picture and music, and the process was hard. it premiered in new york on november 18, 1928, and the audience reacted enthusiastically; walt wept with emotion. but distributors were conservative, so walt bypassed them and worked directly with theaters. from then on, audiences knew that if they loved this film, they would remember the name walt disney. ben the ip flywheel first appears: clubs and merchandise the mickey mouse club was born by accident. in the summer of 1929, a fox dome theater manager proposed a partnership; disney licensed the club charter and merchandise, and it quickly expanded to 800 clubs with over 1 million members. in 1933 kay kamen became the exclusive merchandise agent; within 6 months merchandise sales reached $6 million, and two years later reached $70 million. by 1934 merchandise royalties already exceeded film rentals, and the flywheel began to turn. david the engineering miracle of animation production ben breaks down the disney animation process in detail: storyboards, temporary voice tracks, bar sheets syncing every frame and syllable, a layout department handling scenes and shots, animators drawing frame by frame at 12-14 per second, about 80,000 drawings for a feature. cel animation kept backgrounds unchanged; the inkers were almost all women; the paint lab offered thousands of colors. the multiplane camera stood 10-15 feet tall and produced a parallax effect. this was the three-way intersection of art, commerce and engineering. ben the 1941 strike and walt's hard line the strike lasted 3.5 months. walt gave a nearly 3-hour speech to the entire staff with a hard line: "the strong survive, the weak are eliminated" — which only drove more people to join the union. walt took a government-friendly trip to latin america and left the problem to roy. under federal mediation roy recognized the union, raised wages, and laid off over 500 people, cutting staff from 1,200 to under 700. the studio was badly weakened, and walt's relationship with the company changed completely. david the vault strategy: the compounding of re-releases in 1944, short on cash, disney re-released snow white, taking in $3 million on a cost of only a few hundred thousand. after that it re-released every 7 years, which became the core rhythm of disney's ip operation. walt said that over 8 years the potential audience had grown by 25 million children who either weren't born yet or were too young. roy said "our product is almost eternal" — this is the foundation of ip compounding. david 99.95% of value created after his death ben points out that of the company walt built from age 21 until his death in 1966, 99.95% of its value today was created after he died. in 1966 the market cap was under $90 million, pretax profit was $21 million, cash exceeded debt, and buffett bought in 1966. this highlights the power of disney's long-term compounding game, and shows that walt's flywheel design far outlived his own lifespan. ben park origins: a gamble that wasn't ip extension disneyland did not originate from the company deliberately seeking a new vehicle for its ip; at first there was almost no synergy. the budget ballooned from $5 million to $17 million, the company put in only $500,000, and outside financing was needed. abc invested $500,000 in equity and guaranteed a $4.5 million loan, plus paid $5 million a year in production fees for 7 years of broadcast rights — the largest television program contract at the time. the park ultimately cost $17 million. it was a huge gamble. ben & david davy crockett detonates merchandise revenue in 1955, 10 million davy crockett hats were sold, along with 7 million records, for total merchandise sales of about $300 million; disney received about $7.5 million, more than the cumulative profit of all its previous first-run animated films. this validated flywheel point 3: inject ip into as many auxiliary profit nodes as possible without damaging the core ip. david & ben self-built distribution achieves vertical integration in 1953 disney founded buena vista distributio

h: compression is intelligence: prediction and compression are two sides of the same coin information theory says prediction and compression are mathematically equivalent, so the pretraining objective of a language model can be re-understood as building the most efficient text compressor — not merely predicting the next token. this is part one of a trilogy and covers only the mathematical foundations of the compression limit, with no engineering details and no product judgments; information density is moderate. suited to people who want to build information-theory intuition, not to people who want industry judgments. engineers and researchers who want to build information-theory intuition, especially those who use cross-entropy loss every day but have never thought through why it looks the way it does. andrej karpathy andrej karpathy reinventing entropy | compression is intelligence part 1 information theory compression language models shannon pretraining the pretraining objective is really compression karpathy points out that large language model pretraining is usually described as ‘next token prediction’, using cross-entropy loss, and the term cross-entropy itself comes from information theory. one result of information theory is that prediction and compression are mathematically equivalent — two sides of the same coin. so you can restate the pretraining objective entirely as: not predicting the next token, but building the most efficient text compressor. the value of this restatement is that it makes clearer what cross-entropy actually is and why it is used. andrej karpathy the robot example: probability determines code length a warm-up with a robot far away on the moon: the commands are only up, down, left, right, but the distribution is uneven — half are up, a quarter down, an eighth left, an eighth right, and each command is independent. the naive student gives every command a fixed two bits, averaging 2 bits; the smart student uses a variable-length code: 0 for up, 10 for down, 110 for left, 111 for right, for a weighted average of 1.75 bits. the key constraint is that no codeword may be a prefix of another codeword — this is called a prefix-free code — so that the robot can decode unambiguously. andrej karpathy the output of perfect compression looks like random noise a third, ‘impractical’ student proposes: random noise is incompressible, so the bitstream produced by a perfect compression algorithm should be indistinguishable from random noise. if the compressed n-bit bitstream really looks like random noise, then all 2 to the n messages must be equally likely, each with probability 1/2^n. working backwards, a message that takes n bits under a perfect scheme means its probability is 2 to the minus n. take the log and negate it, and you get n = -log₂(p). this negative-log expression is the fundamental formula of information theory, and shannon's definition of ‘the information content of an event’. andrej karpathy information content is the lower bound on compression perfect compression is not always possible, because the probabilities of real messages are usually not integer powers of 2. the more general statement is: the information content of a message gives a lower bound on how short it can be compressed — at least when averaged over all possible messages. you can absolutely overfit a compression algorithm to one specific case. in the robot example the probabilities are too clean, all powers of 2, so the information content of each symbol is exactly an integer number of bits; but in natural language the probability of each letter depends heavily on context, and none of them are powers of 2, so the computed information content is all fractional. andrej karpathy shannon had his wife guess the next letter shannon started with n-gram statistics, but long strings simply do not appear in a corpus, so the statistics break down. so he switched models: his wife betty. shannon took a book and had betty guess the next letter one at a time; when she guessed wrong he wrote down the correct letter, and when she guessed right he drew a dash. the transcribed text has fewer letters but the same information content — because if he could replicate a betty, he would only need to give her this reduced text to restore the original. in a 1950 paper he changed to recording how many guesses were needed to get it right, and from that inferred the implicit probabilities the human brain assigns to real letters. when he analysed language he was not purely doing data analysis; he was probing an underlying language model, namely the brain of his subject. andrej karpathy entropy is the average information per symbol entropy asks for the average information content per symbol in a signal. because under perfect compression codeword length equals information content, entropy is essentially asking about the compression limit, giving a lower bound on how efficiently a signal can be compressed. for any probability distribution, entropy

h: adhd medication changes behavior, not learning barkley likens adhd to diabetes, yet 64% of people cycle back out of the diagnostic criteria; medication improves compliance but not learning, and the mta long-term follow-up confirms no academic advantage — what actually works is small-group differentiated instruction. high information density, aimed straight at the holes in the adhd medication evidence chain; suited to parents currently making medication decisions. but the host's selection of anti-medication evidence is obvious, so listen critically alongside the original. parents still weighing whether to medicate their child, teachers who want to get the classroom environment right, and clinicians concerned with the evidence on pediatric psychiatric medication. your parenting mojo your parenting mojo 266: if adhd medication doesn’t help kids learn, what does? adhd child education medication efficacy evidence-based teaching behavioral intervention mta his own data refute his own metaphor barkley has long likened adhd to diabetes and argued it requires lifelong treatment. but in his own follow-up study, 64% of children showed a markedly fluctuating course, cycling out of and back into the diagnostic criteria. the host points out: diabetes doesn't do that — a pancreas doesn't work normally for a few years and then fail, you don't cycle out of a diabetes diagnosis. if adhd really were a biological defect of the brain, this kind of "coming and going" shouldn't happen. yet barkley then still insists that over 90% have high symptoms for life. the two claims are in direct logical contradiction. jen lumanlan kids' self-reports differ from parents' by 10x in barkley's milwaukee study, at age 21 only 4% of participants reported enough symptoms in the diagnostic interview, while at the same time the proportion reported by parents was 46% — a 10-fold gap. barkley explains the difference as young people underestimating their own symptoms, and says their reports don't become reliable until around age 30. the host offers another reading: why couldn't it be that parents overestimate? the diagnostic process never really asked the child about their experience in the first place. so the 4% figure may be exactly the result of a diagnostic system that doesn't trust children. jen lumanlan diagnosis asks how much trouble the child causes parents in the textbook barkley edited, the questions in the child diagnostic interview include "what does your child do that bothers you" and "how severe is this for you," rated 1 to 9. the subject of the questions is the degree to which parents are affected by the child's behavior, not the child's own feelings. the same textbook also concedes that symptoms vary with context: high activity during recess is normal, and only becomes a problem back in the classroom. the host asks: if the child is simply unsuited to a motionless classroom environment, why is the disease located in the child rather than in the environment? jen lumanlan drugs let people show what they know, not learn new things barkley states plainly that the premise for using stimulants is that they "work," and that their function is to help an individual perform knowledge they already have, not to increase the amount of knowledge. the host seizes on this logic: if medication only lets what is already known be performed, short-term academic scores shouldn't rise in the first place; and if you expect the amount of knowledge to increase after long-term medication, barkley then complains that existing academic studies are too short to capture long-term gains. she also notes that pharmaceutical companies don't advertise long-term academic gains — which is itself a negative signal. jen lumanlan the same kids didn't learn one more word on medication the pelham study used a crossover design in which 173 children with adhd studied social studies, science, and vocabulary units under medication and under placebo. medication had a huge effect on classroom behavior: 37% more arithmetic problems completed per minute, 53% fewer rule violations per hour — they looked like model students. but knowledge tests showed they didn't learn more content on medication than on placebo, and memory didn't improve either. medication had only a small effect on immediate test scores within the window of drug efficacy, and it vanished once the drug wore off — a performance effect, not a learning effect. jen lumanlan what actually gets kids learning is small classes the host concedes barkley would say pelham's classroom isn't the real world, but also points out the key: in those small classes (1 to 11 per group, averaging 5 to 6), using evidence-based strategies like brainstorming, think-pair-share, modeling aloud, and having students summarize and predict, the children did learn. medication added no learning effect on top of good teaching. this becomes a resource question: put the funding into the classroom, or keep buying drugs? h: ferrari makes 14,000 cars a year and is worth more than ford: it sells exclusion, and inclusion too ferrari builds only about 14,000 cars a year, yet its market cap exceeds ford's. the secret is holding luxury-goods exclusivity and sports-team inclusivity at the same time — manufacturing myth through scarcity, sustaining loyalty through community. this episode runs 3 hours 59 minutes and is dense with information, though the middle history section drags a little. the core insight is in the final hour, on the brand paradox and the business model, and is worth a founder's close attention. founders, brand managers and investors — especially anyone trying to understand how scarcity drives ultra-high pricing power and a durable moat. acquired acquired ferrari ferrari luxury scarcity brand business model racing the ferrari paradox: 14,000 cars a year, a billion people who know the name ferrari sells only about 14,000 cars a year — the equivalent of toyota's output every 10 hours; porsche sells 22 times as many. only about 180,000 people worldwide own a ferrari, but more than a billion people recognise the brand, making it the company with the highest awareness-to-ownership ratio in history. that extreme scarcity underpins its ultra-premium positioning. ben enzo's engine philosophy: sell the engine, give the body away enzo ferrari was known as an engine man, and his lines include ‘i sell engines, the body comes free’ and ‘aerodynamics is for people who can't build engines.’ he resisted mid-engine technology early on, holding that the engine belonged in front — yet in the same period the factory was developing mid-engine models, a contradiction that captures his strategy: publicly conservative, privately innovative. ben luca returns and calls the 348 a bad car in 1991 gianni agnelli brought luca back as chairman of ferrari. luca first bought one of the then-flagship 348s to test, and found it had no personality, was technically behind, underpowered, and would even lose to a volkswagen golf off the line at a traffic light. he said flatly that ‘the 348 is a bad car, the worst car we have ever built.’ it reflected ferrari's decline under fiat management: overproduction, shared parts, and a lost connection to racing. david the geography of expansion: the production cap is per market, not absolute ben points out that ferrari's production ceiling is not absolute but specific to existing markets. as long as the perception of scarcity in existing markets is not disturbed, sales into new markets such as china are permitted. that explains why ferrari can launch product in different regions without diluting the brand. ben how much of the profit the hypercars carry ben works through it: ferrari's current hypercar, the f80, sells for an average of about $4 million, limited to 799 units, generating roughly $3.2 billion in retail sales. assuming a 10% dealer margin, ferrari books $2.9 billion in revenue, delivered over 2.5 years, contributing about $1.25 billion in the first year — 15% of annual revenue. but hypercar gross margins may run as high as 80-90%, so the first-year profit contribution could exceed 30%. ben inclusion plus exclusion is the cheat code ben argues that ferrari's essence is having the exclusivity of a luxury brand and the inclusivity of a sports team at the same time. he draws the analogy to acquired's own strategy: be extremely selective about companies and sponsors, but as inclusive as possible toward the community. he thinks ferrari got there first, and that it is a business cheat code. david agrees, and jokes that acquired needs to reposition itself. ben why no one else has managed to copy it the discussion turns to why there is no other ferrari. david argues the key is continuity: ferrari has kept its core myth and product promise intact since 1947, and is the only team in f1 to have operated continuously. ben adds that lamborghini lacks a racing heritage, aston martin has been badly run, and mclaren failed because of changes in ownership and leadership. david & ben a company is perfect when the number of partners in it is odd and less than 3. david i sell engines and the car i throw in for free. ben there is not a direct correlation between ferrari victories on the track and the number of cars that you can sell. but if for many years you do not win, it means that you do not add wood to the fire of the myth. the myth of ferrari is based on competition, on cars. david the ferrari 348 was a shit car. it was the worst car we ever made. everything was missing. it had no personality. david luca leaving is for me the same as mr. enzo dying. he has become ferrari. you see him, luca, you see ferrari, you don't see anything else. you don't see luca. bernie ecclestone ferrari is both inclusive and exclusive. it has the exclusivity of a luxury brand, but the inclusivity of a sports team. ben we don't sell a car, we sell a dream. ben ferrari annual production about 14,000 cars ferrari owners worldwide about 180,000
